News.title: Reckless thrillseekers ignore police warnings to plunge into sea from children’s charity roof
News.content:
Reckless thrillseekers ignore police warnings to plunge into sea from children’s charity roof

The Harriet Davis Seaside Holiday Trust in Tenby, Pembrokeshire, has warned someone could be seriously injured or killed as groups of young children climb onto its roof

View 4 Images Youngsters have been "tombstoning" from the charity's roof into the harbour below (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

Thrillseekers have been jumping into the sea from the roof of a charity building used by seriously ill and disabled children.

‌



Groups of youngsters have repeatedly climbed onto the Harriet Davis Seaside Holiday Trust building in Tenby, Pembrokeshire, before “tombstoning” into the water below. The charity says the problem has escalated dramatically in recent weeks, with as many as 24 people accessing the roof around high tide and causing damage as they climb up and down the building.

‌



Footage of the dangerous jumps has also been shared on social media with the caption: “Got to keep the Tenby tradition going!”

‌



The trust, which provides specialist holiday accommodation for families caring for children with disabilities, complex medical needs and life-limiting conditions, fears somebody could be seriously injured or killed.

Tourist pulls off extraordinary escape after plunging 180ft down cliff face READ MORE :

View 4 Images The problem has worsened in recent weeks, the charity said (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

'Extremely serious danger to life'

Senior Administrator, Carol Lincoln, said: “The activity presents an extremely serious danger to life - both to the young people jumping from the roof, and to fishing and other boats which may unfortunately be in the water below them.”

‌



She added: “The situation has now escalated significantly. This last month, as many as 24 young people on every high tide have been on our roof, jumping from the adjacent property into the sea and, in the process, causing continued and deliberate damage to the fabric of the building.

“We are now also experiencing youths hammering on our doors and windows as they climb onto and descend from the roof. This is understandably terrifying for the vulnerable families staying inside the property.”

The charity has repeatedly tried to make the building harder to access, including using anti-climb paint and fitting plastic spikes across the roof and three access points and thousands of pounds has also reportedly been spent repairing damage.

‌



View 4 Images Police did not attend on every occasion families called (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

Acts of criminal damage

The charity said families staying at the property had contacted police about the youngsters but were told on some occasions that officers would not attend. When officers did visit, she said the charity was advised to remove bins which had been used to help people climb onto the roof. But this did not deter the children from acessing the roof.

‌



Carol said: “Instead, the youths simply stole fuel bins from the harbour and used those instead. We have followed the advice given to us and have taken every reasonable step within our means to prevent access to the roof.

“This has included installing anti-climb paint and rows of plastic anti-climb spikes across the whole roof and three access points. We have also spent thousands of pounds repairing damage to the roof. Despite this, the problem has continued and is now escalating.

“The young people are deliberately smearing the anti-climb paint over our external walls and are progressively ripping the plastic spikes from the roof. This is causing serious and continuing damage to the fabric of the building.”

‌



The Trust says its biggest concern is the impact on families who use the accommodation for what can be a rare opportunity to enjoy a holiday together. She added: “Our visitors are not tourists coming to the town for entertainment. Most of our visiting families come from Wales, and some are local families.

View 4 Images The charity's building is near the harbour in Tenby (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

‌



'Charity is being let down'

“They are parents and carers looking after children and young people who may have profound disabilities, complex medical needs or life-limiting conditions. Many families are only able to have a holiday because our properties provide the specialist equipment and facilities they require.

“For many of them, this is an extremely precious opportunity to spend time together and create positive family memories in circumstances where ordinary holidays are simply not possible. Instead, they are increasingly finding themselves frightened and distressed by young people climbing onto the roof, banging on doors and windows and shouting as they gain access to and descend from the building.

“This is completely unacceptable.”

‌



The charity has now called for stronger action from police, parents and council officials before the behaviour ends in tragedy. She said: "What was once an occasional problem has now developed into a significant and increasingly popular activity, with ever larger groups accessing our roof.

“The greater the number of people jumping or even simply accessing our roof, the greater the possibility of a fatality. This risk is now very real. We therefore feel that this situation has moved far beyond an issue of occasional antisocial behaviour.

“It is now a serious and escalating public safety issue involving criminal damage, deliberate trespass, risk to life and the welfare of vulnerable families staying within our properties. We cannot wait until somebody is seriously injured or killed before this is treated with the urgency it deserves.”

Article continues below

County Councillor Michael Williams has backed the Trust and written to police calling for action saying their is a genuine fear that there could be a fatality. He said: “In my opinion at the very least criminal damage is being caused by these youths and they are they are trespassing with intent, and I would ask that you consider taking action on these specific activities.

“This amazing charitable organisation provides a unique opportunity for families who often have to contend with some of the most distressing circumstances conceivable and they deserve the support of everyone concerned.

“The Trust and their guests are being let down by the inability or unwillingness of organisations they should be able to rely on to effectively address these activities.”

News.title: Donald Trump's wild week as BBC lawsuit descends into farce and he faces ridicule over 'close aid'
News.content:
Donald Trump's wild week as BBC lawsuit descends into farce and he faces ridicule over 'close aid'

As well as trying to avoid talking about Natalie Harp, Trump has been threatening to bomb the bond markets, blaming Canada, begging the Supremes not to keep him hangin' on and cosying up to Little Rocket Man

View 2 Images Trump has been desperately trying to avoid talking about his Natalie (Image: Getty Images)

Donald Trump spent much of this week trying to avoid talking about Natalie Harp, the 'extremely close' executive assistant whose role in the White House sits somewhere between 'Oval Office gatekeeper' and 'weird security blanket'.

‌



Before we get to the rest of the week's bizarre moments, it's worth addressing why the Natalie Harp story is one that needs to be told. Some would say it's unfair to focus on a member of staff - even one employed by the most powerful and consequential man in the world.

‌



At their most innocuous, Natalie Harp's oddly close relationship with Donald Trump is the story of a young woman, perhaps a vulnerable one, whose enthusiasm and support for a political hero has turned into desperate obsession.

‌



But at worst, it illustrates the kind of messianic devotion with which Trump has surrounded himself in his second Presidency.

Not all of Trump's team are so enthusiastic in their outpourings of love for their President. But Natalie Harp is not the only one who thinks he's an unquestionable gift from god.

Meanwhile, Trump has been threatening to bomb the bond markets, blaming Canada, telling the Supremes not to keep him hangin' on and cosying up to Little Rocket Man.

‌



Here's everything you need to know.

Trump threatens to launch military strikes on the bond market

Donald Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week said he was going to double the Government's purchases of long-term US bonds in a bid to prevent a panic in the bond markets - wobbles in which have sent government borrowing costs skyrocketing.

But that's not what we're looking at today. We're looking at this truly bizarre moment where Trump, asked about the intervention, appeared to have some kind of brain episode and threatened to bomb the bond market.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

They're not even a real country, anyway

Donald Trump has come up with a wizard new scheme for making life more expensive for regular Americans, just in time for the midterms. Blame Canada.

Well, strictly speaking, each side blamed the other for trade talks breaking down on Friday night - but the upshot is both sides have slapped 50% tariffs on the other's goods.

‌



President Donald Trump’s import taxes will hit about 5% of what Canada ships to the United States every year, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Prime Minister Carney said Ottawa would respond with targeted tariff protection for industries exposed to the new US duties, including some steel products. He also mentioned the dairy, appliance, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics sectors.

No further talks were planned. Whatever the eventual outcome, a loss of trust seems one of the earliest casualties.

Carney accused Washington of using “economic integration as a weapon” and said “its signature was written in pencil.” Resorting to the language of battle, he said his country had been “attacked” by the new American tariffs. “You’re at war when you get attacked,” he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond.

‌



Where's the beef?

American ranchers used to be among Trump's fiercest defenders. And why not? He promised them a utopian future during the campaign.

But he has, understandably, gone down in their estimation since it turned out he was perfectly willing to screw them in time for the midterms.

In his second intervention in the beef industry this year, Trump announced he'd struck a deal to allow 300,000 metric tonnes of beef mince to be imported to the States, tariff free, over the next three months.

‌



The importers, Trump said, had agreed to sell it at 25% off market rate - in a move he said would help to "rebuild the herd" of American cattle - which is at its lowest rate for decades due to drought and high working costs for farmers.

But it has the added advantage of making food a bit cheaper until shortly after America next goes to the polls.

Colin Woodall, of the National Cattlemen's Beef Association, told the New York Times that "flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd".

‌



And let's not forget this is the second time Trump has screwed farmers this year - after promising to import 80,000 metric tonnes of beef from Argentina in a bid to shore-up Agrie President Javier Milei's struggling government.

Trump heckled by man in 'kill paedophiles' shirt

Trump gave another one of his pre-midterms rallies in South Carolina last night. The rally was in support of Darline Graham, who is running to replace her late brother Lindsey in the Senate seat - and is rapidly proving to be a liability.

But the most embarrassing thing that happened at the SC rally was the guy who stood up during Trump's speech and shouted something indecipherable, while wearing a tee shirt that read: "Kill your local paedophile."

‌



If what he was shouting was anything like as coherent as what was written on his shirt, Trump probably needn't be worried.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

She's running...

Photos revealed by the Mirror on Friday show Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp sprinting after his cart at his Scottish golf course - confirming just one of the many bizarre tales about the President's "Human Printer."

‌



It came after bizarre letters she sent him confessing her devotion to him were published.

Questions continue to be asked about the 35-year-old executive assistant's unusually close relationship with the US President. Harp is nicknamed the "human printer" because she frequently prints out and hands the President printouts of flattering news stories and cherry-picked poll numbers - acting as a "filter" for information reaching him.

View 2 Images She's running...after his golf cart

‌



You can - and should - read more about the frightening letters she is said to have written to the President here.

But many of the tales about Harp's behaviour are the stuff of legend, and reported, usually credited to anonymous sources, in books and longreads. Like the time she is said to have ridden in the boot of an SUV in order to stay close to Trump.

So it was a pleasure to be able to confirm one of the legends - that she sprinted around Trump's Turnberry golf course on foot in 2023 - as entirely true.

‌



Pictures published by the Mirror show this incident for the first time. Harp is shown running full-tilt uphill after Trump's cart on the first day of his trip to Turnberry on 2 May 2023.

Worried that she had upset Trump, Harp explained in a letter during or shortly after the trip: "The first day I was told there were no carts, and people walked, which is why I walked.

"The second day, I was specifically asked by, I forget who his name was, but one of the main people who worked there, if I could continue walking, and tell any other girls who would head out there to do the same to spare the Course any more Carts.

‌



"If there is anything else I have done to cause you trouble, please forgive me."

And it didn't end there...

Donald Trump on second golf holiday with Natalie Harp

We also revealed today that Trump left his wife at home for another golf holiday in Scotland last year - on which he was accompanied by Hart.

‌



Harp accompanied Trump to Turnberry last July for a second visit - where she followed him on the golf course and sat in on at least one meeting with a world leader.

You can read about that one here...

More shenanigans in Trump's BBC lawsuit

Donald Trump's lawyers have badly miscalculated the President's increasingly preposterous lawsuit against the BBC in many ways. There was the original lawsuit, which would have forced Trump to hand over his financial records - we talked about that in our weekly Youtube roundup here.

‌



There was the bit where they managed to get it written down in evidence that a maximum of 285 people watched the offending Panorama programme in the United States...we talked about that in this episode - and I strongly recommend you give that one a watch if you haven't, because it's super funny.

Anyway... perhaps Trump's biggest blunder was assuming the BBC was just like any other media company - and that they would fold under the threat of a 10 billion dollar lawsuit and settle out of court.

See, Trump sues a lot of people - but his lawsuits seldom end up in a courtroom. Particularly when it comes to media companies, it increasingly seems that a settlement is what he's actually after. It happened with ABC News - who agreed to pay fifteen million dollars after a presenter wrongly stated that Trump had been found liable for rape, when the jury found he'd technically been found liable for sexual assault - a distinction the judge put down to a quirk of New York law.

‌



Later, Paramount settled for sixteen million dollars over an entirely spurious lawsuit relating to the editing of an interview with Kamala Harris on an episode of 60 Minutes. The interview was entirely fine, but Trump decided had been edited to present Harris in a flattering light, and Paramount had a merger they wanted to get through the regulators.

So one can imagine Trump's team saw the Telegraph having a meltdown about the editing of the Panorama programme - which again, was broadly fine - and thought..."easy money."

But from the beginning the Beeb has said they would fight this lawsuit to the end. And their lawyers' assertive approach to the case certainly does not give the impression they're in any mood to tell Trump "oh I suppose you're right, here's a few million quid to go away."

‌



There's just very little incentive for them to do so. They don't have a parent company that needs to do business in America. And while they are technically allowed to settle out of court, the BBC is rarely sued, and has a real appetite for defending claims it thinks are weak - not least because any payment would be taken out of licence fee cash. And suddenly the British taxpayer is effectively paying money to the leader of a foreign country over a spurious lawsuit - and it becomes a diplomatic issue.

Meanwhile, Trump has been getting increasingly upset about the BBC doing entirely normal things to fight its case.

See, they've issued summonses to Donald Trump Jr, Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner to give evidence in the case.

‌



The BBC says all three have personal knowledge of Trump's state of mind on January 6th.

But they've been somewhat reluctant to allow themselves to be served with papers - something that usually has to be done in person in the states. And their secret service protection have declined to facilitate the process.

So the beeb have gone back to the judge to ask for help in making arrangements to get these witnesses to give evidence.

‌



And that's why, on Monday, a spokesperson for Trump's legal team issued a wild statement accusing the BBC of "seeking to harass him, his family, and supporters".

The beeb has now asked the court to allow service of papers to be done by email and certified mail.

What makes this interesting is that in pursuing what he thought would be an easy case of extracting cash from a broadcaster, Trump may have succeeded in prompting a full-scale relitigation of what happened on January 6th - an piece of history he's spent a lot of his second presidency trying to rewrite. This could turn out to be a genuinely massive story when it lands in court next year.

‌



Kim Jong Un

And if all that wasn't enough, Trump is cosying up to North Korean megadictator Kim Jong Un again.

The pair have been talking again. Trump posted a picture of him and Kim taken during his first term - back when a President alienating America's natural allies while cosying up to its enemies was a novel event.

Then on Sunday night he had a direct pop at South Korea, announcing he would be scaling back American involvement in a series of military drills alongside Seoul, and branding the plans "inappropriate and hostile". Trump later explained that his was partly out of revenge for South Korea refusing to help with the war on Iran. Which is not an unreasonable position for South Korea to take, given they get 60% of their oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

‌



And when he was asked about the gruesome twosome rekindling their situationship, Trump casually let slip that North Korea has "57 nukes". Which is something you don't really want to say out loud, especially in front of - as he was - the White House Press Corps and a load of contractors working on his new helipad.

Supremes won't stop Trump's ballroom. Not even in the name of love

Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts is allowing the White House to continue construction on President Donald Trump’s $400 million ballroom project for now. Roberts signed a temporary order on Friday allowing work to continue while the court considers an emergency appeal from the Trump administration. Lower courts had ordered a halt to the project, finding that it must have congressional approval.

Honestly, at this point the structure is like 60% built. Even if building it was illegal, what are they going to do? Order Trump to rebuild the East Wing brick by brick?

Article continues below

Actually, yes, that would be the funniest option.

News.title: Cargo ship with 24 crew members sinks in Bay of Bengal as rescue operation launched
News.content:
Cargo ship with 24 crew members sinks in Bay of Bengal as rescue operation launched

A Panama-flagged cargo ship carrying 24 crew members sank in the Bay of Bengal on Saturday, officials said

View Image File image of the Panama-registered cargo vessel MV Matthew (Image: Mick O'Neill)

A Panama-flagged cargo ship carrying 24 crew members has sunk in the Bay of Bengal, officials say.

‌



The MV Ocean Winner was carrying iron ore from Paradip, a major port in the eastern Indian state of Odisha, to Singapore when it sank about 240 nautical miles off the Odisha coast on Saturday, officials said.

‌



The Indian Coast Guard and Indian Navy have launched a rescue operation. Coast Guard ships Varad and Anmol, as well as a third vessel, Vijit, from Sri Vijaya Puram, have been deployed to support the operation.

‌



Twenty of the 24 crew members are Chinese nationals, while three are from Myanmar and one is Bangladeshi, officials said.

A senior Indian Police Service officer told national news agency PTI: "So far, two persons have been rescued from the waters." Another vessel in the vicinity has also joined the rescue operation, he said.

Article continues below

The bulk carrier set off from Paradip Port at 6.43pm BST (10.43pm UTC) on Thursday, according to Marine Traffic.

News.title: Meghan Markle's role in Netflix series The Gentleman 'is not happening due to public backlash'
News.content:
Meghan Markle's role in Netflix series The Gentleman 'is not happening due to public backlash'

It was understood Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex, was to return to acting in Guy Ritchie’s Netflix drama The Gentlemen, which is about a British duke who unexpectedly inherits his father’s country estate

View 4 Images Meghan Markle had been linked with a new Netflix role (Image: Getty Images)

The Duchess of Sussex’s proposed role in The Gentleman is off just 24 hours after it emerged, reports claimed tonight.

‌



Royal author Tina Brown today said she has been told the decision was made due to what she described as a public backlash against Meghan Markle following reports she was in talks to appear in the Netflix show.

‌



Ms Brown, who previously wrote an unauthorised biography about the former Suits actress, wrote on X: "I have heard that Meghan Markle’s role in Guy Ritchie’s Netflix series The Gentlemen is OFF. Public backlash was too fierce. This does not bode well for Meghan’s acting comeback in the UK."

‌



View 4 Images Tina Brown previously edited Vanity Fair and The New Yorker before writing books about the royals (Image: Getty Images for SXSW London)

Meghan was said to be in talks to appear as what was described as a temptress character in the third series of the comedy drama, which is about an aristocratic family who turn to crime and also features Ray Winstone as a drug lord. The speculation followed the bombshell announcement that Meghan and husband Prince Harry, 41, are returning to live in the UK with their children Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five.

‌



They have already reportedly found a family home and schools for their children in the UK and Harry is said to be keen for his dad, King Charles, on Saturday pictured driving on the A93 near Braemar, to develop a relationship with his grandchildren.

It had been reported Meghan was excited by the prospect of the proposed Netflix role, which would be written specifically for her. She allegedly entered talks for The Gentlemen after meeting film director Ritchie – Madonna’s ex-husband – through mutual acquaintances.

Meghan, who appeared on MasterChef Australia last month, made her name as Rachel Zane in popular US legal drama Suits before leaving in 2017 after she began dating Harry. She has also appeared in other shows, such as CSI:Miami and last year filmed a cameo as herself for comedy film Close Personal Friends with Lily Collins and Brie Larson.

‌



View 4 Images Harry and Meghan are preparing to return to the UK with their children Archie and Lilibet (Image: @meghan/Instagram)

The claim will come as a blow to The Sussexes, who made their autobiographical documentary Harry & Meghan with Netflix in 2024. The streaming giant also aired their documentary Polo. It is understood Meghan, who is said to have toured schools in the Cotswolds during a recent visit to the UK, will continue to run her lifestyle brand As Ever from the UK and hopes to expand it globally.

Ms Brown, who previously edited Vanity Fair and The New Yorker, before writing books about the royals, including The Diana Chronicles in 2007. She was married to legendary Fleet Street journalist Harold Evans, who was voted the greatest editor of all time before he died aged 92, in September 2020.

‌



Writing in The Times on Saturday, before her claim that Meghan's role was off, Ms Brown had commented about the couple's move, including Meghan's apparent new job.

She wrote: "It was always the best option for Meghan to return to acting, something she was genuinely good at until she threw it in to marry Harry. In 2023, when replays of her old hit cable show Suits were inexplicably all the rage on Netflix, it would have been a legitimate pop culture sensation and a major payday if she had let her agents pitch her for a reboot.

View 4 Images Guy Ritchie and Vinnie Jones behind the scenes on The Gentleman

Article continues below

"But no. Duchesses don’t do ensembles. Meghan believed she could pull off some kind of manic multihyphenate mishmash of entertainment enterprises in between accompanying her husband on ersatz royal tours to promote random global uplift." Ms Brown added: "As Martha Stewart noted: “If you’re an actress, it’s hard to then transition to a princess and then from a princess into a homemaking guru on a television show. It doesn’t sort of follow.”

News.title: Young children shown hunted deer corpse in disturbing drone footage
News.content:
Young children shown hunted deer corpse in disturbing drone footage

WARNING: GRAPHIC CONTENT. EXCLUSIVE: The Mirror has seen drone footage from a deer hunt in Somerset earlier this year, which was being monitored by animal rights group the League Against Cruel Sports

Andy Burnham urged to crack down on 'barbaric' deer hunts

Campaigners have renewed calls for a crackdown on hunting after drone footage showed ­children – including a baby – being encouraged to look at a stag’s bloody corpse.

‌



The clip shows a group examining the body of a young stag in the back of a vehicle after a hunt in Somerset earlier this year. The League Against Cruel Sports and North Dorset Hunt Saboteurs monitored the hunt.

‌



The League is now calling on Andy Burnham to strengthen laws on hunting – League chief executive Emma Slawinski explained: “It’s shocking to see adults trying to normalise this cruel and sickening activity with kids, showing them the victims of a hunt.

‌



View Image Andy Burnham has been urged to crack down on deer hunts (Image: Getty Images)

“This harrowing footage shows why we are calling on the Prime Minister to strengthen hunting laws to prevent this barbaric blood sport from still taking place. We are calling for the removal of the exemptions in the Hunting Act.

“[They] are being exploited by the deer hunts to chase stags and hinds for many miles before shooting them.

‌



“The ‘research and observation’ and ‘rescue of a wild mammal’ exemptions are enabling deer hunts in Somerset and Devon to kill wildlife and get away with barbaric behaviour.”

There is no suggestion the hunters in the video acted illegally. Deer hunting is legal within seasonal rules, i.e mature stags may be hunted from early August to October’s end, young stags in March and April and hinds November to early March.

A Countryside Alliance spokesman said: “The Devon and Somerset staghounds are integral to the management of the deer on Exmoor. Hundreds of thousands of deer are culled in the UK every year and go into the food chain to provide healthy wild meat.”

Article continues below

Defra said: “Causing unnecessary suffering to an animal is an offence, and we are committed to upholding the UK’s high standards of animal welfare.”

But it added that sustainable shooting had an important role in rural communities, and that it would work with them to preserve the countryside, wildlife and rural ways of life.

Earlier this year, the government ran a consultation on banning trail hunting, amid fears it was used as a cover to genuinely chase and kill foxes. Defra is still analysing the responses.

News.title: A66 Middlesbrough crash: Andy Burnham leads tributes to police officers killed on active duty
News.content:
A66 Middlesbrough crash: Andy Burnham leads tributes to police officers killed on active duty

Andy Burnham has paid tribute after seven people - including serving police officers PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough - were killed when a wrong-way car collided with a marked police vehicle

Cleveland Police issue statement following tragic A66 crash

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has led tributes after seven people - including two serving police officers - were killed in a horror crash.

‌



The officers were on active duty when their marked police vehicle collided with a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way along the A66 in the early hours of Saturday morning. The officers have since been named as PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough.

‌



The Prime Minister said: “Devastated to hear that two police officers have lost their lives while on duty in Cleveland this morning, as well as five members of the public.

‌



“My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of everyone involved, and with everyone at Cleveland Police. Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances.

“I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time.”

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood also paid tribute, she said: “A devastating incident in Teesside this morning in which seven people have died, including two police officers. Cleveland police have my support as they work to identify all those involved. Police officers put their own safety on the line to protect their communities every single day. The two officers were on active duty, serving the people of Cleveland.

‌



“My thoughts are with all those affected, their families, friends, the emergency services who attended the scene and the wider police family.”

View 3 Images A large police presence remains at the scene (Image: Iain Buist/Newcastle Chronicle)

The tragedy unfolded in South Bank, near Middlesbrough, at around 3.39am. Five members of the public travelling in the Passat were also killed and everyone in both vehicles was pronounced dead at the scene.

‌



A major emergency response was launched following the collision, with the North East Ambulance Service sending 14 resources to the scene, including ambulance crews, a specialist paramedic and its Hazardous Area Response Team.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the crash. The watchdog said it understands Cleveland Police had sighted a suspicious vehicle and a pursuit began before the Passat travelled onto the A66 and collided with the police car.

The pursuit had been abandoned before the crash and the police vehicle involved in the collision was not part of the pursuit and was just travelling in the area, according to the BBC

‌



View 3 Images The road has remained closed

Work is reportedly still ongoing to formally identify everyone who was inside the Passat. Families of those who have been identified have been informed and are receiving specialist support.

The ambulance service said: “Sadly despite the best efforts of everyone attending, a number of patients died at the scene. We send condolences to all of those affected by such a tragic event and thank everyone for all they did to help.”

‌



View 3 Images Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller spoke to reporters (Image: Iain Buist/Newcastle Chronicle)

The deaths of the two officers have left colleagues at Cleveland Police devastated. Lauren Somerville, Chair of Cleveland Police Federation, said: “Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland Police Family are feeling today. Our colleagues who should have been going home to their loved ones at the end of their shifts are not. And that is just unfathomable.

“Cleveland Police Federation will be offering full support to our fallen colleagues families and they have all of our love and care at this time. When the time is right we will pay full tribute to our brave colleagues. But we can assure that their sacrifice will never be forgotten.”

‌



Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said: “First and foremost, our thoughts are with the families of everyone involved in today’s incident. No one should leave their home and not return safely, including police officers serving their communities and protecting the people of Cleveland.

“This tragic incident will be felt across Cleveland, within our communities and throughout the entire policing family. We are providing specialist support to all families involved at this extremely difficult time.

“The investigation has been referred to the IOPC, which is the standard approach when a death occurs following police contact. We will cooperate fully with their investigation. While this investigation takes place, we strongly urge people to avoid speculation.”

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said there were few words that could bring comfort to the families, friends and colleagues of the seven people who died. He added: “Our thoughts are with everyone affected and with those who are continuing to come to terms with this unimaginable loss, including colleagues at Cleveland Police, who will feel the profound loss of two of their serving officers.

“On behalf of everyone at the Office of the Police and Crime Commissioner and the people of Cleveland, I extend our deepest condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of all seven people who lost their lives.

Article continues below

“I also give my sincere thanks to the staff from all our emergency services who responded to, and are continuing to manage, this devastating incident.”

News.title: A66 crash: Two police officers killed in wrong-way crash named
News.content:
A66 crash: Two police officers killed in wrong-way crash named

The two police officers killed in a crash involving a Volkswagen Passat and a police vehicle on the A66 in South Bank have been named as PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough

Cleveland Police issue statement following tragic A66 crash

Two police officers who were killed in a crash on the A66 in South Bank in the early hours of Saturday have been named.

‌



PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were among seven people who died in a crash involving a Volkswagen Passat and a police vehicle near Middlesbrough in Teesside shortly after 3.30am on Saturday.

‌



Five members of the public, who were occupants of the Volkswagen, were also killed. The identities of the five members of the public have not yet been released.

‌



Cleveland Police said the Volkswagen was travelling in the wrong direction along the A66 when it collided with the police vehicle, which was travelling in the opposite direction. The force confirmed that all occupants of both vehicles were pronounced dead at the scene.

Chief Constable Victoria Fuller named the two police officers who died and said their loss is being felt "across communities, by our police family and by our partner agencies".

View 3 Images Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were killed in a crash on the A66 (Image: Owen Humphreys/PA Wire)

‌



"These were brave officers protecting our communities and serving our residents who didn't return home to their families at the end of their shift," she told reporters on Saturday afternoon.

Chief Constable Fuller said she and the deputy chief constable visited the families of both officers to "offer our condolences and support".

She added that the five other people killed have also been formally identified. Specialist family liaison officers are being deployed to support the bereaved families, she said.

‌



The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has opened an investigation into the circumstances leading to the crash in South Bank after a mandatory referral from the force.

Officers from Cleveland Police "sighted a suspicious vehicle and a pursuit began" before the car travelled onto the A66 and collided with the police car, the watchdog said.

View 3 Images Police officers at the scene of a fatal crash involving a police car and a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough (Image: PA Wire/PA Images)

‌



North East Ambulance Service (NEAS) said crews were called to the collision at 3.39am and sent 14 ambulance resources, including ambulance crews, a specialist paramedic, its Hazardous Area Response Team and a doctor from Great North Air Ambulance Service.

A NEAS spokesperson said: "Sadly despite the best efforts of everyone attending, a number of patients died at the scene. We send condolences to all of those affected by such a tragic event and thank everyone for all they did to help."

The A66 is closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane in Eston. Police officers are stationed at both ends of the cordon, and the crash site cannot be seen from the road closures.

‌



A large white tent has been erected over the scene, with multiple emergency service vehicles at the site. Police have implemented a drone exclusion zone around the scene of the collision.

View 3 Images The A66 is closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane in Eston (Image: Ian Buist/Teesside Live)

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "devastated" to hear seven people had been killed in the collision.

‌



"My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of everyone involved, and with everyone at Cleveland Police." he said on X. "Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances. I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time."

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the crash was "devastating", adding that her thoughts were with all those affected.

Cleveland Police Federation chairwoman Lauren Somerville said: "Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland Police family are feeling today.

Article continues below

"Our colleagues who should have been going home to their loved ones at the end of their shifts are not. And that is just unfathomable.

"Cleveland Police Federation will be offering full support to our fallen colleagues’ families and they have all of our love and care at this time.

"When the time is right we will pay full tribute to our brave colleagues. But we can assure that their sacrifice will never be forgotten."

News.title: DVSA shares good news as it reminds learners of changes to practical test
News.content:
DVSA shares good news as it reminds learners of changes to practical test

This will give you motivation to keep going if you are a learner driver

View 3 Images In July 2026 the driving test pass rate increased to 52.1% (Image: Getty)

The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) has shared some good news, calling the pass rate a " testament" to learners.

‌



The agency, which carries out driving tests in Great Britain, said the pass rate rose to 52.1% in July 2026. It hailed the good news as a sign of learners' and instructors’ hard work and urged candidates to use its “Ready to Pass?” checklist to ensure they’re properly prepared for the test's high standards.

‌



A DVSA spokesperson told The Mirror: "In July 2026, the driving test pass rate increased to 52.1%. This is testament to the hard work of learner drivers, their instructors and our 'Ready to Pass?' campaign in ensuring that learners are ready to meet the high standards the driving test demands.

‌



"Improving the pass rate is vital to ensuring that as many test slots as possible are available to people booking for the first time, and that learner drivers are spared an often lengthy wait to retake their test.

"We're determined to reduce waiting times further, building on the over 300,000 additional tests delivered since June 2025 – supported by driving examiner numbers at their highest level in recent years."

Changes to driving test booking rules

View 3 Images Learner drivers are continuing to face lengthy waits for practical tests, but the DVSA says it's taking action to cut delays (Image: Getty)

‌



Following measures announced in November 2025 and a public consultation on changes to the driving test booking system, the DVSA brought in changes to how tests are booked. These changes were made to make the process fairer and crack down on firms reselling slots at inflated prices.

The three changes to how learner drivers can book and manage their car practical driving test appointments are:

A maximum of two changes can be made to a booking - introduced on March 31

Only learners are allowed to book a practical car driving test and make changes to their own booking - introduced on May 12

Learners can move their booked test only to a nearby centre - introduced on June 9

‌



The DVSA warns: "It’s against the law to book a driving test for someone else." It adds: "You’re not allowed to change, swap or cancel a driving test for someone else."

The new rules only apply to car driving tests. They do not apply to other types of tests.

More details on the changes can be found here.

‌



What is the DVSA's Ready to Pass?

The official DVSA Ready to Pass campaign notes that 48 out of every 100 driving tests were failed in Great Britain during July 2026. With this in mind, it's important to c heck you’re ready to pass before test day.

The DVSA shares advice on the skills learners need, handling test-day nerves, doing mock tests and avoiding driving-test scams.

The motoring experts believe that a learner will usually be ready to take their practical driving test when:

‌



You do not need prompts from your driving instructor.

You do not make serious or dangerous mistakes when you’re driving.

You can pass mock driving tests.

You have practised ways of managing your nerves.

Your driving instructor agrees you are ready.

Move your driving test

View 3 Images DVSA email update to learners sent on February 3, 2026 (Image: Sophie Buchan)

If you don’t feel ready, consider postponing your driving test. You’ll improve your chances of passing by giving yourself extra time to sharpen your skills, fit in a few more mock tests and work on managing nerves.

Article continues below

The DVSA reminds learners that changing your appointment is free as long as you do it at least 10 full working days beforehand (Monday to Saturday). Delaying also frees up a slot for someone who is ready to take their test.

News.title: Two police officers among seven killed in wrong-way car crash
News.content:
Two police officers were among seven people killed when a car travelling the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into a force vehicle.

A Volkswagen Passat with five occupants said to be in their late teens struck an oncoming marked Cleveland Police vehicle on the A66 near Middlesbrough at about 03:39 BST.

The BBC understands a pursuit of the car had ended before the crash, with the police vehicle just happening to be in the South Bank area. The occupants of both cars were pronounced dead at the scene.

The officers have been named as PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38. Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said they were "brave officers protecting our communities".

She said it was an "incredibly sad day for Cleveland", adding: "No one should leave their home and not return safely.

"These were brave officers protecting our communities and serving our residents, who didn't return home to their families at the end of their shift."

News.title: Video appears to show police chase minutes before fatal A66 crash
News.content:
Security camera footage appears to show several police vehicles chasing a car just minutes before a fatal crash that killed seven people, including two police officers, near Middlesbrough.

The clip is thought to have been filmed on Lime Road at 03:36 BST on Saturday morning, around three minutes before a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way on the A66 nearby collided into a marked police vehicle.

The BBC understands the police car involved in the crash was not part of the pursuit and that the chase had stopped before the collision.

Following a mandatory referral from Cleveland Police, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has opened an investigation into the circumstances of the crash.

News.title: How this 1960s ex-council house is managing to stay cool without air con
News.content:
After five heatwaves and plenty of advice on how to stay safe in what is set to become the UK's hottest summer on record, many people continue to find it a challenge to stay cool - particularly in their homes.

This is perhaps no surprise. More than half of homes, external in the UK are already at risk of overheating and at current rates of climate change this will rise to 92% by 2050 if we do not adapt.

But in south London, on a 35C day, one 1960s ex-council house with no air-conditioning is managing to beat the heat.

Marion Baeli's home is one of many across the UK being adapted for warmer - maybe even 40C - British summers.

News.title: Watch: Moment humanoid robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m record
News.content:
A robot has outperformed humans by running faster than Usain Bolt's 100m sprint world record at the World Humanoid Robot Games in China.

The humanoid robot, developed by the Beijing Innovation Centre of Humanoid Robotics, ran the distance in 9.39 seconds at the event.

Eight-time Olympic gold medallist Bolt set the world record for humans in 2009, running 100m in 9.58 seconds.

The robot beat two others including one made by Chinese smartphone maker Honor - which the manufacturer says ran the distance in 9.32 seconds in a test run.

Other events at the robot games, which started on Saturday, include boxing and football, but also household tasks such as folding laundry.

The BBC's China correspondent Laura Bicker reports from Beijing.

News.title: More students planning to live at home for university over 'insane' living costs
News.content:
More new students are choosing to live at home for university this year than in the last nine years, new data shows.

Over 81,000 UK 18-year-olds said in their accepted university application that they intended to live at home this year, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) - just over one in three students in that category.

In 2017, it was closer to one in five.

The figures vary across the UK - with 48% of applicants in Scotland intending to live at home, compared with 20% in Wales - but the trend is rising across the board.

Students told the BBC the rising cost of living was a major influence in deciding what to do after school or college.

For friends Beatrice and Amelia, who are from St Helens, Merseyside, the cost of accommodation was a big factor in their decision to live at home while studying.

Both are heading to university in September, but neither will be moving into student accommodation.

News.title: As they return to the UK, Harry and Meghan search for a brand that sticks
News.content:
In late July, the Duchess of Sussex's lifestyle range, called As ever, launched a "rich, vibrant" blackberry spread alongside a softly lit video of her picking the fruit.

A month later, Meghan and her husband Prince Harry are returning to live in the UK just as blackberry season ends. Perhaps we can expect another video soon, shot on these shores.

Or perhaps not, because experts say the Harry and Meghan brand is at a crossroads.

After the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's acrimonious exit from the Royal Family in 2020, the projects marking their fresh start in California - from streaming to signature scents - have mostly failed to find large audiences, and experts say it's unclear where the couple goes from here.

Their return to the UK has surprised many and we don't know their reasons for the switch, but what's clear is that they will not be working royals when they return. So what could they be doing instead?

News.title: GTA 6 leaks - a nightmare or a blip for the biggest video game of the year?
News.content:
Video game journalist Wesley Yin-Poole, director of news at IGN, says the apparent leaks will be tough for the game's developers.

"GTA 6 is an enormous endeavour," says Yin-Poole. "It's being built over the course a decade, essentially, with thousands of people involved.

"To have the game exposed in this way will have been devastating to many people who worked on it."

The group behind the apparent leaks claims to be acting in the interests of players, accusing Rockstar of engaging in anti-consumer practices, such as its decision not to release a disc version of GTA 6 at launch.

Not everyone is convinced about the group's intentions, as each release of new material has invited viewers to send cryptocurrency "donations" to the user uploading them.

Stop Killing Games, which campaigns against all-digital distribution models, criticised the alleged leaks as "destructive" and urged people not to send money to those claiming responsibility.

Yin-Poole says there's "a huge amount of scepticism" about the stated motivation.

"Most people believe this is about money," he says, "it feels like, honestly, the whole 'we're doing this for the gamers' angle is nonsense, and I suspect most people have dismissed it."

So far, two official trailers for GTA 6 have been released, the most recent in May 2025. Since then, ardent fans have leapt on any rumours or apparent clues in official Rockstar posts.

Some famously came up with an elaborate theory, external suggesting an image of the moon included in a promotional post for GTA Online held clues to the release date of GTA 6's first trailer.

"To a certain extent, Rockstar has themselves to blame," says Vermeij. "That's their strategy - and I think it's a good strategy, it's exciting. But the consequence is that every little bit of information, every little event, gets sort of blown out of proportion."

Yin-Poole says while people will likely understand this isn't the way Rockstar had intended GTA6 to be revealed and doesn't show the game in the best light, he believes most will "reserve judgement" about it until they have seen official footage in action, or played it for themselves.

Ultimately, he believes there's little chance the leaks will "derail the potential success of the game".

"GTA 6 will be an unprecedented moment in pop culture history," he says. "So ultimately, this will become a footnote in the history of GTA 6's development."

Vermeij, who has not watched any of the latest leaks, agrees.

"I think it will have no impact at all whatsoever," he says. "People will have forgotten about it by the time the game comes out."

Grand Theft Auto 6 is due to be released on 19 November for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, with a PC release expected at a later date.

News.title: Drugs at their fingertips, intense pressure: Why child stars fall into addiction
News.content:
Hayden Panettiere was 16 when drugs first arrived in her life in Hollywood.

Ahead of a red carpet event for the hit series Heroes, she has said someone on her team handed her a pill to help amp up her energy. The hit sci-fi NBC series had catapulted the teen into a household name - and that brought with it intense pressure and exhaustion she says felt overwhelming.

"Within minutes, a wave of energy washed over me, like I'd just woken up from the most refreshing night's sleep of my life," Panettiere wrote about that pill in her memoir, which was released just months before her death.

She called it "the gateway drug that ushered me toward the good of pharmaceuticals and the downfall of addiction".

The star's sudden death at the age of 36 has placed a renewed focus on her struggles with mental health and substance abuse, and re-ignited a discussion about the pressures of Hollywood on child stars.

The coroner's office in Greenville, South Carolina said crews treated a woman in "cardiac arrest" and her autopsy showed "no signs of trauma".

No cause of death has been released, though additional tests are yet to be completed.

Audio from police dispatchers and crews who responded to the address said they were responding to a "cardiac arrest" and detailed their efforts to resuscitate the woman after a possible "overdose". Panettiere's ex boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack, were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing on their part, according to police.

It is not known if drugs or alcohol played a factor in her death, but the US Drug Enforcement Agency is joining an investigation into her death, according to US media reports.

Panettiere is one of many actors who has openly struggled with addiction after exposure to fame at an early age, which addiction experts told the BBC can put people at risk for mental health and substance abuse issues.

It can sometimes seem to the rest of the world that child actors have "everything" at their fingertips - like fame and money, said Lucas Trautman, the medical director of Oxford Treatment Center, an addiction treatment centre in Mississippi.

"But it's important to remember that they were also exposed during a developmental time to many adult aspects of life that the rest of us weren't - including traumatic experiences - and so that gives them unique risk factors for addiction," Trautman said.

Panettiere's death comes after she published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction, her postpartum depression and the loss of her 28-year-old brother.

Panettiere's decision to publicly share her struggles is worthy of respect, said William Moyers, the vice-president of public affairs for Hazelden Betty Ford, the largest nonprofit addiction treatment provider in the US. But he said the constant public scrutiny she faced may not have allowed her room to address her mental health in private.

"Her entire life from the beginning was centred in the intense public spotlight, and this didn't give Hayden much in the way of a respite," said Moyers, who has been in recovery from an addiction since 1989.

News.title: Vigil held for family who died in sea off Shoreham
News.content:
Alden added: "The way everybody has come together and marked today with this minute's silence, and there were people who met with paddleboards and kayaks over at Kingston Beach as well this morning, it's been a really lovely way to pay to the very sad loss of these lives."

Wesley Horscroft attended on behalf of paddlers in the Kingston beach community.

He said he had originally planned to go out alone and "put some flowers on the water" to honour the family, before he decided to invite others.

"It's kind of grown and a lot of people wanted to turn up to do the same," he said.

He said Saja's death had added an "another layer" to the grief felt in the town.

News.title: Economic adviser O'Neill rules out government job but backs PM's devolution plans
News.content:
Economist Lord Jim O'Neill, who has been advising the prime minister, has said he will not be taking a job in Andy Burnham's government.

As first reported by, external the Financial Times, Lord O'Neill, a crossbench peer who was once a treasury minister under the Conservatives, said he did not want the constraints involved in taking on a formal role.

The former chief economist at Goldman Sachs had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser.

He said he was enjoying what he was currently doing too much and did not want to have to give up control of his business interests to comply with official rules.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he had "lots of other things that are going on that I very much enjoy" and, having been a minister before, he knew the job included "all the constraints that understandably go with it, like a blind trust and to abandon everything else you do, never mind the fact that it's 24/7".

In placing shares in blind trusts, ministers have no knowledge of how their investment is being handled, to avoid any potential conflict of interest.

He said he concluded he would rather be a voice to talk to and "get on with the rest of the things in my life".

He earlier told the Financial Times it was "not because of any policy disagreements", adding "I'm a massive fan of the focus on devolution and I hope Andy and his team will be bold on this and everything else."

He pointed to Greater Manchester as an example of economic growth and said if you could repeat that around populated areas, "then national economic performance will improve".

Asked by the BBC whether the new government in the upcoming October budget would need to raise taxes, Lord O'Neill said it was a choice for the prime minister and his team "based on the things they're saying they want to do more of - defence spending is obviously the one that catches the eye", among other things.

Pressed on whether the government could turn to something such as wealth taxes, Lord O'Neill said he was "not a fan of further increases in these kind of taxes, particularly as it relates to capital gains for genuine risk taking things like venture capital".

He noted that the country has boosted government spending "dramatically" in recent years and needed a "more sensible approach to welfare spending under genuine welfare reform".

From 2015-2016, Lord O'Neill was commercial secretary to the Treasury under the then-Chancellor, George Osborne.

The peer, who grew up in Greater Manchester, was a key figure in pushing the Conservatives' Northern Powerhouse agenda, which was aimed at boosting the economy of the North of England.

Lord O'Neill is also known as the economist who coined the term Bric in 2001 to describe leading developing or newly industrialised countries with potential for fast growth and, therefore, investment returns.

The original four nations - Brazil, Russia, India and China - later became the Brics when they were joined by South Africa.

News.title: Welsh county becomes global hotspot for carbon emissions after wildfires
News.content:
A county in Wales had one of the world's highest carbon emissions per square kilometre due to wildfires in July, according to a charity.

The fire above Blaenavon, Torfaen was described as "one of the largest and most challenging" in south Wales in recent years by the fire service.

Save the Children said it was concerned about possible health consequences after data, external published by the European Union's earth observation programme, Copernicus, showed Torfaen behind Malanje in Angola, Spain's Ãvila and Annaba in Algeria in terms of wildfire emissions in July.

Torfaen council said it was unaware of the EU data but its own air quality monitoring showed "elevated particulate concentrations".

A blaze the size of about 300 football pitches broke out on Mynydd Garnclochdy, between Abersychan and Blaenavon, with people reporting smelling smoke about 30 (48km) miles away in Cardiff.

Combined with others across the region it contributed to a major incident being declared, which eventually required assistance from the military.

Blaenavon councillor Janet Jones said the smoke had been "particularly bad" on 13 August - about three weeks after the fire first ignited.

"There was great concern about air quality and the impact on elderly people and those suffering with respiratory issues such as emphysema and COPD."

Jones said she had spoken with GP practice nurses two weeks ago and was not aware of any increase in patients complaining about respiratory problems, but added this "could change in the months ahead".

News.title: Third arrest in murder probe after cyclist punched
News.content:
A third person has been arrested as part of a murder investigation following the death of a "loving and loyal" man in Leicester.

George Glover, 27, was punched as he cycled along Narborough Road, close to the junction with Noel Street, at about 06:30 BST on Monday, Leicestershire Police said. He died in hospital on Thursday.

A 24-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder on Friday and remains in custody.

A 31-year-old man and 39-year-old woman, who were previously arrested on suspicion of robbery and conspiracy to commit murder, also remain in custody, the force said.

In a tribute released by police on Friday, Glover's family said they were "so proud of the young man he'd become".

They said: "George was a much-loved son and big brother to his three siblings. His loss is already felt so deeply."

Officers from the East Midlands Special Operations Unit are continuing to appeal for anyone who may be able to assist with their inquiries to get in touch.

Det Insp Kevin Hames said: "If you can help but haven't yet contacted us, please be assured it's not too late and anything you're able to provide â including any footage â could be vital to our investigation."

News.title: Hidden museum gallery to reopen after 83 years
News.content:
A gallery that has remained closed to the public since World War Two is to reopen at London's Natural History Museum next month.

The gallery, which has remained hidden from view since 1943, will reopen from 16 September, featuring 50 objects which show our evolving relationship with the natural world.

The exhibition, named Nature and Us, is part of a transformation project called NHM150, which aims to open a new or revamped showcase every year until the museum's 150th anniversary in 2031.

Dr Doug Gurr, director of the NHM, said: "For the first time in over 80 years, visitors will be able to step into this beautiful historic space and explore our changing relationship with the natural world."

News.title: Two men re-arrested after death of soldier
News.content:
Two men have been re-arrested on suspicion of manslaughter after the body of a soldier was found in a river.

Northumbria Police recovered the body of Liam Potts, 22, who served with the Coldstream Guards, close to Wylam Bridge on 18 August.

Prior to his disappearance in the early hours of 15 August, the force said it received reports of a disturbance at The Boathouse pub and a subsequent collision at the bridge between a car and group of pedestrians. Police are investigating whether the incidents are linked to the soldier entering the water.

Two men, aged 22 and 23, have been re-arrested on suspicion of manslaughter and remain in custody.

A man and woman, both in their 20s, sustained serious but not life-threatening injuries in the collision.

The woman has since been discharged, while the man remains in hospital for further treatment.

Police said the soldier was on the bridge at the time of the collision, but was not in the car or hit by it, yet entered the water "within minutes" of it happening.

News.title: Police investigate car crash into house in Glasgow suburb
News.content:
Police are investigating after a car crashed into a house in a Glasgow suburb.

Officers were called to the property on Low Borland Way in Eaglesham, East Renfrewshire, at about 13:20 on Friday.

A large police presence was seen on the street on Friday, which was sealed off behind a cordon. The house was protected by temporary fencing on Saturday.

BBC Scotland News understands that Police Scotland is not ruling out links to Operation Portaledge - its investigation into gangland activity across central Scotland.

The crash happened at the end of a quiet cul-de-sac of detached homes.

The brick wall of the property was caved in near the front door, with smoke marks visible to the upper floor.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "There are no reports of any injuries. Officers attended and inquiries are ongoing."

News.title: Brief break from rain as sunshine returns for weekend
News.content:
After the spell of showery weather earlier this week, a strong area of high pressure is set to bring bright and sunny weather to much of the UK this weekend.

Daytime temperatures will feel pleasantly warm - though a long way off from the record heat experienced earlier this month.

Nights are expected to be mostly clear, leading to a significant temperature contrast from morning lows to afternoon highs.

While Saturday and Sunday will bring a brief break from the rain for many, unsettled weather will return early next week.

There is a respectable case to be made for cryptocurrencies. They offer a store of value that is independent of governments and central banks – which is partly why they are associated with economically liberal or libertarian politics.

But there is, equally, a case to be made that cryptocurrencies are a form of Ponzi scheme; that they have no intrinsic value and therefore rely on a kind of confidence trick in order to work.

There are other reasons for being sceptical about digital coins, including the anonymity they can confer, which makes them useful for money-laundering, concealing the proceeds of crime.

Nothing of that kind is alleged in the case of the donors to Reform UK, but there are questions to be asked about a party that is so dependent on financial support from a small number of rich people who have made their money in this subsector of the financial world.

The Independent’s research has established that 60 per cent of the party’s funding has come from such people since the general election. The most generous donor is Christopher Harborne, the Thailand-based entrepreneur who was an early investor in Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether.

Not only has he given £15m to the party, but he also gave Nigel Farage, the party leader, a personal gift of £5m just before he became an MP. Mr Farage’s failure to disclose that gift, as would appear to be required by the Code of Conduct for MPs, is the subject of a parliamentary inquiry.

That personal gift is part of a larger story of a party that has been funded to an unusual extent by the denizens of the crypto subculture.

There is no necessary problem with such a narrow funding base, except that Mr Farage has acted as an advocate for the crypto “industry”, if it can be called that. He has promised to cut taxes on crypto profits if elected, and to create a Treasury bitcoin reserve fund.

As Stella Creasey, the Labour MP, has said, “even if there is no connection between Mr Farage receiving substantial sums of money and his views on cryptocurrencies, the appearance of it undermines our democracy”.

It is possible that Mr Farage’s support for policies that favour crypto merely reflect his ideological alignment with libertarians, but the appearance of possible influence by donors reflects badly on his judgement.

Nor is it just donations that could give rise to the appearance of influence. Mr Farage holds shares in Stack BTC, a British bitcoin company, which would risk the appearance of a personal conflict of interest if he were to seek to enact pro-crypto policies if he were ever in government.

We would not compare Mr Farage with his ally Donald Trump, who has corrupted American politics with his brazen personal enrichment – including issuing his own very much Ponzi-like cryptocurrency.

By Mr Trump’s standards, Mr Farage is a sea-green incorruptible. But the dependency of Mr Farage and his party on crypto interests, and his advocacy of policies that appear to favour those interests, does not look good.

We hesitate to give Mr Farage advice about electoral strategy, but his closeness to crypto interests risks alienating fair-minded voters who might otherwise be prepared to give him a hearing.

Ben Stokes starred again with bat and ball as Durham boosted their Rothesay County Championship promotion hopes with a crushing 338-run win at Derbyshire with a day to spare.

The former England captain followed up his half-century and two wickets in the first innings by making an unbeaten 66 before taking five for 17 as Derbyshire were skittled out for 84 while chasing an unlikely 423 for victory.

After resuming their first innings on 127 for six, trailing by 156, Derbyshire were all out for 156, with Durham’s Matthew Potts finishing with five for 46.

Durham opener Ben McKinney then made a brilliant 140 off 162 deliveries and Will Rhodes made 52 before a 55-ball 66 not out from Stokes saw the visitors declare on 295 for six.

Stokes then took three wickets in four balls as Derbyshire’s second innings capitulated, with Potts chipping in with three for 22.

Division One leaders Nottinghamshire wrapped up a 145-run win against Surrey at The Oval despite Ollie Pope’s 111 for the hosts, who were all out for 183 in their second innings.

Nottinghamshire’s Olly Stone and Dillon Pennington shared seven wickets between them after Joe Clarke’s 95 helped the visitors to 306 all out after they had resumed on 147 for three.

Warwickshire completed a thrilling one-wicket win against Sussex at Edgbaston to climb up to second in Division One.

open image in gallery Chris Woakes helped Warwickshire to victory in a one-wicket thriller ( Getty )

Chris Woakes edged the winning boundary after Warwickshire had slipped from 149 for three to 202 for nine as they chased 203 for victory after restricting Sussex to 207 in their second innings.

Essex batter Charlie Allison made 105 not out at Taunton to lift his side to 314 for three after they had followed on against third-placed Somerset, to lead by three runs with seven wickets remaining.

Gloucestershire pair Ollie Price (63 not out) and James Bracey (45 not out) helped their side reach 248 for three in Cheltenham and they lead Worcestershire by 131 runs with seven wickets in hand.

Northamptonshire opener Ricardo Vasconcelos made 100 to put his side in control at Old Trafford against Lancashire.

The visitors declared on 298 for four and then removed openers Keaton Jennings and Marcus Harris before close to leave Lancashire needing 422 for victory.

Middlesex reached 184 for four in their second innings before close at Northwood and require 170 runs to win against Kent, who had made 254 all out.
