World.title: Tragically Hip band members reflect on Gord Downie and farewell tour 10 years after final show
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ten years after The Tragically Hip��’s emotional final concert, band members Paul Langlois and Rob Baker tell CBC’s Eli Glasner about how they remember that night in Kingston, Ont., and what grief looks like a decade after losing lead singer and friend, Gord Downie.

It’s been a decade since The Tragically Hip’s final concert in Kingston, Ont., but Paul Langlois feels he hasn’t fully processed it yet.

"It’s hard to believe it’s been 10 years since that last show, since our last show," the Tragically Hip guitarist said in an interview with CBC’s Eli Glasner, which aired on The National Thursday night.

"I’m just trying to be in a place of appreciation for what we did and how it seems to have affected people."

It was a bittersweet night as Hip lead singer and lyricist Gord Downie said goodbye to thousands packed into Kingston’s Rogers K-Rock Centre (now known as Slush Puppi Place) and millions watching across the country. Fans and Downie cried together as Downie sang hits like Ahead by a Century and Bobcaygeon for the last time.

Downie sings during the Tragically Hip's final show in Kingston, Ont., on Aug. 20, 2016. (David Bastedo)

The Canadian band, which released 13 studio albums since its formation in 1984, toured for the final time in 2016. They capped it off with a show in their hometown on Aug. 20, 2016. Downie had been diagnosed with terminal brain cancer in Dec. 2015 and died just over a year later, aged 53.

CBC will rebroadcast the band’s final concert on Saturday to commemorate its 10th anniversary. You can find a list of screenings of The Tragically Hip: A National Celebration here.

WATCH | The Tragically Hip: A National Celebration 10th Anniversary Rebroadcast: The Tragically Hip: A National Celebration | 10th Anniversary Rebroadcast COMING UP Relive the night Canada stood still for the live broadcast of The Tragically Hip’s 2016 Man Machine Poem concert from Kingston, Ont., re-broadcasting and streaming commercial-free on Saturday, August 22 on CBC TV, CBC Gem, CBC Radio and CBC Music’s YouTube page.

"I really appreciate that it matters to people, that people still care — about the band, the music, that they want to pay their respects to Gord in some way," said guitarist Rob Baker.

"It’s not so much a celebration for me, it’s a remembrance … the last show was the last day of a career that I loved."

Langlois recalls feeling uncomfortable and uneasy before the final performance.

"I went to the arena early, for some reason I was just kind of going a bit squirrely," he said. “It was starting to seep in that this is the last show, so I kind of had a heavy feeling."

But as soon as Downie showed up to the soundcheck, Langlois’s mood changed.

"[Downie] looked around and he's just like, 'This is going to be so great,'" Langlois recalled.

"It just changed me. I’m like, 'You think so?' and he’s like 'Yeah. It’s going to be so fun.' It lightened me up."

Downie is seen performing on a screen as a man in Vancouver watches during a viewing party for the final stop of The Tragically Hip's tour in Kingston. A decade on, band members said they had no idea how much the final show meant to Canadians until after. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Baker said he was focused on his friend and bandmate on the tour.

“I was there to support Gord, and to help Gord realize his last wish. He really wanted to do it again, and he wanted to look every last person in the arena in the eye, and make a connection, to say thank you to them.”

But Baker said it wasn’t always easy.

"I had to keep all of my emotions jammed down, corked down inside the bottle — much to my detriment later on. But I couldn’t have gotten through it otherwise," he said.

"There’s no way I’d get through it. You can’t stand on stage, blubbering. I had a job to do, and that’s to be attentive to where Gord’s going to take a song … and to be there to support him."

From left, Paul Langlois and Rob Baker speak with the CBC’s Eli Glasner at the Glenn Gould Theatre, in Toronto, on Tuesday. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

At first, the band members were worried that Downie’s condition would affect him on stage. But, they said, the singer seemed to improve physically throughout the farewell tour.

At the time, the band didn’t realize how big a deal their last show would be.

“I don’t think it crossed anyone’s mind that there might be big screens in a small town, or on a campground, or in someone’s backyard,” Langlois said.

People who couldn't get a ticket to the band's final show gather in Springer Market Square to listen to the Tragically Hip in downtown Kingston, Ont., on Aug. 20, 2016. (Lars Hagberg/The Canadian Press)

“It wasn’t really until the days after where I think we all started to realize, ‘Oh, that was maybe a bit bigger than we thought.’”

Baker and Langlois are emphatic that the band won’t be getting back together.

Hip release new album

But the band did release a new album on Friday, Live July 22 – August 20, 2016, which features recordings from across the 2016 tour.

Baker said the members of The Tragically Hip were always forward-looking, so putting together an album of past performances was difficult at times.

But, Baker added, music can have a healing quality.

He recalled when he burst into tears at a remembrance of life for Downie’s father, Edgar, who died in 2015. He later told Downie he felt it happened because he hadn’t grieved when his own parents died.

"And [Downie] said, ‘You’re so full of shit. I see you up on the bus at four o’clock in the morning listening to Artie Shaw, or Benny Goodman or something.’ He said, ‘What do you think you’re doing?'" Baker said. "I was like, 'You’re absolutely right.' I didn’t think I was grieving, but of course I was."

“Music helps you through things. Sometimes you have no idea it’s even happening.”

World.title: RCMP search for suspect in shooting that injured 3 in Fort Smith, N.W.T.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

RCMP are searching for a suspect in what they described as a “mass shooting incident” that injured three people early Saturday in Fort Smith, N.W.T.

In a noon update, police said they were alerted at approximately 2:12 a.m. MT to shots fired outside a local business in the community of just over 2,000 people situated on the Slave River next to the Alberta border.

The shooting took place outside Dirty O'Fergies bar, witnesses said, as the opening event of Fireweed Festival, a community music festival was drawing to a close.

The three injured people are receiving medical care, police said, without providing information about their identities.

The community was ordered to shelter-in-place just before 3 a.m. Members of emergency response teams from the N.W.T. and the Yukon are assisting RCMP, alongside police dogs, remote piloted aircraft, and the major crimes unit.

Residents should lock their doors and remain inside, not open the door for anyone, and refrain from posting photos of responding officers on social media, police said.

Police described the suspect as male with a heavy build, medium complexion, black hair and facial hair, wearing a gray sweater. He is believed to be armed and the public is urged to not approach him and call the RCMP immediately if spotted.

While the RCMP shared photos of the suspect, they also warned that images generated by artificial intelligence have circulated on social media.

“We are advising the public that these images do not match the descriptors of the subject,” the RCMP said. “We are requesting the public to not share it any further as it is inaccurate."

Police have opened a community portal for the public to collect digital evidence from witnesses.

The suspect is described by police as male with a heavy build, medium complexion, black hair and facial hair, wearing a gray sweater. RCMP are warning people against sharing AI generated images of the suspect, and instead rely only on images provided by RCMP. (RCMP)

Fort Smith Mayor Dana Fergusson asked the community to remain calm.

“Just hang in there and be strong because we know what a beautiful, great and amazing community we are,” she said. “This isn’t us and this isn't what represents us.”

Fergusson was in the parking lot with her son outside Dirty O'Fergies when the incident took place. The bar, located in the Pelican Rapids Inn, is owned by her family.

“We were escorting people off the property like, you know, 'Hey, time to go, night's over,' that kind of thing. And it happened right in front of us,” said Fergusson. “It just happened very quickly.”

What started as an altercation between a group of men resulted in multiple shots being fired, witnesses said.

Fergusson said she first went to help the injured, along with two staff members, before getting everyone else on the scene back into the safety of the building until emergency responders arrived.

“It's just sad because it didn't need to be this way,” she said. “It’s not the community, it's these bad apples bringing their bad energy.”

The suspect is still at large as the community remains under a shelter-in-place order, for over 10 hours. RCMP are asking for the public's help in identifying the suspect, but warn against relying on inaccurate AI generated images that are circulating on social media. (RCMP)

One of the organizers Fireweed Festival said she is “devastated.”

“I put my blood, sweat and tears into this festival. To have someone take that in a moment,” Melissa Faith-Johns told CBC. “We have people here from all over Canada.”

Festival organizers were still waiting for direction from police on what will happen with the festival for the rest of the weekend, she said. The Park Party originally planned at Queen Elizabeth Territorial Park has been postponed. Further updates would be posted to the Festival's Facebook page.

The Fort Smith Health Centre is open for emergency access only, and is under lockdown. A mass casualty protocol was lifted at 7.45 a.m. MT, but the health authority said the lockdown will remain in effect until police advise it is safe to return to normal operations. Residents are asked to call ahead if possible before seeking care.

The Fort Smith Community and Recreation Centre is also closed until the shelter-in-place order is lifted.

The CBC's Jared Monkman is in Fort Smith. He'll be broadcasting live from the community on Sunday from 6 a.m. to 9 a.m. Tune in on your radio or on CBC Listen.

World.title: How will the British press cover Harry and Meghan this time around?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Prince Harry and Meghan Markle return to Britain this month, they will be stepping back into a country that has spent six years talking about them from afar.

Their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, are due to attend school in Britain in September, and the couple are expected to live privately outside London for an extended period, according to reports. They will remain non-working royals.

Many questions have already been asked about the couple's return — but after being away for years following a tumultuous relationship with the British press that appeared to have been a factor in their decamping to California, could the tabloids' fascination with the couple peter out this time?

Speculations about the life plans and movements of Royals are nothing new in Britain, but in the mythology that can sometimes be fomented around them, Harry and Meghan were often seen as "the evil, the bad cops, it's all very black and white," said Steven Barnett, a professor of communications at the University of Westminster.

"It's very binary… There is a tendency in certain elements of the British press to go in for very personal witch hunts."

The early coverage included the Daily Mail's "(almost) straight outta Compton" headline about Meghan's mother and The Sun's "Harry's girl on Pornhub," which involved the tabloid discovering scenes from Markle's time on the American TV series Suits on a pornographic website, then apologizing for it months later.

A Guardian analysis of 843 articles across 14 U.K. newspapers from May 2018 to January 2020 found 43 per cent of coverage about Meghan was negative, compared with just eight per cent of 144 articles about Kate Middleton.

Royal commentator Afua Hagan said that interest would ramp up in Britain as they return.

She told Reuters while the couple were essentially walking back in to the "lion's den" they were better prepared this time: "They're not bringing a knife to a gunfight. They know what they have to do, what ​they're going to come up against, and will prepare themselves better."

It's not just the couple that has changed, Barnett said; "other soap operas" may be occupying the minds of the British public.

WATCH | What do people in the U.K. think?: Londoners react to Prince Harry and Meghan’s move back to U.K. | Duration 2:25 The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are reportedly returning to Britain this month – six years after they quit royal duties and relocated to the U.S. While details around the decision behind their shift are unknown, the British public has mixed feelings about the move.

When Meghan and Harry first lived in the U.K., Barnett said, the country was in a different place.

"We didn't have, you know, two wars; the possibility of this country being drawn into a war with Russia; the ravages of climate change. Not to mention, cost of living problems and people struggling to get by."

Still, the court loss Prince Harry and several others recently suffered in privacy lawsuits they had filed against the Daily Mail could lead to more "nasty and vitriolic" coverage, Barnett said.

British media scrutinized after professor's death

The couple's return comes at a time of reckoning for British media.

The death this month of Jason Arday, a 41-year-old Cambridge professor who had resigned after allegations about his academic record, has prompted an intense debate over the boundaries of legitimate scrutiny — and whether the British press crossed them in its treatment of a Black public figure.

Some have made a connection between the nearly 250 articles that were published about Arday within two weeks, according to The Independent , and the negative coverage Markle received.

"The pile on that Meghan … got for years and years and years is akin to what Professor Jason Arday had. She was piled on for years and years and years and it still goes on," Nina Myskow, a former Sun columnist, said this week on Jeremy Vine, an eponymous chat show on Channel 5.

Barnett said the "personal assault" to which Arday was subjected was unfair, despite legitimate questions about plagiarism in his work and and Cambridge University's lack of vetting of it.

People hold up a sign at a vigil by Stand Up To Racism to remember former Cambridge professor Jason Arday, who died aged 41 on Friday after resigning amid plagirism allegations he denied, at Trafalgar Square in London, Britain, Aug. 17, 2026. (Chris J. Ratcliffe/Reuters)

"The same thing, I think, has happened in the past to Meghan, as it has to other public figures, because that's what the British tabloid press does," he said.

Arday's death has prompted questions about the way his story became entangled with much larger arguments about race, diversity and who belongs in Britain's elite institutions.

Marcus Ryder, chief executive of the Film and TV Charity and co-founder of the Sir Lenny Henry Centre for Media Diversity, sees the issue as stemming from a lack of diversity within British media.

Black people, as a result, he said, are too often denied the freedom to succeed or fail simply as individuals.

"White people are allowed to succeed and fail as individuals," Ryder said. "Whereas Black people, when we succeed and fail, it is used for good and ill as part of wider narratives."

Arday's rise became evidence for one narrative about racial progress. His downfall became evidence for another about diversity and merit.

Ryder applies that directly to Meghan: he says her presence exposes contradictions in British society — a Black woman entering one of Britain's most privileged institutions while that institution itself is rooted in hereditary privilege.

Now, the couple are no longer working royals. They have lived in California for six years. Much of the drama surrounding their departure has already been litigated, televised, published and repackaged. There may not be much more left to say.

Ryder said he hopes the perspectives reflected in the coverage of the couple reflect "the real positivity that large swaths of, of the population, especially Black women, feel towards Meghan Markle."

World.title: Churchill, Man., residents say year-round shipping would benefit town but tourism, environment must be considered
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Churchill, Man., residents are welcoming findings suggesting a longer shipping season is possible but say any expansion must weigh the impacts on tourism and the environment.

A series of studies commissioned by Port of Churchill owner Arctic Gateway Group say year-round shipping through the Hudson Bay might be feasible without the use of the most expensive icebreakers amid shrinking sea ice.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said Friday the studies bolster hopes the province could ship liquefied natural gas through the country's only rail accessible deepwater port on Arctic waters.

Dave Daley of Churchill tour operator Wapusk Adventures said year-long shipping would help increase a dwindling population by bringing more people to town and provide economic opportunities for youths.

But he said many questions remain as to what an extension would mean for the environment and the town's burgeoning ecotourism industry.

"A lot of people are talking about is it going to interfere with the seal birthing grounds? Is it going to interfere with polar bears out on the sea ice?" Daley said.

"W e've built our tourism industry in Churchill, that is recognized around the world as one of the most amazing places on the planet to come to. So … people are excited, and people are against it, too."

Churchill tour operator Jeremy Allen says balancing tourism and environmental needs with increased shipping activity will be difficult. (Jonathan Dupaul/CBC Radio-Canada)

Jeremy Allen, a tour operator with Lazy Bear Expeditions, said striking a balance will be a "tough challenge."

"In my experience, a lot of times when the big ships pull in, the whales are kind of gone for the day. But that's something we'll have to deal with," he said, adding he believes most residents would be in support of expanding the shipping season.

"There's a lot people … here in this town that grew up with the port and didn't grow up with tourism and say they would rather have the port than tourism."

Kinew said Friday the environmental effects of LNG shipments are not on the same level as those of shipping oil, dismissing the idea there would be as much Indigenous and local opposition to that activity.

Any expansion would pose 'real risks': wildlife ecologist

Ryan Brook, a professor at the University of Saskatchewan and an expert on the ecology of the Hudson Bay lowlands, said the local landscape is so sensitive any kind of industrial accident "would be catastrophic."

"LNG is different than oil … but LNG would come with its own unique impacts and risks," Brook said. "Any shipping and any industrial expansion is going to come with some very real risks. And I think we can't just sweep those under the rug."

Kristin Westdal, a marine mammal expert and vice-president of science at marine conservation non-profit Oceans North, said the potential impacts on local wildlife — including belugas, narwhals and polar bears — and mitigation measures need to be studied before moving forward with this kind of economic development.

But Westdal added year-round shipping is "extremely speculative."

"We're still in that place where we're talking about ideas — really future ideas," she said.

Belugas whales near the Churchill port last September. (Darren Bernhardt/CBC)

"I think we really need to get back to this idea of figuring out what we want to do with that environment first and how to protect it."

The vessels required to expand the shipping season year-round will cost in the range of hundreds of millions, significantly cheaper than the multibillion-dollar ice breakers needed to traverse the thickest ice in the Arctic Ocean, according to the findings in the commissioned studies.

They say the class of tankers that would be able to travel through the icy waters might not be able to manoeuvre the narrow entrance of the existing port when fully laden with LNG.

Kinew said Friday an expansion that would include an offshore LNG terminal in the Hudson Bay would cost $70 to $80 billion. He said he plans to travel to Toronto in September to pitch investors on the expansion.

Joe Stover, who worked at the port before pivoting to tourism after previous owner Omnitrax shut down operations in 2016, said the town would benefit from having a more diversified economy.

"Certainly nobody wants … climate change to have all the effects that we see happening right now," he said. "But in the meantime, you see what's happening, you have to take advantage of an opportunity that's there … responsibly, of course."

World.title: Visitors outfoxed by footwear thieves at provincial park in Sask.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Cunning and furry thieves are outfoxing campers and cottagers at Great Blue Heron Provincial Park.

Sonnet McGuire, manager of the park located about 50 kilometres north of Prince Albert, says she started getting reports about shoes going missing in early July.

Visitors found single shoes left in bushes, on the side of the road, or even at the boat launch.

The culprits: a group — sometimes known as a skulk — of sly foxes with a taste for footwear.

“We have five foxes that are moving about the campground and they seem to love stealing people's shoes,” McGuire said.

The behaviour isn’t new, but this year the thieves are more active.

“We knew it was gonna be foxes because we've had this before, the odd time, just not to this level,” McGuire said.

At first, the park kept the lost shoes in the back of the campground office, but it quickly had to upgrade to outdoor storage bins to hold them. So many shoes.

Dozens of Crocs, flip flops, runners and Birkenstocks were stolen by the foxes and returned to the campground office to wait for their rightful owners. (Aishah Ashraf/CBC)

McGuire said there were about 70 in the bin on a recent day, but she suspects over 100 have passed through it this summer.

“It's kind of like a scavenger hunt in the campground because as you're walking around the campground on the trail or wherever you might be, people are just finding shoes," she said.

“We had one story where people were walking down the street and they saw one fox sitting on the road and the other one kind of on the edge of the campsite. And it was almost like the one fox was on lookout and the other one went into the campsite, stole a shoe, and then they both took off running.”

WATCH | A fox took your shoe? Get in line at this Sask. campground: A fox took your shoe? Get in line at this Sask. campground | Duration 2:26 Five foxes at Saskatchewan's Great Blue Heron Provincial Park have gotten their paws on more than 100 shoes this summer — turning the campground lost-and-found into a growing collection of stolen footwear.

Camper Brenda Andres said she’s also seen the furry criminals at work.

“We just turned onto the first highway and a little fox ran across the road, and sure enough, he had a little shoe in his mouth,” Andres said.

She’ll be keeping her shoes inside during her camping trip.

One of the shoe-swiping foxes caught in the act in the Sunnyside subdivision at Emma Lake. (Doreen Smuda/Facebook)

‘Kind of a fun game’

Cottager Rachelle Kelln doesn’t mind the sneaky visitors.

“It's kind of a fun game,” she said.

Her cottage is in the Carwin Park subdivision near Emma Lake. It’s also a favourite dumping ground for the shoe-swiping foxes.

“We just started noticing more and more shoes,” Kelln said.

She’s found at least six on her property since July 10, and even more left on the side of the road — all types of shoes, including flip flops, Birkenstocks, even Adidas Sambas.

“Those are expensive shoes and there's a bit of panic around those ones,” Kelln said.

She’s had a few people stop by to pick up their shoes, and they’ve all been excited to get back on the right foot.

McGuire said visitors to the park are advised to keep their kicks inside, as the foxy thieves will remain at large.

World.title: Why a B.C. wildfire evacuee wants to see an haul of emergency support services
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Dawne Young knows what it is like to answer the call when emergencies strike.

A retired 911 dispatcher, Young spent years answering calls for help, from house fires to crimes in progress.

But when the Bald Range wildfire in Summerland broke out, it was an emergency that she believes the province could have prepared better for.

Young said when the fire broke out on Friday, Aug. 7, not everyone in her family received the emergency alert.

"My family members were all standing beside each other, and one got it, and the other one didn't," she said.

The Bald Range fire is pictured burning between Summerland and Peachland on Aug. 8. It led to the evacuation of the entire community of Summerland. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Her troubles didn't end there, she said.

Once she fled and found a place to stay at a friend's house, she tried to register as an evacuee.

She said she downloaded the app, and was told she would be verified Monday to Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

"The following day I did get verified, so I was able to get online to register, then it told me to proceed to the reception centre — which I thought was the whole point of registering online, was so that you didn't have to go to the reception centre," Young said.

What followed was several phone calls, being put on hold and conflicting information. Young said the experience was stressful and frustrating.

"When people are fleeing, they need help right away — not 12 hours later," she said.

Dawne Young, a retired 911 dispatcher and Summerland evacuee, describes her evacuation experience as 'unsettling.' She's urging the province to invest more into emergency management so people fleeing wildfires can get help faster. (Marc D'Amours/CBC)

Young is not blaming the volunteers that run emergency support services. Instead, she believes the province needs to invest more into emergency management.

"I just think that we have had enough big fires in the Okanagan. It is not going to get any better with climate change — the way things are, this is our way of life now," she said.

"People need to be prepared and the government needs to be prepared."

WATCH | Premier says lessons to be learned from Bald Range wildfire's growth: B.C. premier says lessons to be taken from how quickly wildfire spread | Duration 2:58

During a visit to Penticton, Premier David Eby said the current emergency support services system is a lot better than previous years, but admitted it still has its faults.

His government committed to an after-action review of how emergency support services dealt with the aftermath of the fire.

"We are going to take the lessons learned from this fire and apply them and make sure it's better," he said.

The premier said the review will include a pool of experts, including those with expertise in wildfires and local government.

Issues with support are common: researcher

Some wildfire researchers say troubles with the emergency alert system are not entirely uncommon.

"Sometimes the communication systems can be overloaded, so text alerts that are supposed to go out, in fact don't make it to residents," said University of British Columbia researcher Kathryn McConnell.

"In other cases, fires can happen at the same time as electricity outages, so ... accessing television for alerts and landlines for alerts may not be possible."

WATCH | What it's like fleeing B.C.'s raging wildfires: 'Really quite scary': What it's like fleeing wildfires in B.C.'s Okanagan | Duration 4:36

McConnell added that wildfires typically start in rural and remote regions, areas where cell phone coverage may be spotty or non-existent altogether.

To combat this issue, McConnell said the province should look into analog alert sirens as an alternative to telecommunications-based alerts. She said the systems are already used in countries like France to alert people about fires and floods.

But she cautions that a good emergency management system should include more than one method.

"I think big picture the goal with these systems is redundancy —so that if one mode fails, for instance if the telecommunications method fails, than you still have these backup modes," she said.

World.title: Israeli settler blockades part of escalating violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The recent siege of Palestinian homes by militant Israeli settlers in the village of Qusra in the occupied West Bank is far from an isolated incident.

But the U.S. citizenship of one of the Palestinian homeowners has drawn more media attention than the near-daily acts of aggression by hardline Jewish settlers aimed at pushing Palestinians from their land typically receive.

Ohio-based businessman Loui Ridi returned to Qusra on Monday, August 17, to protect his home – and his brother and nephew, who live there — as settlers encircled it and two nearby homes.

"I called my brother and he said, 'I have no food. I don't want to leave the house, but I need food,'" Ridi told CBC news in a video call from Qusra after his arrival.

For them to leave, he said, would be to invite the settlers to take his home.

WATCH | Palestinian-American pleads for U.S. to help end Israeli settler siege:

"Just two months ago [settlers] were at my neighbour's village in Jalud," he said. "They put a siege on the family for a couple of weeks. And unfortunately, they managed to kick them out of their own house."

Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal under international law. They have expanded significantly under the current government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his ultranationalist coalition partners, who critics accuse of giving tacit approval to settler violence.

One of Ridi's first acts after returning to Qusra was to fly an American flag from the roof of his building. He's asked the U.S. Embassy for help.

Qusra is about 16 kilometres south of Nablus as the crow flies and is surrounded by settlement blocs, including Migdalim and Shilo, as well as a growing number of outposts occupied by radical settlers.

Settler attacks causing casualties or property damage are averaging about six incidents a day this year, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs — "higher than in any year on record."

LISTEN | Palestinian-American returns to Qusra as Israeli settler violence surges in West Bank: The Current 24:11 American-Palestinian trapped in West Bank amid Israeli settler siege We hear from Loui Ridi who travelled from Ohio to the village of Qusra in the West Bank to help his brother and nephew who have been trapped in their home, after Israeli settlers surrounded their house last week. Then political analyst, Dahlia Scheindlin, on what this situation means in the larger context of surging Israeli settler violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank, and where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government stands on the issue.

The violence in Qusra prompted a rebuke from the U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who denounced those responsible as "Israeli terrorists" on social media.

"We're appalled at some of the things that have happened to families who are the victims of just criminal activity that is inexcusable and repugnant," he told Reuters in a later televised interview.

"I don't call them settlers," he said. "They're un-settlers."

Huckabee is a strong supporter of Israel's settlement policy and of Jewish claims to a biblical right to the land, referring to the West Bank as Judea and Samaria.

More than 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied Palestinian territories, including East Jerusalem. Many live in large, long-established blocs, while others live in unauthorized outposts considered illegal even under Israeli law, at least on paper.

Huckabee has dismissed violent settlers as a small minority.

Critics say that ignores what they describe as a de-facto institutional annexation of the West Bank that increasingly relies on violence.

A young Palestinian boy is seen at a mosque allegedly burned by Israeli settlers in the village of Qusra, south of Nablus in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on July 26. Palestinian officials said Israeli settlers set fire to two mosques in the occupied West Bank overnight on July 26, after this week's deadly clashes in the territory left six people dead. Violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank has surged since the Gaza war began with Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel. (John Wessels/AFP/Getty Images)

"I think Mr Huckabee is missing the main point," said Dror Etkes, founder of Kerem Navot, an Israeli NGO that monitors Israeli settlements.

"The problem is not the specific house in Qusra. The problem is the system which produces this type of violence," he said.

"The idea that Israel can rule three million Palestinians in the West Bank through its military while more and more land is being grabbed and given to Israeli settlers."

At Qusra, Israeli border police and units from the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) were deployed. The IDF said the forces were deployed to restore order and remove settlers blockading the Palestinian homes.

"IDF and Border Police forces acted to restore order and remove the Israeli Civilians from the area," an IDF statement said. It also said illegal structures erected in the area had been removed and that troops would remain.

Ridi said IDF soldiers declared the area around his home a closed military zone and urged him to stay inside, while allowing one settler to approach his property and intimidate him.

"I told the IDF guy, or the soldier, even though it's a military zone. I'm on my property…. Your job, you were sent here to move that settler and arrest him."

On Friday, Reuters published a video apparently filmed by Ridi showing an Israeli soldier throwing items from the balcony of one of the besieged houses in Qusra and another dumping things into a well on the property.

WATCH | Israeli soldiers appear to throw items from balcony of besieged house in West Bank's Qusra: Israeli soldiers appear to throw items from balcony of besieged house in West Bank's Qusra | Duration 3:23 Video obtained by Reuters, filmed by Palestinian-American Loui Ridi, that appears to show one Israeli soldier throwing items from the balcony of one of the besieged houses in Qusra and another dumping things into a well on the property.

For Palestinians, scenes like those contribute to an increasingly blurred line between soldiers and settlers. IDF units operating in the West Bank can include ideological settlers, and the military also trains settler security units.

The IDF referred a query from CBC News about whether any Israelis had been arrested in connection with the Qusra blockade to Israeli police, who have not responded.

The fact that the settlers have not been permanently removed has fuelled a belief among Palestinians that the IDF is there to enable Israel's settlement enterprise.

"Because if the Israeli army wants to move the settlers they can move [them] in just one hour," said Rabia Odeh, 22, another Qusra resident who lives on the other side of the village from Ridi.

"But the settlers and the Israeli army are playing together, just in front of our eyes."

Israeli settlers and people in military uniforms stand outside a Palestinian's house in Qusra, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, in this screengrab taken from a handout video released August 10. (Reuters)

CBC News first met Odeh in the fall of 2023 after her family's home was attacked by militant settlers from a nearby outpost on a hill overlooking Qusra.

They threw rocks at the house and set cars outside it on fire.

Four Palestinians were killed in the confrontation that followed. Two more men from the village were killed during their funeral.

Odeh says the outpost has grown since then.

Now married and expecting her first child, she lives in a home equipped with exterior security cameras.

"Even when I have to go to my mother's house I check the cameras," she said. "So if the settlers [are] outside, I can't go outside."

Both Odeh's former and current homes are on the outskirts of Qusra, as is Ridi's.

"What we see happening in the past month is that this violence is targeted more and more to the outskirts of Palestinian built-up areas," said Etkes.

"To reduce the area where Palestinians can live, where Palestinians move," he said.

Settlement watch groups say the strategy is aimed at pushing Palestinians into smaller areas and making it easier to connect settlement blocs and outposts across different parts of the West Bank.

"Qusra, this is probably, you know, one of the best examples of what we have seen in the last month," said Etkes. "But this is not something which happens only in Qusra. This is happening also in dozens of other Palestinian villages in the West Bank."

Settlement expansion is also continuing on a much larger scale elsewhere.

On Thursday, Canada joined France, Germany, the United Kingdom and several other countries in condemning Israel's decision to publish construction tenders for a new settlement known as E1, just outside occupied East Jerusalem.

"The E1 settlement will undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank and harming the territorial contiguity of the Palestinian Territories," said a joint statement.

World.content:
Article content

“It’s one thing for (Carney) to come to Canadians and say, ‘look, we’re not able to sign a trade deal today.’ It’s another thing for him to go back to this, you know, anti-American sentiment where, essentially, he’s arguing that this relationship is not as consequential as many people believe it is,” said Jivani.

World.title: ‘You’re at war when you get attacked,’ Carney says after trade talks collapse
World.content:
Article content

World.title: Read Mark Carney’s full statement on the collapse of trade talks with the U.S.
World.content:
Our objectives in our trade negotiations have been to:

Preserve tariff-free access to the U.S. for the vast majority of Canadian business;

Provide greater stability to our trade relationship;

Significantly reduce U.S. tariffs on our key strategic industries, so that Canadian businesses in these sectors would have the best access of any in the world;

Protect our small and medium-sized businesses – the lifeblood of our economy – including by removing the imminent threat of new tariffs; and

Maintain our flexibility, independence, and sovereignty so we can keep building the Canada we want.

We have recognized from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship. Our government understood, before many, that America is altering all its trade relationships. Putting tariffs on its closest allies and charging for access to its vast market.

We have worked in that context. To strike a fair deal that would provide the best access to the U.S. market and greater certainty to Canadian businesses and workers. Throughout, our goal has been to secure the best deal for Canadians, never a deal at any price or on any deadline.

In recent weeks, we made important progress toward improving Canada’s position as having the best deal in the world with the U.S.

However, that progress has not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians. As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa. They have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute. However, last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.

At midnight tonight, the U.S. intends to impose a 50% tariff on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods. Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses.

In the coming days, the government will introduce additional measures to support Canadian workers and businesses, building on the nearly $25 billion in support provided over the past 18 months.

These actions complement Canada’s core economic strategy. From day one, we have been focused on building our strength at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.

That strategy is working. We are advancing nearly $500 billion in major infrastructure projects. In parallel, we are unlocking new export markets for Canadian businesses. Our existing free trade deals already provide Canada with preferential access to 1.5 billion consumers, and we are on track to double that market access by the end of this year.

Canadian economic growth is accelerating, and we are on course to have the second-fastest growth in the G7 over the next two years. Our economy is creating jobs at four times the rate of the United States. Our exports to non-U.S. markets are on track to double over the next decade. Foreign direct investment in Canada is at its highest level in two decades, running at twice the rate of our nearest G7 competitor. Canada now ranks as the most attractive country in the world for infrastructure investment.

Canada has what the world wants. And we will not allow any nation to determine our future. We will set our own course to keep building Canada strong for all.
