We must continue and give new momentum to democratic, anti-corruption, economic and public administration reforms,” the prime minister stressed.

Government plans for the next five years

According to the new programme, the Armenian government will pursue the following goals in 2026-2031:

strengthening and further institutionalising the peace established between Armenia and Azerbaijan;

maintaining and further developing a favourable security environment around Armenia, in particular by normalising and developing relations with countries in the region and deepening existing partnerships beyond it;

unblocking Armenia through the Crossroads of Peace project and the “Trump Route” (TRIPP) transit programme;

liberalising the visa regime with the EU for Armenian citizens;

deepening democratic, anti-corruption, economic and public administration reforms.

With whom does Yerevan plan to deepen partnerships under its “balanced foreign policy”?

In 2026-2031, the Armenian government will pursue a “balanced and proportionate” foreign policy.

“It has proved effective in stabilising Armenia’s external environment. Regionalisation plays a key role in foreign policy, whose goal is to ensure conditions in which Armenia can not only live without external support, but do so comfortably,” the document says.

Based on this approach, the government places particular importance on further developing relations with Georgia, Iran, Turkey and Azerbaijan. The government has outlined the following steps for each neighbouring country:

Georgia

Yerevan will continue implementing the measures set out in the Declaration on Establishing a Strategic Partnership between Armenia and Georgia. This will create new mutually beneficial opportunities for political, trade, economic, energy and transport cooperation, as well as regional and joint infrastructure projects.

Iran

Armenia will continue energy cooperation with Iran, develop cross-border infrastructure and expand transport routes through Iran, including North-South and Persian Gulf-Black Sea corridors.

Turkey

The Armenian government will continue efforts to establish diplomatic relations with Turkey, open the Armenian-Turkish border and put at least two modern border crossing points into operation. It also plans to restore and expand transport, energy and digital infrastructure, as well as bilateral and multilateral trade.

Azerbaijan

The government plans to continue efforts to sign and ratify a peace agreement and carry out work on the delimitation and demarcation of the state border. Contacts between civil society and business communities in the two countries will continue, helping to establish bilateral trade.

The foreign policy priorities specifically include deepening strategic partnerships with the European Union, the US, France and China. With Russia, Armenia plans to “transform and deepen its partnership”.

Against the backdrop of tensions over the ban on Armenian food and other exports to Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), which Russia leads, the programme says:

“Work will continue to ensure the full and uninterrupted exercise of the EAEU’s fundamental freedoms — the free movement of labour, services, goods and capital — as well as to develop relations with member and observer states.”

Regarding relations with the European Union, the programme stresses that Armenia will continue working to meet standards in democracy and the rule of law, as well as in the economic, financial and other spheres.

Armenia intends to deepen its partnership with the United States further. Cooperation will continue based on the principles set out in the Strategic Partnership Charter and bilateral memorandums of understanding.

“The TRIPP project, the ‘Trump Route’, will be implemented, at least in terms of operating energy and railway infrastructure, while integrating Armenia into major regional infrastructure projects,” the programme says.

Armenia’s 2026–2031 government programme

World.title: Parrots Rocky and Kiki: Tbilisi Zoo’s brightest residents – video
World.content:
Macaws at Tbilisi Zoo

Tbilisi Zoo is home to two species of macaws: scarlet macaws (Ara macao) named Rocky and Kiki, and blue-and-yellow macaws (Ara ararauna) named Chico and Paco. Their bright plumage catches visitors’ attention at first sight.

The macaws at Tbilisi Zoo are currently in the middle of their breeding season. Chico and Paco are expecting chicks. They usually incubate their eggs for 24–28 days. During this period, both parents actively protect and care for their future offspring.

Rocky and Kiki have become particularly cautious during this period. They often hide from people and rarely leave their enclosure. If you are planning to visit them at the zoo, keep in mind that they may be difficult to spot at the moment.

Macaws are known for their strong bonds. Pairs almost always stay together: they preen each other’s feathers, look for food together and protect each other when danger threatens.

With proper care, macaws can live for 50–60 years, and sometimes even longer — more than 70 years. Rocky’s exact age is unknown, but he is the oldest parrot at Tbilisi Zoo. Despite his advanced age, Rocky still has the same short-tempered and grumpy nature he has always had.

Once, when a keeper was a little late with a treat — a nut — Rocky immediately made his “protest” known by biting him on the finger. Because of their powerful beaks, macaw bites can be very painful and may cause serious injuries.

Macaws are incredibly intelligent birds. They have excellent memories, and some can even imitate human voices and words.

Although macaws are often kept as pets, caring for them is no easy task. They need plenty of space, daily attention, mental stimulation and constant variety in their surroundings.

It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. World.title: Opinion from Abkhazia: ‘Nika Gvaramia said nothing new about resolving Georgian-Abkhaz conflict’
World.content:
An interview with Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Georgian opposition, about ways to resolve the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict attracted considerable attention in Georgia. In Abkhazia, however, it attracted almost no attention.

In his blog, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda, offered his view on why. He believes the lack of interest among Abkhaz people is mainly because Gvaramia said nothing new in the interview and offered none of the things Abkhaz people would want to hear.

Inal Khashig: “From my strictly Abkhaz perspective, Gvaramia did not say anything radically new. If anything, he simply revived the old idea of resolving the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict through Georgia’s integration into the European Union, which would serve as an attractive incentive for Abkhaz people.

Georgian politicians have periodically put forward this idea since the presidency of Mikheil Saakashvili. The most recent was Georgia’s current prime minister, Irakli Kobakhidze, who in 2024 even set a specific deadline for achieving the goal. ‘Georgia will join the European Union together with our Abkhaz and Ossetian brothers by 2030,’ he declared at the time from a high-profile podium. In short, the EU idea has already been discussed many times.”

From Gvaramia’s interview, I also understood that Georgia cannot resolve the conflict through military means at present because it lacks the resources needed to guarantee the desired outcome. In this context, economic development and shared security interests should form the basis for resolving the conflict.

The only “new” idea proposed by the opposition politician is that Georgia needs to overcome the trauma it suffered after the Georgian-Abkhaz war of the 1990s because these memories “prevent it from moving forward and hold back development”. And on this point, I completely agree with Nika Gvaramia.

In my view, Georgia’s constant insistence on the need to regain Abkhazia is actually a heavy burden that prevents the country from achieving its full potential.

It is like a man who devotes all his energy and the rest of his life to trying to win back a wife who left him long ago. You can consider his life wasted.

I am convinced that if Mikheil Saakashvili had not abandoned his reform agenda in favour of “restoring territorial integrity” during his presidency, Georgia would almost certainly have made much greater progress in building its statehood.

I can well imagine that when Nika Gvaramia speaks about the need to overcome the trauma, he actually means giving up once and for all on claims to the lost territories. But as a politician, he understands the consequences of making such an admission openly.

As for the idea of restoring trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians, Gvaramia talks about this as well. But his understanding of “trust” is not very different from that of other Georgian politicians: essentially, “we will open up the world to you and shower you with benefits, but first come back to us”. In other words, it is a kind of bargain, with no guarantee that the other side is not bluffing.

But genuine trust looks very different.

In my view, a tangible step towards beginning the process of rebuilding trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians would be for Tbilisi to abolish the discriminatory Law on Occupied Territories, which does little short of preventing Abkhazia and South Ossetia from breathing freely without Georgia’s permission. But Nika Gvaramia did not mention this law even once. Perhaps that is why his interview went unnoticed in Abkhazia.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.



Nika Gvaramia interview

World.title: Opinion: ‘Removing Kobakhidze would be logical move for Ivanishvili if prime minister does not move against him first’
World.content:
Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

According to Eka Gigauri, executive director of Transparency International Georgia, removing Prime Minister Kobakhidze could eventually become a logical step for Ivanishvili — provided the prime minister does not manage to seize political power himself.

Eka Gigauri: “The Garibashvili case has once again confirmed what we already knew:”

None of this has anything to do with fighting corruption. Ivanishvili is reshuffling his inner circle, while Kobakhidze — with his approval and Mdinaradze’s assistance — is getting rid of political rivals. In “Georgian Dream”, no one is surprised when people enrich themselves at the public’s expense or engage in corruption: they all steal. The entire system is built on corruption, and Ivanishvili gave them the freedom to do so. So the “fight against corruption” is merely a staged performance designed to conceal a settling of scores. Kobakhidze does not get his hands dirty himself. He has Mdinaradze to do that for him, who has become his loyal executor and servant. It is obvious that the overwhelming majority of “Georgian Dream” supporters genuinely support Garibashvili. The same cannot be said of Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Look at the reactions from “Dream” supporters to statements by Garibashvili and his wife. If the authorities imprisoned Mdinaradze and then Kobakhidze, “Dream” supporters would not say a word in their defence. To them, Kobakhidze is still a former NGO worker and employee of international organisations. He is not a churchgoer and has no particular ties to the Church. The same applies to much of his team. There is no friendship, brotherhood or willingness to support one another in the “Georgian Dream” party. Apparently, none of them possesses that quintessential Georgian sense of honour. Out of fear of Bidzina, and now of Kobakhidze as well, they will betray one another, throw each other under the bus and abandon one another in times of trouble. Ivanishvili is deliberately deepening divisions within his own team and turning its members against one another. His goal is to prevent them from uniting against him and to force them to constantly undermine and confront each other. Today, Kobakhidze is clearly Ivanishvili’s favourite. However, he appears to have been carried away by this status. He often talks about his personal achievements, as though he had the power to act even without Ivanishvili. He may not have many genuine supporters within “Georgian Dream”, but today he exercises almost complete control over state institutions. “Georgian Dream” members appear to fear Kobakhidze greatly — perhaps even more than Bidzina. They know that Kobakhidze has direct access to Bidzina and can tell him something about a fellow party member that could ultimately destroy them. Even Garibashvili did not have this kind of influence. Kobakhidze has placed his people almost everywhere, while parliament is under his complete control. He has gradually concentrated enormous power in his hands. If this continues, even Ivanishvili may find it difficult to dismantle the system.

The experience of authoritarian regimes around the world also shows that dictators manage their inner circles according to the principle of “divide and rule”. They periodically replace their favourites and involve everyone in corruption schemes and other crimes, so that they can later use their weaknesses and complicity against them. At the same time, they pit influential groups against one another and keep everyone in a constant state of fear through selective punishment.

Thus, no individual or group can accumulate enough power to pose a real threat to the leader. However, such a system also carries a significant risk: a favourite who has concentrated all the levers of power in their hands may eventually begin building an independent political force. That is why dictators often get rid of their most loyal and influential allies.

At the same time, members of an authoritarian ruler’s inner circle often initiate changes of power. In other words, autocrats and dictators have good reason to fear their own inner circles. Today, if Kobakhidze wanted to, he could even remove Bidzina, and no one in “Georgian Dream” would dare oppose him. Therefore, removing Kobakhidze would eventually become a perfectly logical step — unless he managed to remove Ivanishvili first.

Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

World.title: Weekly review of oil prices in Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. The average prices of Azeri Light CIF, Azeri Light FOB Ceyhan, Dated Brent, and Urals crude oil increased last week (August 17-21).

According to Trend's calculations based on data from the oil market source, the price of Azeri Light CIF crude, produced at the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli field in Azerbaijan, grew by $0.48, or 0.51%, compared to the previous week (August 10-14), to $95.03 per barrel. Data shows that the maximum price for this grade of crude oil during the week (August 10-14) was $97.12 per barrel, and the minimum was $91.31.

The average price of Azeri Light crude oil on a FOB basis at the Turkish port of Ceyhan was $91.52 per barrel, which is $1.31, or 0.12%, less than the previous week (August 10-14). During the week (August 17-21), the maximum price was $93.70 per barrel, and the minimum was $88.20.

The price of Urals crude oil rose by $3.3, or 5.14%, compared to the previous week (August 10-14), standing at $67.48 per barrel. During the week (August 17-21), the maximum price was $70.29, and the minimum was $63.08.

The Dated Brent crude oil price averaged $92.95, up by $0.23, or 0.25%, compared to the previous week (August 10-14). During the week (August 17-21), the maximum price was $94.43 per barrel, and the minimum was $90.16.

World.title: U.S. court overturns suspension of immigrant visa issuance to citizens of 75 countries
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 22. The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York has blocked the U.S. Department of State’s decision to suspend the issuance of immigrant visas to citizens of 75 countries. According to the court ruling, the restrictions violate the law and exceed the department’s authority.

In January, the U.S. Department of State suspended the issuance of immigrant visas to citizens of 75 countries.

The countries subject to the restrictions included Russia, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Belarus, Brazil, Georgia, Egypt, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Cuba, Syria, and Uzbekistan.

World.title: Traditional owners relieved they won't have to watch another Juukan Gorge disaster
World.content:
Avelina Tarrago feels a sense of relief as she walks into the Nganganterre gorge.

At the site also known as Painted Gorge, the familiar rolling dunes of Pilungah Reserve are interrupted by rocky walls dotted with ritual geometric shapes depicting song lines involved in old Wangkamadla ceremonies.

The Wangkamadla woman, mother and barrister had worried that her family might be forced to watch the destruction of cultural sites by mining in a potential repeat of the Juukan Gorge disaster in Western Australia.

Isabel, Avelina and Valentina Tarrago visited the sacred site for the first time after it was permanently protected. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

In 2023, the ABC reported the Wangkamadla people had applied for Pilungah and Ethabuka reserves to become special wildlife reserves, but that existing resource exploration permits would first have to be withdrawn.

As a director of Mulligan River Aboriginal Corporation, Ms Tarrago eventually convinced mining and petroleum companies to withdraw four exploration leases from the remote reserves on Queensland's border with the Northern Territory, including at Nganganterre.

"I was really worried … I was quite upfront about the risk of harm to this site, that it would be more significant than what happened in Juukan Gorge," Ms Tarrago said.

The Wangkamadla petroglyphs are too sacred to show publicly. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Now she is relieved, after the state government granted the request in April to permanently protect Pilungah from industry activity.

Sitting down in the gorge, her mother Isabel breaks into song, continuing her people's ceremonial history at the site.

"When we come onto country, we always sing out to the old people, let them know that we're here, making sure that we're caring for country, we're not doing the wrong thing, going in the wrong places," Ms Tarrago said.

The celebration on country began with a smoking ceremony. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

Mining concerns laid to rest

Cattle operations were wound down on the former pastoral property, then known as Cravens Peak, more than 20 years ago when it was purchased by Bush Heritage Australia for conservation in partnership with Mulligan River Aboriginal Corporation.

In 2021, the Wangkamadla people were awarded native title over their land in Queensland, including the 446,000-hectare Pilungah Reserve.

But to permanently rule out the possibility of mining, they had to pursue its designation as Queensland's third special wildlife reserve.

Pilungah is a 21-hour drive from Brisbane. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

"No doubt it would have been destroyed," Ms Tarrago said.

" If anything had happened to the site, it would be like personally harming our people, our Wangkamadla people, the holders of knowledge here. "

Special wildlife reserves are unique to Queensland and all three are owned by Bush Heritage Australia.

Pilungah was the first to also achieve the status based particularly on cultural values.

Wide-reaching rock art

Archaeologist Iain Davidson has spent a career piecing together the significance of Aboriginal art and has worked with Wangkamadla people for more than 40 years.

Iain Davidson has researched Painted Gorge/Nganganterre over four decades. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

He said he was "blown away" when he first saw the petroglyphs of Nganganterre.

"You can link the images … at Painted Gorge with images at Roma Gorge, images in the middle of the Sandy Desert, and images in the Burrup Peninsula," Professor Davidson said.

"You've got a long stream of related ceremonial behaviour across Central Australia."

Professor Davidson says the songlines rock carvings demonstrate shared Indigenous ceremonial behaviour across Central Australia. (ABC Western Queensland: Lachlan Ford)

He said his research tied into analysis by late linguist Louise Hercus, demonstrating how songlines threaded through the land.

"This is just a highly impressive ceremonial landscape," Professor Davidson said.

Nation-leading laws

Bush Heritage Australia's national covenant lead Felicity Shapland said the protections would also help the conservation of wildlife, including the rare fat-tailed Pseudantechinus.

"When we started this about three years ago, this seemed like the impossible dream," she said.

But the not-for-profit will need to report annually to the government on how it is protecting the land as part of its new legal requirements.

The reserve is the only known location of the rare fat-tailed pseudantechinus in Queensland. (Supplied: Bush Heritage Australia)

"The monitoring and management requires us to look at the different species that we have here, to monitor them, and make sure that they're healthy, that they're not in decline," Ms Shapland said.

Bush Heritage wanted to achieve the same status for each of its properties in Queensland, including the nearby Ethabuka Reserve.

Felicity Shapland says advocacy for national park-level protections in other states have concentrated on New South Wales and South Australia. (ABC Western Queensland: Lachlan Ford )

It said it hoped the example set in Queensland would inspire other states to introduce a similar set of laws for private reserves.

"This is such an advantageous thing for conservation to have access to something like this," Ms Shapland said.

"It's the only national-park-equivalent-level protection in the whole of Australia."

A pond at Pilungah Homestead pays tribute to a spring destroyed by previous owners, named Pilungah. (ABC Western Qld: Lachlan Ford)

With the region "teeming with life" after recent rainfall, Ms Tarrago said the story of Pilungah could demonstrate the possibility of incorporating Indigenous knowledge into the land-conservation movement.

World.title: The Canadian province set to vote on becoming a breakaway country
World.content:
As he walks around his cafe refilling coffee and delivering baskets of gravy-laden poutine, Christopher Scott wears his politics on his T-shirt.

"Free Alberta!" the shirt declares.

The Whistle Stop Cafe's signature dish is the "heart attack burger", which boasts eight beef patties and various other meats. A MAGA baseball cap rests on the cafe's jukebox, but on this side of the US-Canada border, the acronym stands for Make Alberta Great Again.

The cafe has become a meeting point for Alberta's separatists, who are pushing for the province to break away from Canada and form a new country.

The movement is exposing deep fractures inside one of the world's most stable federations and shares striking similarities with Western Australia's historical secession attempts.

Some Alberta separatists have co-opted a Trump slogan as part of their campaign. (ABC News: Lauren Day)

Cafe patrons stop Scott to shake his hand. "Nice to meet you. We're fans," one says.

Scott, who founded the pro-separatist group Let's Talk Alberta, hopes enough of those fans will vote in an upcoming referendum that could set Alberta on the path to independence.

"The facts point to an independent Alberta being far superior to what we're experiencing right now," Scott told the ABC.

"So I don't have a crystal ball, but I have hope."

Alberta is a province of vast skies, endless prairies, towering mountains and abundant oil and gas fields that have made it one of Canada's economic powerhouses.

Those natural resources provide for high employment and high incomes. They also generate a lot of money for Canada's federal budget, a factor that is fuelling the separatist movement.

Scott feels like the province is being forced to subsidise a country that neither respects nor represents them.

Alberta fast facts Alberta is the fourth largest of Canada's 10 provinces.

It has a population of more than 5 million people.

Its biggest cities are Calgary and Edmonton, the province's capital.

It is one of three "prairie provinces" (Manitoba and Saskatchewan are the others).

Like Australia, Canada has a federal system where funds from wealthier provinces are redistributed to other regions. The idea is to spread the country's wealth and enable each province to provide similar public services.

According to the conservative Fraser Institute, Alberta contributed over $CA300 billion ($304 billion) more to the federal government than it got back between 2007/08 and 2026/27.

"Albertans aren't exercising their sovereignty and it's costing them billions of dollars," he says.

The business owner has become a prominent voice in the movement.

Christopher Scott's Whistle Stop Cafe has become a meeting place for Albertans who support the idea of separating from Canada. (ABC News: Lauren Day)

He spent two decades working in the oil industry before buying the cafe in 2019, only to be ordered to close the following year due to the COVID pandemic.

He kept the cafe open despite public health orders, and it became a rallying point for Albertans opposed to pandemic restrictions.

It led to his arrest and a short stint in jail.

"As I was laying in a jail cell for three days for the crime of protesting government policy and doing so on my own property legally, that kind of changed things for me," he says.

"I came to the conclusion that Alberta independence is necessary and inevitable.

"Not just for economic reasons or policy and things like that, but because it's an opportunity to rewrite the rules from the people's perspective instead of the governing party's perspective."

Albertans will vote on the secession question in October, but the referendum is non-binding. (ABC News: Lauren Day)

Echoes of Brexit

Support for the movement has gone from a small fringe minority to up to 30 per cent of the population, according to some polls.

On October 19, Canada will learn whether those polls reflect reality.

The vote is technically a referendum on whether to hold a referendum.

Albertans will be asked whether the province should remain in Canada or whether the government should begin the legal process required to hold a binding vote on separation.

Alberta is home to stunning natural features, including part of the Canadian Rockies. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

Alberta's Premier Danielle Smith says she personally opposes separation but she believes Albertans should have a democratic opportunity to express their views.

"Those who are unhappy with confederation are not fringe extremists and must be listened to," she said in May.

Separatists say the premier could also be in for a shock result akin to Brexit in 2016, when British voters defied the polls to break away from the EU.

Scott says many separatism supporters are too nervous to declare how they'll vote publicly.

"Many people find it difficult to talk about this because it's like, 'What's my boss going to think?' or 'What are my customers going to think?'" he says.

Polls suggest a majority of Albertans want the province to remain part of Canada, but support for secession has grown. (ABC News: Lauren Day)

It's not just the pro-separatists who are invoking Brexit.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was governor of the Bank of England during the Brexit vote, has reminded Albertans of the turmoil that followed.

"They're still, 10 years later, trying to undo what people didn't think they were voting for but what they ended up having," Carney has said.

The province's former deputy premier, Thomas Lukaszuk, says that argument should be a powerful motivator.

"When you think you're going to win, a lot of people tend to be passive and not vote, so I'm reminding them of what happened in the UK with Brexit," he told the ABC.

" They woke up the next day and said, 'What have we done?' … and now their economy is in shambles and they're on their seventh prime minister in 10 years. "

'Opening the gate for Donald Trump'

Lukaszuk has been driving an old motorhome, decked out in maple leaf decal, around Alberta on a "unity tour".

The former politician grew up in communist Poland. Now he heads up the Forever Canadian group and says spreading the message is his way of "giving back" to Canada.

Thomas Lukaszuk has been on a "unity tour" to promote the benefits of remaining Canadian. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

For him, the most troubling aspect of Alberta's separatist debate is not the prospect of Alberta leaving Canada, but the growing interest in the idea from south of the border.

Alberta separatists sparked controversy this year by meeting with US State Department officials three times, in a move strongly criticised by the premier of neighbouring British Columbia.

"To go to a foreign country and to ask for assistance in breaking up Canada — there's an old-fashioned word for that, and that word is 'treason'," David Eby told reporters earlier this year.

Some Albertan residents feel their province is providing too much to the rest of Canada and receiving too little in return. (ABC News: Lauren Day)

The US's interest could run deeper than Donald Trump's trolling of Canada as the "51st state".

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told a conservative news network in January: "I think we should let them come down into the US, and Alberta's a natural partner for the US."

And in June, the Trump-aligned Heritage Foundation think tank published an article provocatively declaring "Canada's Texas is threatening divorce, and it could eventually become the 51st state".

More than 240,000 people have now put their name to a petition calling for the US ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, to be declared "persona non grata".

The petition accuses Hoekstra of undermining US-Canada relations and normalising Trump's "51st state" taunts.

At a Forever Canadian event in the town of Diamond Valley, long-time Albertan Mary Papais echoed the fear on many people's minds.

Mary Papais fears separatists are "opening the gate for Donald Trump". (ABC News: Lauren Day)

"I believe that they are opening the gate for Donald Trump," she told the ABC.

" Donald Trump wants into this province, he wants the resources that are here, and he will take them and he could [not] care less what any Albertan felt or thought. "

The separatist movement is also facing strong opposition from Indigenous leaders, who say separation would affect their treaty rights, which were signed with the Crown, not the province.

They also fear the debate will fuel racism and deepen divisions in Alberta.

"[This] is really another step to try and eliminate First Nations," Piikani Nation chief Troy Knowlton told the ABC.

Troy Knowlton fears the vote will fuel division and racism. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

Earlier this year, First Nations groups took the issue to court, successfully arguing that Alberta had a duty to consult them before allowing the separatist petition to proceed.

The premier pushed ahead with the non-binding referendum anyway, but cited the court ruling for preventing a direct vote on separation.

"I told her this to her face: where you're going to fail in separatism, you're going to succeed in division," Chief Knowlton says.

"First Nations are under attack right now because of what they opened the door for."

Parallels with Western Australia

The debate in Alberta has drawn comparisons to Western Australia.

In 1933, angry over the perceived unfairness of the federal system and the distribution of the state's vast natural resource wealth, WA voted overwhelmingly to secede.

Western Australia lobbied to leave the Australian commonwealth in the 1930s. (Supplied: State Library of WA)

Its petition was ultimately rejected by the British parliament.

Tanya Clemens, a fourth-generation Albertan farmer who supports separatism, sees clear parallels.

"Western Australia voted yes to secede from Australia, but the difference is that they didn't have a legal pathway," she says.

"They had the democratic mandate, but they didn't have the legislative mandate to be able to do that.

"Canada has a legal pathway."

Like Scott, the cafe owner, Clemens was also motivated to get involved in the separatist movement during the COVID pandemic and what she saw as government overreach.

The mother-of-two says the biggest hurdle for many Albertans is that they still have a deep love of Canada, even while being critical of the way the country is run.

Tanya Clemens says she grew up with a "deep patriotic spirit" but she wants better for Alberta. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

"I have [the] Canada maple leaf tattooed on my shoulder and grew up with an ideal of what Canada was and loving it and singing the anthem and having a very deep patriotic spirit to it," she says.

" It's tough for people to move past that and realise that you can still love Canada and want better for Alberta. "

When asked what she would do about her maple leaf tattoo if the referendum was successful, Clemens says she would probably add an Alberta flag beside it.

"People have asked me if I would remove it. Heck no. I do love Canada and I love the people of Canada."

World.title: 'We're all gonna make it': What gymbros are getting wrong about Zyzz
World.content:
For a certain generation of Australian men, the path to the gym began with a photograph of a shirtless young man from Sydney.

His videos were brash, his poses were deliberately ridiculous, and at times he said deliberately provocative and offensive things to garner attention.

His catchphrases spread through bodybuilding forums, YouTube and social media, and some are now resurfacing as a new documentary hits our screens about one of Australia's earliest social media celebrities.

Aziz Shavershian had the muscles, the tan, the hair, the confidence, and he's the subject of Stan's new movie, Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz.

Zyzz was one of Australia's earliest social media celebrities. (Supplied: Stan)

But for all this renewed attention, Aziz won't hear or see it, having died in Thailand at just 22 years of age in 2011.

Fifteen years after his death, Aziz, known by his online moniker Zyzz, has become part of a new wave of online content celebrating an earlier era of gym and rave culture.

But it also comes at a time when a new generation is encouraged to pursue physical perfection through so-called looksmaxxing by a slightly amorphous online world of male influencers pushing misogyny broadly referred to as the manosphere.

Psychologist sounds alarm over looksmaxxing While it's a bit of fun for some, the social media trend known as looksmaxxing can have major impacts on young men's physical and mental health.

It is a strange moment to watch for his older brother, Said Shavershian, also known as ChestBrah.

He says the culture around young men's bodies and masculinity now looks very different to the one he and Aziz helped create.

"What me and Aziz always preached was we're all going to make it," he said.

"It's a message of just that, 'Hey man, if I made it, so can you.' And that was what we're always about, just uplifting the little guy and uplifting anyone to be the master of their destiny."

Before Tate, there was Zyzz

Andrew and Tristan Tate are now among the world's most recognisable figures in the online manosphere, building enormous audiences around a highly performative version of masculinity, wealth and status.

The brothers are currently in custody in the United States as the British government tries to extradite them to face charges of rape, assault and facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.

Why the Tate brothers were arrested Everything you need to know about the arrest of the Tate brothers.

In Poster Boy, it is put to the audience that the blueprint for the modern male influencer was being tested years earlier in Sydney, with Zyzz at the head of an "aesthetics movement".

But Said does not see the Tates as inheritors of his brother's message or goof representations of masculinity.

For him, masculinity is something far less flashy than fast cars and fancy watches.

"Being someone that's vulnerable, that's kind, that's loving," he says.

"Young men out there, young boys don't really have many positive role models to look up to in society and ones they can kind of feel relatable to."

From Sydney gyms to the looksmaxxing era

Said Shavershian said he and his brother wanted to uplift young men. (Supplied: triple j)

Together, the brothers helped turn bodybuilding into something less about standing on a competition stage and more about being part of a lifestyle.

"Shredding for Stereosonic" became a cultural in-joke, and Aziz became its poster boy.

But the pursuit has become much more extreme online since the height of Zyzz, with communities obsessing over facial structure, perceived attractiveness and where an individual sits in a hierarchy of male beauty in what is known as looksmaxxing.

Said sees the connection and the merits in taking pride in your appearance, but says "deep, deep down, it's quite toxic".

He points to practices, including "face pulling" and "bone smashing" as examples of where the pursuit of physical perfection can go, with men ultimately ranking themselves against others.

The aesthetics movement appears to be a precursor to the current phenomenon of so-called looksmaxxing. (Supplied: Stan)

"With the digital age and social media, there's more information out there," he says.

"Anyone could just post anything, rage bait, any kind of content to kind of reel an audience in."

And once the algorithm finds an audience, it can keep serving them the same message, particularly targeting boys and young men at impressionable ages.

Documentary asks pertinent questions of peptides

Beyond its examination of modern masculinity, the film examines Zyzz's death and his use of steroids and peptides.

For years, the story repeated online was simple: the impossibly fit 22-year-old had suffered a heart attack in a Thai sauna.

The film reveals that Zyzz died from acute respiratory failure after taking a combination of morphine, cocaine and benzodiazepines.

He also had an enlarged heart, although the cause of that enlargement remains unclear.

Said Shavershian remembers Aziz as his "younger, goofy, dorky, highly intellectual brother". (ABC News)

There is no direct attribution to his use of steroids and other performance-enhancing substances.

Said, who is not a medical expert and uses some performance-enhancing drugs, has defended their use in controlled and managed settings.

"I think they definitely have their place in competitive sports, in bodybuilding, and in recovery," he said.

The ABC has reported not only on the booming unregulated trade of peptides, but also the severe health complications they can pose.

There are also medical concerns about the illicit trade of peptides and separately the side-effects of prescribed peptides.

It is a particularly pertinent question for the legacy of a man whose image has become synonymous with the pursuit of the perfect physique, and a confronting detail in a story that has otherwise been relentlessly mythologised, because Zyzz became something larger than the person his brother remembers.

"To me, I always would see him as my younger, goofy, dorky, highly intellectual brother," says Said.

He understands why people still idolise Zyzz, but is less comfortable with the comparisons that have turned his brother into a larger-than-life figure.

"Az was just as much human as you and I," he says.

Reflecting on Zyzz's life, Said said his flaws are what make him relatable.

"Why does a role model always have to be completely virtuous?" Said asks.

Aziz, he argues, was "imperfectly perfect".

A young man with faults, ambitions and insecurities who happened to become extraordinarily good at making people watch him.

World.title: Why can't clinicians override inaccurate algorithm decisions?
World.content:
"The idea of an Independent Assessment Tool didn't drop from the sky, we didn't come up with it."

"It was a very important recommendation of the Royal Commission into Aged Care."

That's what the Minister for Health, Mark Butler, said at a press conference last Tuesday, when asked about the aged care algorithm, featured in our Four Corners investigation the night before.

For clarity, the "Independent Assessment Tool", or IAT, that the minister refers to, is not the algorithm. It's the questionnaire completed by a clinician when assessing someone for aged care services. It was recommended by the royal commission.

On the other hand, the computer algorithm is a secretive formula devised by the government which scores people on the amount of aged care funding they should receive. It was never recommended by the royal commission.

Conflating the two — the questionnaire and the algorithm — has been a common tactic of the government and the Department of Health.

The reality is that these are two very different things, and their development and testing processes stand in stark contrast.

Loading...

Not a job for public servants

The questionnaire or IAT was tested on 22,000 people; there were three working groups involved in its development which included some clinicians; and there's a detailed report on its development and trial which is publicly available.

The algorithm underwent no live trial before it was launched; the Department of Health has been unable to give the name of any clinicians who signed off on it; and there's no detailed report explaining how it was developed and tested.

In fact, despite senators making a formal Order for the Production of Documents, the government has refused to release anything beyond publicly available Department of Health material.

The algorithm's design, evaluation and implementation are all details that have only been gleaned through some rigorous questions from the Coalition, the Greens and Senator David Pocock at Senate estimates.

Waiting for aged care A long-time ABC reporter is one of nearly 100,000 Australians waiting on a crucial aged-care assessment.

Through those responses, it's been revealed there was a prototype of an algorithm — believed to have been designed by a consultancy — which was taken in-house by bureaucrats, modified and validated by them, and launched on November 1 last year.

Public servants have given evidence that they used data from 200,000 assessments to test and verify the algorithm at the back end, but there was no live trial.

Professor Kathy Eagar, honorary professor at UNSW, has a strong opinion on that: "[Public servants] should never have been asked to do a job that is so technically sophisticated."

Eagar should know. She designed a classification algorithm used to allocate funding to people in residential care. She led a team of researchers and experts in the field and her report was published in the Medical Journal of Australia. It contrasts starkly with what's happened with the algorithm at the centre of this controversy.

For our Four Corners, Eagar reverse-engineered the Support at Home algorithm and explained its flaws — that there's more than 500 questions in the IAT but the vast majority do not feed into the algorithm; that the detailed notes recorded by the clinician in more than 100 text boxes cannot be read by it; and that issues such as frailty, cognitive problems, mental health and carer fatigue come into the equation far too late to have any impact on someone's funding, and therefore the amount of care they receive.

Regarding other problems, she revealed that a one-point difference at a particular juncture in the algorithm equates to almost $40,000 a year lost or gained in funding.

Questions linger for government

There's little doubt that the government is aware of the problems.

Thousands removed from official aged care waitlist A Four Corners investigation can reveal the number of people waiting for full aged care funding at home stands at almost 154,000 — not 100,000 as officially reported.

The Senate has now voted for it to be ditched; the Ombudsman is investigating it after 800 complaints; and the government itself has committed $18 million to reviewing both the IAT and the algorithm.

Independent MPs are comparing it to Robodebt — something the Coalition has avoided doing for obvious reasons — and backbenchers report being inundated with calls from their constituents.

When summing up the issue on Tuesday, Butler acknowledged the problems, saying the government was "doing everything we can to monitor the rollout of this scheme" and "where we think we need to modify it, we've indicated a commitment to do that."

The question is, why doesn't it allow clinicians to override the algorithm's decisions when they think it's wrong — at least while it is being reviewed and refined?

It could compare funding decisions made by clinicians and the algorithm, as would have occurred in a real live trial.

Instead, the government voted down a Senate amendment to allow human override.

It says it will legislate a new pathway, allowing assessment agencies to ask for reviews of decisions when necessary.

That's not much different to what's in place now, except it's the older person or their family who has to lodge an appeal.

Loading

'People are giving up'

In its first five months, more than 1,000 people asked to have the algorithm's decision reviewed — that's six times the number from the entire financial year before its implementation.

The government says that's still less than 1 per cent of all assessments, indicating that it's not a real problem.

Eagar disagrees. "The reason that it's a very small percentage is because it's too hard and complex to appeal and also people are giving up," she told Four Corners.

"They know that if they appeal, the appeal is being considered by the very department that developed the system."

If the government wants a true indication of the level of feeling in the community, perhaps it should read the thousands of comments on Facebook where discussions about the algorithm, long waitlists, and people dying are growing by the day.

World.title: Dog, rabbit and fox fur found in toys and key rings sold in markets and online
World.content:
Laboratory testing of seven fluffy toys and key rings sold by online retailers and at stalls in markets in NSW has found every product contained real animal fur despite some being marketed as fake fur.

The testing identified rabbit and fox fur and in one case, dog fur, imports of which have been banned in Australia for decades.

In most cases the fur had been dyed, making it difficult for consumers to recognise it was real animal fur, particularly where some products were advertised as fake fur and did not have a label identifying the material.

One key ring sold to look like an animal tail, sold online for $2.61 and described as a "tail bag pendant" made with "soft fake fur", was consistent with real dog hair.

The online retailer, based in Hangzhou, China, describes itself as a leading wholesale platform for fashion jewellery, accessories and clothing.

A key ring sold online as "fake fur" contained material consistent with real dog hair, laboratory analysis found. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

The findings come as Four Corners continues to investigate whether consumers can trust the products they buy, following its Duped investigation into food fraud, misleading labels and hidden supply chains.

Animal welfare organisation Four Paws commissioned UK-based lab Microtex Analysis to carry out the testing.

"There is a proliferation of these types of cheap products online and I believe most consumers would believe these to be faux fur given the cost and look," said Louise Ward, the programs lead for Four Paws.

"What makes these results so concerning is that we're not talking about luxury fur coats. We're talking about cheap children's toys, fluffy key rings and small trinkets that no reasonable consumer would expect to contain real animal fur," Ms Ward said.

"Consumers have a right to know what they're buying, and right now our laws and regulations are letting consumers down."

Do you know more? Contact Adele Ferguson using ferguson.adele@abc.net.au and Chris Gillett on gillett.chris@abc.net.au

using and on If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

Microtex tested the products using microscopy analysis, which identifies animal species by examining the microscopic characteristics of individual hairs. It found all seven had real dog, fox or rabbit fur in them.

"I am wholly certain that the furs are animal fibre. I have been doing these identifications for over 50 years," Microtex Analysis principal Phil Greaves said.

A pink toy rabbit, resembling a small teddy and selling for $10 at a market in Sydney, was found to contain hair consistent with real rabbit fur.

A yellow fluffy toy priced at $16 was also found to contain hair consistent with rabbit fur.

Laboratory analysis of this toy found hair consistent with rabbit fur. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

A leather kangaroo key ring, with a fluffy pom-pom, selling for $8, was found to contain hair consistent with fox fur.

Some of the products, including the kangaroo key ring, were sold with tags marked "I [heart] Ugg Australia".

Ugg Australia said the toys and key rings were not its products, and others were trading on its name and misleading consumers. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

Contacted by the ABC, Australian sheepskin tannery and Ugg boot maker Ugg Australia said the toys and key rings were not its products.

"Ugg Australia is our brand and trademark, built on 45 years of sourcing and tanning our own raw materials in Australia," Ugg Australia CEO Lena Fishman said.

"Offshore goods with mislabeled materials and often missing country-of-origin information are trading on that name."

"It doesn't stop at misleading Australian shoppers. Because these products carry Australian branding, they're often resold internationally as if they were genuinely Australian-made, trading on a reputation built by real Australian manufacturers and farmers."

It is unknown where the products were made because most of them did not have a label.

The ABC was unable to contact the manufacturers.

But Ms Ward said China was the most likely source because it dominated the global fur trade.

Dr Greaves said he had not expected to find fibres consistent with real dog hair in the key ring, but he had seen it before in similar products such as "items with 'fur' trims, the hood of a coat, decoration on shoes and a key ring novelty".

NSW Fair Trading said in a statement it was assessing the information to determine whether compliance or enforcement action was warranted.

It said traders who misrepresented products may be in breach of Australian Consumer Law and face significant penalties, while noting that the import ban on dog and cat fur products was enforced by the Australian Border Force.

In a statement, Australian Border Force said it actively enforced the prohibition using intelligence-led border checks and had seized 15 consignments of suspected prohibited cat or dog fur products since the ban was introduced in 2004.

The agency said it continued to work with partner agencies to detect and prevent prohibited animal fur from entering Australia.

Four Paws said a lack of enforcement was allowing these products to be sold to consumers.

"It's consumer deception," Ms Ward said.

"Toys are not covered by mandatory labelling laws under Australian Consumer Law."

There is no prohibition on rabbit or fox fur being sold in Australia.

World.title: How artist Khaled Sabsabi remains optimistic after weathering recent storms
World.content:
Khaled Sabsabi has one thing on his mind: coffee; specifically Lebanese coffee. And it's not because of the obvious reasons, although the bags under his eyes suggest it could be.

It's been a tiring few months for Sabsabi, as anyone familiar with the controversy surrounding his current history-making double-showing at the Venice Biennale would know.

After being appointed, sacked, then reinstated to represent Australia at the 'Oscars of the art world', Sabsabi is the only Australian artist, and one of only three artists in the event's 131-year history, to present work in both a national pavilion and the biennale's main exhibition.

But that is a topic of conversation that Sabsabi is tired of discussing.

The reason he has coffee on his mind is that it's the central thread, recurring motif and medium for his current exhibition at Vessel Contemporary, in Fremantle.

Memory and art

Between Suns is a major survey, bringing together work from 1998 to 2026, including new and previously unexhibited pieces. It includes Sabsabi's first visual artwork Aajyna, a deeply personal piece which has been recreated specifically for the Vessel venue.

Loading Instagram content

Like much of Sabsabi's work, it is an immersive experience, combining sounds and smell — while viewing the piece visitors are hit with the scent of Lebanese coffee. Sabsabi is aware of the power of the olfactory to reignite memories.

"This is pretty much the only childhood memory work I've ever created in my creative practice," Sabsabi tells ABC Arts.

He's overcome with emotion as he retells the memory of seeking shelter in makeshift bunkers as a child during Lebanon's civil war and of sniper bullets whizzing past his head in the moments in between.

But he also says it conjures joyful memories of his mother reading the fortunes of other women in the residue of their coffee cups after they migrated to Western Sydney.

"I'm interested in memory and how humans can recreate memory and even essentially change memory in a very subtle way," Sabsabi explains.

The original work was "lost with time" and recreated again in 2021 for the Campbelltown Arts Centre. Now, coffee drips from walls of an aptly bunker-like structure on the side of the main Vessel building.

"The use of the medium of coffee — it was like reconnecting with an old friend that you haven't seen for 20 years," Sabsabi says.

It doesn't hurt that he is also partial to a cup or two of Lebanese coffee, enjoying the taste of the dark roast as much as the ritualistic aspect of making it.

"You can't go to Khaled's studio without being force-fed coffee," exhibition curator Mikala Tai says.

Khaled Sabsabi and exhibition curator Mikala Tai. (Supplied: Ebony Vukelic)

Coffee also features in the titular works Between Suns C and Between Suns D, one of which is a 3-metre mural Sabsabi created in sections in his Western Sydney studio, a converted garage.

He only saw the canvas in its entirety for the first time when it was hung in Fremantle. It's the first time the pieces have been exhibited, although they were created in 2024.

"The way I work, I work in a continuum. So for me as a living artist or a living human being, I think as I progress or regress, learn or unlearn, I have the capacity to go back and revisit work," Sabsabi explains.

Like the first work visitors are greeted with upon entering Vessel, called Knowing Beyond, also made using coffee, the Between Suns works nod to duality, imagination and mysticism — recurring concepts in Sabsabi's work.

"It's the third space that I'm interested in, the idea of the yet to be imagined, yet to be defined space. Where that comes from, whether you say spirituality or inspiration, it's all interconnected," he says.

Khaled Sabsabi's latest exhibition is inspired by memory and his love for coffee. (ABC News: Jade Barker)

All the way west

Western Australia already held a special place in Sabsabi's heart — his first ever exhibition took place at Perth Institute of Contemporary Arts in 2005 as part of the Hatched National Graduate Show.

The gallery then held his first solo show in 2018 and the Art Gallery of Western Australia holds one of his works in its collection.

"WA takes a lot more risks, creative risks, than it's given credit for and it's experimental and it's open to new things," Tai says.

"It's the way WA reaches out and forms connections through art; it's different to everywhere else in the country and I think Khaled has benefited from that. Even though he is Western Sydney's artistic poster boy now, it was only built from recognition from WA and also from South Australia," she elaborates.

Axed Biennale artist to take not one but two huge installations to Venice The Lebanese Australian artist, controversially dropped then reinstated to represent Australia at the biennale, brings two installations to the 'Olympics of the art world'.

Another recurring theme that runs through Sabsabi's work is hope and optimism. Does he still feel hopeful in the face of a tumultuous global political climate and after everything he's gone through in his professional life over the past 18 months?

"I mean, the past year or year and a half has had quite a heavy impact. But to have the people at Vessel reach out to me and say, 'look, we believe in your work, we value your work, and we respect your work …'," he trails off.

"In that moment where everything was rescinded, it felt like his career was collapsing, like that people wouldn't touch him, that opportunities were going to dry up and his ability to be able to even provide for his family was going to be challenged. So to have this invitation from Vessel, it made him feel that he could still be seen for his work and who he was," Tai says.

Sabsabi worked across painting, video, sound, installation and performance with Between Suns. (Supplied: Aaron Claringbold)

In the wake of what happened with Sabsabi's appointment to represent Australia at Venice, Tai resigned from her role at Creative Australia.

They had never worked directly together before but now she describes them as having a unique bond and "innately trusting each other".

Now his confidence has been restored Tai thinks the world is Sabsabi's oyster.

"I think as an artist that if he had been working in Europe or in Asia, he would have had this kind of recognition that he has now much earlier in his career," she says.

"I'm excited for him to actually be recognised beyond everything that's just happened in the last year, but back to being about his art and what he's proposing as a form of coexistence and shared futures."

Sabsabi is also excited for the spotlight to be back on his work. After doing a cathartic clear-out of his studio in Sydney when he returned from Venice, he has a new 10-metre artwork in progress and is keen to get back to it.

" I take every day as it comes — that's my nature — so this notion of acceptance, I have referred and mentioned acceptance many times, it's part of the spiritual belief for me. "

He lives by the concepts he explores in his work — from his deep love of coffee, to his ever-evolving exploration of spirituality and Sufism, to his optimism.

"I mean if we don't have hope then why do we get out of bed? It's as simple as that, so we're always gonna have hope."

Between Suns is at the Vessel Contemporary, Fremantle until September 20.

World.title: Salt-N-Pepa say they weren't always respected in hip-hop
World.content:
Hip-hop fans love a feud.

Decades before Kendrick Lamar took on Drake, even well before Biggie and Tupac's storied rivalry, the first hip-hop diss track came from a teenage girl from Queens, New York.

In 1985, Roxanne Shante released Roxanne's Revenge, a searing response to rap group UTFO's 1984 hit Roxanne, Roxanne, the 14-year-old clapping back with a devastating mix of confidence and sass.

Noticing the attention it received, two fellow young New York women, Cheryl James and Sandra Denton, tried a similar tack.

Double J — a place for music lovers Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

As Super Nature, they recorded The Show Stoppa, in response to Doug E Fresh and Slick Rick's song The Show.

"That was how women kind of got their recognition back then," James, aka Salt, tells Double J's Hau Latukefu.

"We ain't have no beef with [Doug E Fresh and Slick Rick] for real, but we saw Roxanne Shante do it, so we was like, 'Oh, we could do that. They're gonna pay attention if we do that.' It caused a lot of controversy."

It also opened a lot of doors. Not just for James and Denton, but for a string of women who would come after them.

Super Nature soon became Salt-N-Pepa, who alongside DJ Spinderella would become one of the first all-female rap groups to achieve mainstream success and prove women belonged at the centre of hip-hop.

The moment it became real

The group would go on to make some of the most enduring hip-hop of the 80s and 90s, with hits like Push It, Shoop, Let's Talk About Sex and Whatta Man still staples of the genre today.

But that first track started it all. After countless accolades, its success still means the world.

Salt-N-Pepa's Very Necessary was the sound of a confident group revelling in who they were Very Necessary is the essence of a group joyfully owning and occupying the distinctiveness of their identities.

"We just wanted to hear our song on the radio," James, aka Salt, says.

Their producer, Hurby Luv Bug, sent the Salt-N-Pepa recording to DJ Marley Marl, the only man who could get the song out to the hip-hop-loving public.

"You could only hear hip-hop for 2 hours on the weekend, so everybody was tuned in," Salt recalls. "You just wanted to hear this new music."

The women jumped in Denton, aka Pepa's, car, a beat-up yellow Datsun with a hole in its floor, and cruised the streets with Marley Marl's show blaring through the radio.

"Then the record comes on and we go crazy," Salt says.

"Pep puts it in park in the middle of the boulevard. She jumps out the car. She's going, 'They're playing my song on the radio!'

"I swear, with all the accolades, all the awards, the Grammys — Salt-N-Pepa got them all at this point — that moment for me still remains the most exhilarating moment. Because that's when we knew this was really going to be something."

Salt-N-Pepa were a dominant force in hip-hop in the 80s and 90s. (Getty: Michael Ochs Archives)

It became something enormous. Tens of millions of records sold, countless world tours, a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award and their 2025 induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.

"The reason that you even know Missy Elliott's name is because of Salt, Pepa, and Spinderella," Missy Elliott said when inducting the group.

"They are the bricklayers, the foundation that hip-hop stands on."

There's an endurance to their success too, which on one hand speaks to the timeless nature of the music and its subject matter.

Loading Instagram content

But Salt reckons the quality of their material is only one part of the secret to their long-term success.

"I be taking breaks sometimes," she says frankly. "Every time I take a break, it ups the ante.

"You can't saturate the market. You gotta step away sometimes. You can't just be out there!

"But every time I do take a break and come back, it's like the floodgates just fly open. All of a sudden, we're back in the 90s and we're doing all the things.

"We're trying to keep up at this point. But it feels amazing: it's the people, it's really the fans. It's real love for Salt-N-Pepa out there."

Built to last

Salt-N-Pepa shaped the musical tastes of many, and they did it as underdogs.

It's hard to imagine now, but in the 80s and 90s, Salt-N-Pepa weren't just focused on whether a female hip-hop group would have staying power. They were wondering whether hip-hop could survive as an art form.

"That era [was] a challenging the time for hip-hop. [We were] wondering if it would last," Pepa says. "We were celebrating 10 years, 20 years …"

While they were flying the flag for the music that spoke to them, Salt-N-Pepa weren't always offered the reciprocal respect such a pivotal force in the popularisation of the genre deserved.

"We were getting flak back in the day," Pepa says.

" They used to call us pop. We were sellouts when we was getting hit records. Now everybody wants to be popular, right? "

No matter what naysayers might have said, the truth was in the material and the way audiences responded. In Australia alone they released over a dozen charting singles, four of them reaching the top five on the ARIA charts.

And while Salt-N-Pepa's songs are undeniably of their time, they have aged well.

A beginner's guide to women in hip-hop From Queen Latifah to BARKAA, here are some of the female rappers who have brought their own flavour to a male-dominated scene.

Supplanting the machismo from sexualised hip-hop, the women rapped about female desire through a lens of safety and body positivity.

"It's so memorable for us when [people] tell us we were the soundtrack to their lives. It means a lot," Pepa says.

It turned out to be exactly what people were looking for.

More than 40 years on from their formation, and with over 15 million album sales, James and Denton keep the Salt-N-Pepa legacy alive.

This November they return to Australia for the first time in eight years, playing shows with fellow era-appropriate superstars Boyz II Men and Bell Biv DeVoe.

Demand has been rampant, with most shows sold out, and comment sections are packed with fans excited to reconnect with such a formative musical presence in their lives.

"It makes us feel like we're such a part of people's history," Salt says. "It helps us to understand the impact."

Salt-N-Pepa start their Australian tour in Perth on November 26, before shows in Sydney, Geelong, Hunter Valley and Brisbane.

Join Hau Latukefu for a massive hip-hop-fuelled party on The Block Party, Friday evenings from 7pm on Double J, or any time on ABC listen.

World.title: Sydney Swans fans grapple with scandal ahead of double header
World.content:
Sydney Swans fans are grappling with an emotional week of developments ahead of a historic double header, as a scandal continues to engulf the team.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are separately investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

The lawyer representing two of the women present on the evening says his clients will be claiming damages for "pain and suffering", while the lawyer representing a third woman involved says a potential civil lawsuit is being looked at.

On Sunday, the women's side is set to take on Essendon in the AFLW's round 2 before the men's side finishes its regular season with a clash against North Melbourne.

The scandal has rocked the AFL and the wider community, with Swans fans left to reckon with their support ahead of the double billing.

Support swells for women's side

Lulu Clarke has been a Sydney Swans fan for as long as she can remember, and says this week has made her feel "pretty awful".

"I'm like, so incredibly disappointed … just to be a Sydney Swans fan," she told ABC News.

Lulu Clarke (left) has been a Swans fan for years. (Supplied: Lulu Clarke)

Before the scandal erupted, the 24-year-old says she had initially purchased tickets to the men's game this Sunday.

"I actually had no idea that the women were playing, I didn't see it publicised at all," she said.

"And then the news broke on Monday and I thought, 'Oh, I'm not going to that AFL game anymore.'

" There's no way I can go and support the men's AFL team, even if those five players aren't on the field; it's not something I can do. "

Ms Clarke says she "flipped" her plans after learning how significant the double header was for the women's side.

"I decided that I'm just going to go to the women's instead of the men's, and do whatever I can to support them because they don't deserve to be overshadowed."

The GWS Giants have encouraged members to support the AFLW Swans, despite their rivalry. (Sarah Reed/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

The GWS Giants have also put rivalries aside and encouraged their fans to turn out for the Sydney Swans women.

The Giants had their own double-fixture last weekend, and have urged members to support their "cross-town compatriots, be it wearing orange or red".

AFLW anger over Swans As the Sydney Swans AFLW side gear up for a historic double header, they have been put under an uncomfortable spotlight through no fault of their own.

"This Sunday, the Swans AFLW will play in their own historic double header at the SCG, in what should be a celebration for their own team and support base," a statement read.

"As we will be playing the Demons away from home in Melbourne, we would like to encourage our Sydney-based and non-travelling fans to continue supporting the spectacle of women's football in Sydney by attending the match, before watching us play Melbourne.

"This is a moment to put rivalries aside and bolster the women's game in NSW by showing up and supporting the league and women in football".

Lucy McEvoy says the support for the women's side has been "really special". (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

On Friday, Sydney AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy and coach Colin O'Riordan said the women's program supported the sanctions imposed on the five male players, and said their actions did not reflect the Swans as a club.

McEvoy said the women's team has received a groundswell of support through social media in the wake of the allegations, which she described as "really special".

"The best way that we can support us in this moment is to get to the game on Sunday and hopefully break a record crowd that we once set a few years ago," she said.

Fans standing by club 'through the good times and the bad times'

Other Sydney Swans fans are opting to attend both matches.

"Everyone is entitled to do what they feel is best for them," says Liz, a Sydney Swans fan who wanted to be referred to by her first name only.

"Personally, I will be there to support the club, the girls and our boys, and support them as I always have," she told ABC News.

"Nothing for me for the club has changed. I can't comment on anyone else, I can only comment on how I'm feeling.

"I will be there for the boys and the girls and I will be cheering them on, because that's what I should be doing because we look after our club through the good times and the bad times."

Some fans are opting to attend both games, while others plan to just attend the women's game. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Madison Clarke is the co-host of the unofficial Swans fan podcast, True Blood, and believes the notion of a "walkout" before the men's game is "coming from parts of the community that aren't necessarily Swans".

"I think there's a mainstream sentiment that is suggesting there may be a walkout," he said.

"We think all feelings on this matter, because it's a complex matter, we feel that all feelings are valid, broadly.

"But the overarching theme should be that while there are five guys that have seemingly dropped their standards and done the wrong thing, there's going to be 23 guys and the AFLW team, running out on the SCG on Sunday, that haven't done anything wrong, that need our support broadly."

The week that blew up the Swans The Swans scandal is creating a greater conversation about the AFL's handling of allegations of violence against women.

Mr Clarke added this week had no doubt been difficult for many fans, and that coming together could be beneficial to navigating the news.

"It's felt for a lot of people to be quite isolating over this week," he said.

"I think what we've found therapeutic and comforting is actually having a dialogue with other Swan supporters.

"So there's nothing better to do, if you're able, than to get to the SCG and be around like-minded people who know how the week's been and know how you're feeling and it can be a really galvanising moment.

"So I think it's very important that we get there.

"Getting around the girls is absolutely paramount at this time as well.

"Getting around the girls and getting around the guys who haven't done anything wrong because I don't think we should be abandoning either the AFLW team or the AFL men's team."

World.title: The other Australian Wolverine: Liam McIntyre on donning the adamantium claws
World.content:
TechnologyVideo games The other Australian Wolverine: Liam McIntyre on donning the adamantium claws Tim Biggs August 23, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 25 years after Hugh Jackman first portrayed the character, another Australian actor is stepping into the yellow armour of one of Marvel’s most violent and most popular heroes. Liam McIntyre, 44, stars in Sony’s upcoming video game Marvel’s Wolverine, developed by Insomniac Games, creators of three highly acclaimed Spider-Man games. This new take on the character is bloody and action-packed, but has a complex emotional narrative at its core. A new PlayStation video game follows Wolverine as mutants and humanity clash for the first time. Set in a world where the X-Men don’t exist, and few people are even aware there are super-powered mutants among them, the game puts Logan — a practically indestructible mutant with retractable claws, traumatised by flashes of a past he can’t remember — in a power struggle between human and mutant factions who each want to eradicate the other’s species.



While there’s plenty of screaming and growling from McIntyre, his portrayal is more grounded and open than most. Still, as the character remains canonically Canadian, it begs the question; why do we keep seeing Australians in the role? “Australians don’t have a lot of self-importance. Tall poppy syndrome, help your mates out, that sort of thing,” said Mcintyre, in Melbourne to promote the game. “Wolverine is an unassuming, get-things-done kind of gruff, rugged [character]. I think his ethos aligns with what a lot of Australians view as some of the best qualities about ourselves. Maybe through that worldview, Australians are like, ‘I kind of think I get this guy’.” Liam McIntyre plays the unstoppable mutant in Marvel’s Wolverine. Despite Wolverine being a mutant, many stories feature him as a relatable, sympathetic character constantly under pressure. His abilities give him a responsibility to help people, but his powers also make him a liability. His lethality and animal-like instincts frequently open him up to manipulation from villains, and he’s only too aware of the possibility he could hurt the people he cares about.



In the game, Logan leaps around the screen tearing enemies apart, with consecutive kills filling a rage meter that unlocks even quicker and more violent attacks, and lets him shrug off damage. But we also see the character in quieter situations, struggling to understand his purpose. “A lot of superheroes have special powers, they’re doing special things and saving people, whereas it’s almost a burden for Logan. He’s most useful when he’s a weapon, that’s when he can enact the most change. But the way that he enacts that change takes a heavy toll on him,” McIntyre said. “He’s not necessarily excited to go out and save the world. He doesn’t want fanfare. He doesn’t want to get his name up in lights as a hero.” The camera is a lot closer, and the action a lot bloodier, than in Insomniac’s previous Spider-man games. McIntyre, born in Adelaide, has been based in the US since he was cast in the lead role of the Spartacus TV series in 2012. Since then, he’s had brushes with super-heroism in The Flash TV show and an animated Justice League feature, and he’s had success in video games as JD Fenix in the Gears of War series. But his latest role feels particularly special because he’s a long-time fan of Wolverine, and he’s still adjusting to seeing his face on the character.



At a preview event for the game at Marvel Stadium, the signboards and screens around the ground were all lit up with promotional images of the character. Sony has introduced special edition PlayStation 5 consoles with Wolverine printed on them. And at Disney’s recent D23 event in California, Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige introduced a look at the game on stage. “He pointed straight at my face! He might not have known that, but I mean, even tangentially, that’s just the wildest,” McIntyre said. “I was watching X-Men: The Animated Series as a 13-year-old thinking, ‘That Wolverine dude is cool.’ And now I’m here. There are these moments in your life where you’re just like, I can’t believe that guy became this guy. Me. It seems impossible.” Editor's pick Video games May the choice be with you: The next great Star Wars story might be a game Acting for blockbuster video games is no longer necessarily just about providing your voice and face. In addition to sound booth work, McIntyre spent four years off-and-on recording performance capture — which minutely tracks facial as well as whole-body movements — alongside stunt people and a core group of co-stars portraying mutants Sabretooth, Mystique and Jean Grey, who he says have all become friends.



But it was performing opposite prolific video game actor Troy Baker, who McIntyre has known for a long time, that he cites as a highlight of the process. “To work with someone who is that good is such a joy. He’s so in the moment, so fresh ... You don’t get many jobs like this in a career, where you really feel like everybody’s trying to make something truly special.” Releasing on September 15, the game comes at a time when Marvel’s also beginning to pull the X-Men and mutants into its big screen efforts. A key character featured in the game was also just introduced to the Marvel Cinematic Universe in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Troy Baker’s character in the game is Nathaniel Essex, who in the comics becomes the villain Mister Sinister, who was just announced at D23 as heading to the MCU portrayed by Adam Driver. While Insomniac could not have known any of this during development, the game’s senior project director Jess Reiner-Reed said that these characters have decades of history, and that fans are happy to see multiple versions of them at once as long as the stories are compelling and ring true. “Having exposure around all these different characters only enriches the universe. We can take inspiration from the movies and TV shows, and they take some inspiration from us,” she said, referring to the well-documented impact of the Spider-Man video games on Brand New Day’s choreography and effects.



“Audiences trust the care we put into these uniquely Insomniac stories, and they can trust that we’re going to do the same thing with Wolverine.” Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

World.title: High rents a roadblock to productivity
World.content:
NationalNSWRenting Editorial High rents a roadblock to productivity The Herald's View Editorial August 23, 2026 — 6:00am

August 23, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A
