The interests of renters are often treated as a footnote in Sydney’s never-ending conversation about property prices. But even with the recent dip in house prices, buying a property remains out of reach for many – especially buying a home that is within reasonable reach of the workplace. Rents are high in central Sydney. Dominic Lorrimer New data revealed in The Sun-Herald today shows there has been little respite from rental rises across Sydney, with the price of owning your own home keeping large numbers of people in the rental market, especially in the inner cities where they compete with international students to lease apartments. Senior economics correspondent Shane Wright reports that in some parts of the country, rents have risen by 80 per cent since the COVID-era rent freeze.



In Zetland, Chippendale and Haymarket in inner Sydney, rents have jumped by between $367 and $452 a week, Wright reports. The picture is mixed, though, with some Sydney suburbs – such as Hunters Hill, Avalon Beach and Hornsby Heights – recording rental price growth slower than the city’s 23.6 per cent inflation rate since mid-2021. The NSW South Coast has bucked the national trend, with landlords in some towns asking less on average than they were in 2021. These falls are attributed to less demand since the COVID-era surge of people seeking to leave Sydney and Canberra. Effects of the current house price slump on the rental market are unclear, but in theory the slump may enable more renters to become home owners, which in turn would ease price pressure in the broader rental market.



There are many other factors at play, though, including federal changes to negative gearing that some fear will force landlords to lift rents to compensate for their lost tax breaks. Related Article Renting Rents spike up to 80 per cent as people are pushed from homes to units The national data that Wright reports on today suggests local factors – including proximity to major employment and education zones, transport and the regional cost of living – heavily influence how much landlords can charge. The most obvious remedy is to increase housing supply in areas where people want to live. In Sydney, the Minns government has taken steps in the right direction with its overhaul of the planning system and focus on transport-oriented development.



Higher densities are a central mechanism for solving the housing crisis for renters and home owners alike. Related Article Analysis

Home loans Five charts that explain what’s really happening with housing It is true that existing high-density areas of Sydney have been home to some of the nation’s biggest rent rises since COVID. But as more high-rise development takes place in well-located areas of the city, tenants will have more options and landlords can be expected to curb rent rises to attract them. Landlords need a fair return on their investment. But affordable housing lifts overall living standards and can benefit the wider economy, as people are able to spend more of their money on things other than housing.



Young people especially can be caught in the trap of paying high rents and being unable to save a deposit to get their feet on the first rungs of the property ladder. Everyone deserves a place to call home, and the end goal for policymakers must balance the needs of investors with equitable outcomes for ordinary residents of NSW. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Heather and Hugo met at drama school 40 years ago. They haven’t stopped working together since
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a familiarity within the Australian creative scene that gives audiences a unique kinship with the actors who appear on our screens and stages. These are the faces we have grown up with, who we have aged with, and who we innately feel like — were we to run into them at the pub — we could share a beer with. It gives our home-grown productions a warm, fuzzy feeling because, not only do we recognise familiar streets, landmarks and cafes used as filming locations, but we feel an instant intimacy when recognisable faces appear. The pride is palpable. Occasionally, a production comes along that is so successful in creating that feeling of familiarity you can’t help but smile when you watch it, even if the subject makes you cry or shift uncomfortably in your seat. And that, in a nutshell, is Dalliance. Hugo Weaving and Heather Mitchell in Dalliance. The good friends have worked together for more than 40 years. The six-episode drama series charts the fallout from one big, life-changing event and the ways it radically upends a group of 60-something friends. Exploring everything from female friendship and the path to parenthood to sex, desire and ambition, it’s the latest endeavour from John and Dan Edwards, the father-and-son production duo behind Bump and The F Ward. The series also marks a reunion for long-time friends and collaborators Heather Mitchell and Hugo Weaving, who star as would-be romantic interests, Dani and Billy. Their on-screen rapport is instant, but when you’ve shared stage and screen for over 40 years, that’s to be expected. Related Article Review What to stream this week: A juicy holiday-from-hell Brit drama, plus five more picks “I feel so blessed every time I get to work with him,” Mitchell says of her decades-long friend. “From when we first worked together … there’s always been a lot of laughter, a lot of fun and ease. It hasn’t changed, really, over the years. And that’s the thing about getting older. [With] people you’ve known for a long time, you sort of slot right back to where you were.”



The pair first met at the prestigious National Institute of Dramatic Art (NIDA) in 1979, began working together at Sydney Theatre Company in 1982, and, most recently, shared the screen in Binge’s acclaimed multi-generational drama Love Me. “I adore Heather,” says Weaving. “Working with her is being embraced. She has a capacity to care about others like no one else and I consider myself hugely lucky to get to play with her whenever we work together.” Georgie Parker as Rose, Hugo Weaving as Billy, and Heather Mitchell as Dani in Dalliance. Dalliance is a reunion for many of the cast, and remarkable in that most of them are in their 50s and 60s. Mitchell was most excited by the prospect of giving talented friends, such as Catherine McClements, an opportunity to expand their creative horizons. “I loved watching her play a character who’s sexy, funny and complex when she’s so often cast as brittle and tough.” She also knew the perfect person for the role of Rose, Billy’s wife of 40 years, pleading with Home and Away producer Julie McGauran to release Georgie Parker, who has spent 16 years working on the soap, for Dalliance. “I’ve known Georgie Parker since we were in our 20s, and I think this role shows people the depth of her talent.” Related Article Australian TV This TV legend has guided us through every decade of life. Next up? Our 60s By nature of the series’ time-jumping format, Weaving worked mostly with Mitchell and David Wenham, who plays Billy’s volatile younger brother, but relished the chance to connect with old friends. “Our read-through days were very special, all the cast together for two days. It was so lovely to catch up with everyone.” And like all great 21st-century friendships, Mitchell adds, the WhatsApp group is still going strong. “We’re constantly writing to each other on because we formed such a close relationship between all of us. It’s beautiful.”



For 68-year-old Mitchell, this was a project particularly close to her heart. Despite a career rich with experience (she won her second AACTA Award in February for The Narrow Road to the Deep North), this is her first time in the producer’s seat. She was quick to accept when John Edwards made the offer. “One of the beautiful things about being older is the challenges are less risky because you’ve got less to lose, if that makes sense.” “And I have loved it,” she adds, pointing out that her age gave her the confidence to ask questions. “I haven’t beaten myself up if I don’t know something. I just say, ‘Can you help me with this?’ I’d go to the production manager and say, ‘I have no idea what this means.’ I think as I’m getting older, I ask for help more.” Georgie Parker as Rose and David Wenham as Gary in Dalliance. Camaraderie played a pivotal role in not only the chemistry between the actors and behind the scenes – Mitchell’s husband of 34 years, Martin McGrath, is the show’s director of photography – but also in the writing room, where lived experience and a willingness to be vulnerable gave depth to each character’s journey. Related Article Opinion

Australian TV If you are still complaining about Australian TV, it’s time to shut up Louise Rugendyke National TV editor “We talked a lot about sexuality,” says Mitchell. “Passion, love, sex. People who’ve been through cancer, how medication affects your sexuality, how desire changes for each person as they get older. Some people just do not want to be touched any more. Other people long for it desperately. For me personally, I’m probably saying too much … [but] I’m more sexually satisfied in my 60s than I ever have been. And I know what I want. “We really wanted to explore both men and women and whatever gender, that there is no time limit to love and companionship and sex. And that sex is not the driving thing for everybody. That often people go online looking for very different things. And sometimes it is sex with no other attachments. And other times, someone is really looking for a true love. The past can turn up.



“So we talked at length about what is sexuality, and how is it perceived? And I would hope that for younger people, if any younger people watch this show, that they will also feel that life doesn’t stop. You don’t stop growing. You don’t stop living. You don’t stop wanting.” Mitchell and Weaving in the 1984 miniseries Bodyline. It was the first time they played partners on screen. Dalliance, and Mitchell’s own sharpened focus on life, touches on what psychologists call “socioemotional selectivity theory”. It argues that we shift our priorities and goals depending on how long we think we have left. Young people who see the future as long and open-ended prioritise knowledge and building their social network, while those further along in life, faced with their own mortality, grow more selective. They chase emotionally meaningful goals, avoid obvious risk, and prioritise close relationships over new connections. “The older you get, you’re looking closer to the idea of death. More friends die around you, more things happen which you might feel will result in an ending,” reflects Mitchell. “Certainly within this show, we want to say, no one’s ready to end anything. These characters aren’t thinking of endings, they’re thinking of beginnings, like how do I want to live the rest of my life? How do I want to be with the people I love?” Loading Endings, as it happens, are fresh in Mitchell’s mind. She recently starred in black comedy The Fox, which would become one of the late Sam Neill’s final roles (though with Neill as the voice of a magpie, they didn’t actually share the screen). “Sam was a very, very dear friend of mine,” says Mitchell, who also paid tribute to Neill at the recent Logie Awards. “I’ve spent a lot of time with him, and my husband was a close friend of Sam’s. He’s directed me, I’ve acted with him, but our main relationship is a non-professional one – I actually went out with him when I was 22 – and I still feel his presence enormously. “And there again, a man in his late 70s who was working and had jobs lined up. So much of his identity and his love was in his work, the people and the industry. I think it’s important for people to know, he was not a weakened person. He was strong right up until the end.”

World.title: It was the critics’ pick of Cannes. Now the same film has won Melbourne’s $140,000 cinema award
World.content:
CultureMoviesMIFF It was the critics’ pick of Cannes. Now the same film has won Melbourne’s $140,000 cinema award Kerrie O'Brien August 23, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What would happen when a group of teenagers collides with 2000-year-old ruins? That is the premise of La Gradiva, the French film that has won the Melbourne International Film Festival’s top gong, the Bright Horizons Award. Director Marine Atlan and her creative team win $140,000, one of the richest film prizes around the world. She also co-wrote the film, with Anne Brouillet. La Gravida, winner of the Bright Horizons Award, also won the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival’s Critics’ Week. MIFF Set mainly in Naples, La Gravida follows a group of high school students as they discover Pompeii – and themselves. “I wanted to explore what happens when you become aware that you belong to a span of time far greater than your own lifetime,” Atlan says, speaking from Paris on the eve of the announcement.



It is her first feature, as she emerges from her role as a cinematographer to take the reins. “The most difficult thing was allowing myself to occupy the position of filmmaker and to feel legitimate in doing so.” The winner was announced at Saturday night’s MIFF Awards ceremony. Short-listed for the prestigious Bright Horizons Award, from left to right, are Paloma Schneideman, Beth de Araújo, Maryam Ataei, Hossein Keshavarz, Rakan Mayasi, Abinash Bikram Shah, Alex Huston Fischer, Eleanor Wilson, and, seated in front, are Harvey Zielinski and Sophy Romvari. Also short-listed but not present are Marine Atlan and Félix de Givry. Wayne Taylor Dario Russo took out the Blackmagic Design best Australian director award for the absurdist black comedy The Fox. He pockets $50,000 in cash, plus a fully kitted URSA Cine 12K $27,500 camera. Currently in New South Wales at a writers workshop, Russo was not able to attend the ceremony. The Fox stars Jai Courtney with voiceovers by Olivia Colman and Sam Neill.



Related Article MIFF Young people are struggling like never before. These films ask why Other nominees for the directors awards were Harvey Zielinski for Sweet Milk Lake, Hyun Lee for French Girls and Maddelin McKenna for Mad Rush. Arrernte and Luritja director, writer, and producer Talia Liddle took out the Uncle Jack Charles Award, worth $20,000, for her direction of short film Protest on the Dance Floor. As the name suggests, it explores how Indigenous people in Melbourne use music – and dance floors – to create spaces of sovereignty, connection and liberation. Sad Girls, directed by Fernanda Tovar, won the MIFF Schools Youth Jury Award, worth $10,000. Special mention went to Phenomena, directed by Josef Gatti. The MIFF audience award will be announced next week, after votes have been tallied.



This year’s MIFF judges included president Sophie Hyde, along with Desiree Akhavan, Courtney Eaton, Noora Niasari, Joe Swanberg and Tan Si En. La Gradiva won the prestigious Cannes Critics’ Week Grand Prize and is also a likely contender for Best Foreign Film at the Oscars. French cinematographer turned director Marine Atlan has won the $140,000 Bright Horizons award at MIFF, one of the world’s biggest cinema prizes. Atlan says she puts a lot of herself into making films: “Trying to unfold the opacity of the world, of reality, through images and sounds remains one of the most essential experiences for me.” Her experience as a cinematographer informs how she directs. “Operating the camera and framing are important to my relationship with actors,” she says. “Sometimes being behind the camera gives me a more direct way of working with and directing them.”



Thought it’s hard to nominate just one element of filmmaking that appeals, Atlan says she loves its collective nature, “that moment when an entire crew is completely alert and focused on the same purpose for the duration of a single shot”. Related Article Cinema Total basket case: How Alexander Skarsgard became the perfect husband in Wicker Real-life and filmmaking partners Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, whose film Wicker – starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgard – opened this year’s festival, were also shortlisted for the Bright Horizons Award. Speaking on Friday, they said they didn’t expect quite this explosion of interest. “We knew that he was a beautiful creation and we were excited to share him but it has definitely taken on a life of its own now,” Wilson says with a laugh when asked about the proliferation of memes posted to social media about the Skarsgard’s wickerman. Remarkably, all of her short films were rejected by MIFF, so she’s thrilled to be here and to be nominated.



“When we were writing it, we were thinking about specific characters and their very specific journeys,” says Wilson. “But if you step back and look at it the context of the state of dating now, it does feel strangely prescient.” Related Article Cinema This scientist quit her job in animal testing to fight for monkeys caged in the labs BRIGHT HORIZONS AWARD 2026 SHORTLIST Big Girls Don’t Cry – Paloma Schneideman

Blue Heron – Sophy Romvari

Elephants in the Fog – Abinash Bikram Shah

Goodbye, Cruel World –Félix de Givry

Josephine – Beth de Araújo

La Gradiva – Marine Atlan

Sweet Milk Lake – Harvey Zielinski

The Friend’s House Is Here – Hossein Keshavarz and Maryam Ataei

Wicker – Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer

World.title: Too pretty to be funny? Why Brooke Shields is still fighting to be taken at more than face value
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brooke Shields can’t play funny because she is too pretty. So say some male network executives with whom she locked horns over her new murder-mystery, You’re Killing Me. In the series, by Mother of the Bride writer Robin Bernheim, Shields plays crime-romance novelist Allison Chandler, the bane of the local detective (Tom Cavanagh) in a cosy fishing village in Maine, the kind where nothing much happens – except a worrying number of homicides. Allison is funny, clumsy, sensitive and smart. But, according to the network higher-ups – despite Suddenly Susan, Lipstick Jungle and a legendary guest spot on Friends – Brooke Shields couldn’t be all those things at once. Brooke Shields plays a romance novelist-turned-sleuth in You’re Killing Me. “As an executive producer I’m privy to the comments from our bosses,” she says on a Zoom call from her home, an hour outside of New York City. Her expressive hands embellishing her words, Shields radiates warmth and passion. “A lot of it is still stuck in the old times. It’s like, ‘oh, no, she can’t be clumsy because she’s pretty’. And the more modern way of looking at this is: she’s all of that. She can be sexy and she can be faulted and that’s fine because she’s earned it. At 61 you earn all of your flaws and your experience. And it makes you so much more interesting. It was important for me to play a character like that to show the multifaceted nature of women.” Strong, complex female leads are as old as storytelling itself, she says. Just look at Homer’s Odyssey, now a box-office hit. Editor's pick Streaming Heather and Hugo met at drama school 40 years ago. They haven’t stopped working together since “Anne Hathaway’s character [Penelope] and Calypso [Charlize Theron] – these are unbelievably strong women,” says Shields. “This is since the dawn of time … Women have been the forebears of strength before we even know. It’s why we have the children. I think that’s starting to become more part of the zeitgeist and not as threatening.” The disconnect between Hollywood’s feminine ideal and the female experience is a topic she explored in her memoir Brooke Shields Is Not Allowed to Get Old: Thoughts on Ageing as a Woman.



“You look at Irene Dunne movies and Lucille Ball, who was a beauty queen,” says Shields. “You look at true female comedy back in that day. Even the Marilyn Monroes. They were brilliantly funny and used their looks as a vehicle. So that by the time they had more dramatic moments, your heart was breaking, because they threw you off balance.” Brooke Shields with Andrea Walker, who plays a cocky true-crime podcaster in You’re Killing Me. Much of the comedy in You’re Killing Me stems from the generation gap between Shields’ character and cocky true-crime podcaster Andrea Walker (Amalia Williamson from Canadian romance drama Sullivan’s Crossing), with whom Allison is forced to collaborate to solve the murder of a fellow writer. The Gen X-Gen Z misfires yield hilariously awkward verbal slapstick to match the physical theatre. “A woman of this age needs this young person in her life,” says Shields. “She can teach this young person and she can learn from her, too. And together, they’re stronger.” Related Article Streaming He’s TV Mr Nice Guy, but Nathan Fillion’s ‘unlikeable’ superhero could be his greatest hit She needed look no further for dramatic motivation than her relationships with her daughters, Rowan and Grier, with her filmmaker husband, Chris Henchy. “A lot of [inspiration] came from my trying to set up my phone with Apple Pay, and my daughters being like, ‘Oh my god, Mum! Here!’ Or I’ll be saying to them, ‘Are you on the polly?’ And they’re like, ‘It’s not polly, it’s molly [the street name for party drug MDMA], and no!’ They make fun of me all the time. And so I went to Robin [Bernheim] and said, ‘We’ve got to put this stuff in there’.”



Retaining the dignity of the characters amid the rivalry was “a fine line”. “If you’re the one being made fun of, you get more leeway. And it’s never mean. My older daughter [Rowan] has all this TikTok stuff that she does, and most of it is her making fun of me. I’ll learn the dance or whatever it is. I don’t understand what they’re saying. But it’s funny and I don’t take offence.” Loading After Rowan was born in 2003, Shields suffered postpartum depression, the subject of her memoir Down Came the Rain, and an infamous clash with Scientologist Tom Cruise, who criticised her use of antidepressants. In June this year, Rowan made her reality-television debut, joining the cast of Bravo network’s Next Gen NYC, which follows young professionals making their way in the Big Apple. Her mother wasn’t happy. Related Article Review What to stream this week: A juicy holiday-from-hell Brit drama, plus five more picks “I was horrified. But she held her own,” says Shields. “I got a message from [the show’s host] Andy Cohen that said she maintained her integrity and she is the grounding force. I said to her, ‘Don’t be the one throwing up. Hold the hair back of the person throwing up. Do not succumb to being mean. That’s not going to get ratings. I don’t want to hear that from you because that’s not who you are.’ So she stayed pretty steady.” Shields barely recognises the industry in which she got her break in 1978 in the film Pretty Baby, and then shot to stardom in 1980 with The Blue Lagoon, before becoming a Calvin Klein model and Time Magazine’s Face of the ’80s.



“I’ve had to hire people to help me with social media. I hate it,” she says. “I’m not good at it. My younger daughter was modelling for a while, and she had a contract, and she had to do all of her own photography. I was like, ‘You’re working for Tommy Hilfiger. How are you doing your own photography?’ She’s like, ‘That’s the way it is, Mum’. And I mean, the word ‘influencer’ – what does it mean? And [fame] is so short-lived but that’s where the money is going. Someone has this many followers or this many TikToks and they pay them numbers that they would never get paid for a hard job. How do you battle that?” Brooke Shields with her daughter Rowan. Their relationship inspired some of the plots in You’re Killing Me. Getty Images As president since 2024 of the Actors’ Equity Association, Shields is lobbying the US government for better wages and working conditions for performers, particularly those employed by Disney’s theme parks and the Trey Parker/Matt Stone-owned restaurant Casa Bonita. “The battles we’re fighting right now are heartbreaking,” she says. “You’re watching people work so hard and they’re not compensated. They’re not protected. They weren’t part of the union prior and they want to organise now. We’re going up against this massive industry and this conglomeration that doesn’t care about the people that are busting their asses for them. Related Article ★★★★

Review Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more “At Casa Bonita you’ve got cliff divers and there’s no safety. The idea that ‘the show must go on’ is not fair. I’ve had so many injuries myself from being on Broadway – taping up my knees and continuing to go on. Actors are considered disposable, and the amount they work, and the money they generate, it’s amazing. And that’s male and female.” In Washington, DC, where “everyone wants a selfie”, she has heard shockingly dismissive statements about her craft.



“If you’re a plumber, you don’t have to pay taxes on your plunger, right? Well, under [former US president] Reagan, if actors had to pay for anything to do with their field – tap shoes, headshots, singing lessons – they didn’t have to pay taxes on them,” she says. “And then, in 2017, that miraculously just went away. We obviously know why, and so that’s another thing that I’m fighting for. I’ve had people in DC say, ‘Oh, wait, so you want funding so someone can follow a hobby?’” Brooke Shields and Christopher Atkins in The Blue Lagoon, which launched her career. Her experience at the age of 18, appearing in Bob Hope’s variety show for US troops in Beirut, was an early lesson in the value of entertainment. “Those 20 minutes of gags, monologues and songs for all these fresh-faced young people who were staying on the USS Guam – that was all we could give them. And it meant the world to them. We’re talking about entertainment as a form of escape and medicine, in a way. I’m not overstating it.” Her new show, she says, “is a little escape … It’s just entertainment. It’s not too heavy.” But she hopes You’re Killing Me plays a part in challenging those pervading perceptions about women that she has faced throughout her lifelong career. “Attractive females can also be smart and not afraid to be flawed. I’m OK with not being pristine and perfect.” You’re Killing Me is now streaming on Stan (which is owned by Nine, the publisher of this masthead).

World.title: Rents spike up to 80 per cent as people are pushed from homes to units
World.content:
PoliticsFederalRenting Rents spike up to 80 per cent as people are pushed from homes to units Shane Wright August 23, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rents in parts of the nation’s capital cities have soared by 80 per cent since the end of the COVID-era freeze on rents, but there are pockets of the country where landlords are getting less from their tenants than they did five years ago. Houses have become so unaffordable for many that people are turning their attention increasingly towards either buying or renting inner city units where they also face competition from international students, figures compiled by property data company Cotality show. Rents have climbed by up to 80 per cent in some parts of the country since the end of the Covid-era rental freeze. Louise Kennerley The property market, including the drop in values in Sydney and Melbourne plus record-high rents, has become a political lightning rod since the May budget when Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealed changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. It has sparked accusations from the Coalition that Labor is destroying the economy and the wealth of people invested in the property market, with the government arguing it is giving first home buyers and future generations a chance to own a home.



The pace of growth in rents has slowed this year after they took off in the period after the end of a COVID-era freeze on rents. That freeze ended in early 2021. Since then, the biggest increase recorded by Cotality has been in the working-class Perth suburb of Balga where they have jumped by 80 per cent or more than $320 a week over the past five years. Perth’s overall inflation rate over the same period was a nation-leading 25.8 per cent. International student-loaded areas in Sydney and Melbourne have experienced rent increases almost as large. In Zetland, Chippendale and Haymarket in inner Sydney, rents have jumped by between $367 and $452 a week. Central Melbourne rents have lifted by 72.6 per cent with similarly large increases in Southbank (69.6 per cent) and Docklands (64.2 per cent) while in Carlton, home of Melbourne University, rents have jumped by 58.5 per cent.



All inner city areas of capital cities have seen huge increases except Canberra where a long-run building boom has added to its supply of apartments. Canberra’s largest rent increase, of 22 per cent, was recorded in its southernmost suburb of Banks. Related Article Renting Tenants caught in crosshairs of angry rent-hike debate Cotality’s head of research, Gerard Burg, said the strong growth in rents in capital city centres and nearby suburbs suggested the impact of the return of international students. He said another factor had been the low affordability of homes. Prices exploded during the pandemic, climbing by more than 30 per cent in some markets while the international border was closed. Burg said as standalone homes had become more expensive, potential buyers had moved either into the apartment market or been forced to continue renting.



“You get these spillover effects. We had that big increase in house prices during Covid while rents didn’t move much at all,” he said. “But [we’re] getting to the point that houses aren’t affordable, so we’re seeing the market for units hold up better than houses. And we’re seeing rents for units higher.” Rents have fallen in a handful of places across the country over the past five years, almost all on the south coast of NSW. In the holiday centre of Manyana, rents have dropped by 30.2 per cent since mid-2021 or by $237.50 a week. In the nearby town of Sussex Inlet, rents have tumbled by more than 17 per cent. Parts of the south coast such as Mollymook (minus 7 per cent) and Ulladulla (minus 0.3 per cent), areas that became huge attractions during the pandemic for people seeking to escape Sydney and Canberra, have experienced a fall in absolute rents.



Substantial falls in asking rents over half a decade, even in deeply depressed property markets, are unusual. But there are many more urban and regional centres where rents have fallen by less than inflation, which itself is being pushed up by rent increases. Across Melbourne’s growing western fringe, rental growth has fallen short of inflation in places such as Diggers Rest (15.8 per cent), Eynesbury (16.5 per cent) and Bonnie Brook (16.9 per cent). In Sydney, rents in Hunters Hill (17.8 per cent), Avalon Beach (20.9 per cent) and Hornsby Heights (21.8 per cent) have also grown slower than the city’s 23.6 per cent inflation rate since mid-2021.



There have been some relatively modest rent increases in Brisbane’s south-west, such as Pullenvale (13 per cent), Fig Tree Pocket (15.6 per cent) and Silverbark Ridge (20.8 per cent). But in the hottest rental market in the country, Perth, tenants have been unable to find any respite. The smallest increase since mid-2021 has been in Brigadoon, about 40 kilometres from the Perth CBD, with rents up by 27.2 per cent. Cottesloe is one of the more expensive property markets in the country. Rents there have grown by 35.8 per cent over the past five years, pushing the median weekly impost to almost $1042. Canberra is again the outlier. The smallest increases in the country have been recorded in the nation’s capital, including in well-heeled and central suburbs such as Forrest (3.5 per cent), Ainslie (5.2 per cent) and Reid (8.7 per cent). World.title: There is a time for all things, including winter
World.content:
And so we are still in winter, just; the season of mittens and beanies, good thick socks and an extra layer or two of clothing; the season of unfurled umbrellas dancing dangerously as commuters hurry to trains and trams and the wet fug of blazer becomes the scent of the season.

Enjoy winter while you still can. Getty Images/iStockphoto

We seek the warmth and light of home, to snuggle in, to block out the wind and rain, to hunker down for a few brief hours. Winter and her meteorological mood swings; the arctic kisses, the cold shoulder, the glacial smile, the spectral pall of grey as clouds scowl and dimmed streams of sunlight leak through the sky.

In the morning, men in black stare out into the weather. A bleak overture, the grey blue notes of wind whistle in subways and car parks, sending papers fluttering like small, doomed kites.

A collective shiver ripples through the passengers as they await the 7.11 to Flinders Street via the City Loop. School students stare into their phones. Office workers who left home gleaming find their lustrous locks have been frizzed into odd topiary shapes. I am tea-cosy warm, unfashionable, anonymous, looking up and about, watching the weather.

World.title: It’s been 25 years since Tampa. A documentary aims to show the story behind it isn’t ‘black and white’
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV It’s been 25 years since Tampa. A documentary aims to show the story behind it isn’t ‘black and white’ Bridget McManus August 23, 2026 — 5:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When multi-award-winning Sydney producer Dan Goldberg first approached the subject of the 2001 Tampa crisis for an ABC documentary, he did so as a “bleeding heart, small-l liberal”. A descendant of Jewish refugees who fled Russia at the turn of the 20th century, his work includes The Hunt for the Last Nazis and Passport to Hope, about a soccer program for Australian refugee children, for which he won the 2010 UN Human Rights Award for TV. He is now in post-production for an SBS documentary on the Bondi massacre. But as filming began on Tampa: The Turning Point, a three-part series marking 25 years since the diplomatic stand-off at sea that redefined Australia’s border protection policy, he began to see two sides to the story. Saereh Rezaee, who was an eight-year-old asylum seeker on the Tampa, is interviewed in the documentary. “The image of that giant, orangey-red container ship is seared into my mind,” says Goldberg, who was a journalist at The Australian Jewish News when the crisis unfolded. “At the time, I questioned the hardline reaction of the government. We all come from our own lived experience. That’s intergenerational for me. “But now that I’ve made the series, I can see that it’s not black and white. I’ve come out of it understanding that there is a genuine clash between two rights – the right to refuge and the right to sovereign borders. The penny dropped for me. I was very vocal in the edit suites. It’s complicated. The shades of grey are difficult to wrestle. And that’s what we hope we’re presenting.”



Related Article Australian TV ‘It’s a really intense experience’: The reality show that’s more like a ‘therapy session’ In the miniseries, directed by Kriv Stenders for Mint Pictures, former prime minister John Howard sits alone in an office meeting room, the camera tight around his face, as he recalls his involvement in the crisis. The same starkly corporate setting is used for other politicians, including then foreign minister Alexander Downer, former Greens leader Bob Brown and former New Zealand prime minister Helen Clark. Other interviewees include the captain of the Norwegian freighter, Arne Rinnan, who refused to return the 433 rescued Hazara Afghans bound for Christmas Island to Indonesia, and asylum seekers themselves, such as Saereh Rezaee, who was eight years old at the time, and Abbas Nazari, who wrote the book After the Tampa. Journalist Dan Goldberg, producer of the three-part documentary Tampa: The Turning Point. Their stories might be very different, but whether they experienced the historical moment from within the halls of power, or on board that perilously overcrowded ship for eight fearful, blistering days, the Tampa has left an imprint on all their lives.



Finding similar, neutral backdrops in Canberra, Jakarta, New Zealand, Britain and Oslo proved surprisingly easy. “Kriv Stenders wanted uniformity, no matter where we were filming,” says Goldberg. “We wanted the people and their stories to be front and centre. There was a uniformity to these offices that, after COVID, are largely empty, which was the practical solution.” Asylum seekers on the Norwegian container ship Tampa in 2001. Underscoring the “ticking-clock political thriller” that unfolds using only these personal accounts and archival footage, is a soundscape that heaves and groans like a drifting ship by Adam Gock of production company The D.A’s Office. “Music is often undervalued, and it has a massive role to play in elevating the experience of the audience,” says Goldberg. “The audience might not feel it. But most of the audience feels something.” The creative team, which includes series producer Ili Bare, was conscious of placing the topic in a contemporary context. “The Tampa happened 25 years ago, but it couldn’t be more relevant today,” says Goldberg. “We’ve taken a historical story and catapulted it into the present tense. We’ve got people [in the series] talking about the 2015 refugee crisis from the Syrian war.



Related Article Australian TV A Country Practice was more than TV. It taught us to be better human beings “We’ve got commentators from Europe looking at the Australian [Pacific] solution and saying, ‘We saw that as a template. And now we’re basically copying it’ … There is this return to right-wing populism. But at the heart of this series is a deeply human story. We hope that the audience will feel swung like a pendulum between these two competing rights.” Tampa: The Turning Point premieres at 8.30pm on Tuesday, September 1, on the ABC and ABC iview. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: The other Australian Wolverine: Liam McIntyre on donning the adamantium claws
World.content:
TechnologyVideo games The other Australian Wolverine: Liam McIntyre on donning the adamantium claws Tim Biggs August 23, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 25 years after Hugh Jackman first portrayed the character, another Australian actor is stepping into the yellow armour of one of Marvel’s most violent and most popular heroes. Liam McIntyre, 44, stars in Sony’s upcoming video game Marvel’s Wolverine, developed by Insomniac Games, creators of three highly acclaimed Spider-Man games. This new take on the character is bloody and action-packed, but has a complex emotional narrative at its core. A new PlayStation video game follows Wolverine as mutants and humanity clash for the first time. Set in a world where the X-Men don’t exist, and few people are even aware there are super-powered mutants among them, the game puts Logan — a practically indestructible mutant with retractable claws, traumatised by flashes of a past he can’t remember — in a power struggle between human and mutant factions who each want to eradicate the other’s species.



While there’s plenty of screaming and growling from McIntyre, his portrayal is more grounded and open than most. Still, as the character remains canonically Canadian, it begs the question; why do we keep seeing Australians in the role? “Australians don’t have a lot of self-importance. Tall poppy syndrome, help your mates out, that sort of thing,” said Mcintyre, in Melbourne to promote the game. “Wolverine is an unassuming, get-things-done kind of gruff, rugged [character]. I think his ethos aligns with what a lot of Australians view as some of the best qualities about ourselves. Maybe through that worldview, Australians are like, ‘I kind of think I get this guy’.” Liam McIntyre plays the unstoppable mutant in Marvel’s Wolverine. Despite Wolverine being a mutant, many stories feature him as a relatable, sympathetic character constantly under pressure. His abilities give him a responsibility to help people, but his powers also make him a liability. His lethality and animal-like instincts frequently open him up to manipulation from villains, and he’s only too aware of the possibility he could hurt the people he cares about.



In the game, Logan leaps around the screen tearing enemies apart, with consecutive kills filling a rage meter that unlocks even quicker and more violent attacks, and lets him shrug off damage. But we also see the character in quieter situations, struggling to understand his purpose. “A lot of superheroes have special powers, they’re doing special things and saving people, whereas it’s almost a burden for Logan. He’s most useful when he’s a weapon, that’s when he can enact the most change. But the way that he enacts that change takes a heavy toll on him,” McIntyre said. “He’s not necessarily excited to go out and save the world. He doesn’t want fanfare. He doesn’t want to get his name up in lights as a hero.” The camera is a lot closer, and the action a lot bloodier, than in Insomniac’s previous Spider-man games. McIntyre, born in Adelaide, has been based in the US since he was cast in the lead role of the Spartacus TV series in 2012. Since then, he’s had brushes with super-heroism in The Flash TV show and an animated Justice League feature, and he’s had success in video games as JD Fenix in the Gears of War series. But his latest role feels particularly special because he’s a long-time fan of Wolverine, and he’s still adjusting to seeing his face on the character.



At a preview event for the game at Marvel Stadium, the signboards and screens around the ground were all lit up with promotional images of the character. Sony has introduced special edition PlayStation 5 consoles with Wolverine printed on them. And at Disney’s recent D23 event in California, Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige introduced a look at the game on stage. “He pointed straight at my face! He might not have known that, but I mean, even tangentially, that’s just the wildest,” McIntyre said. “I was watching X-Men: The Animated Series as a 13-year-old thinking, ‘That Wolverine dude is cool.’ And now I’m here. There are these moments in your life where you’re just like, I can’t believe that guy became this guy. Me. It seems impossible.” Editor's pick Video games May the choice be with you: The next great Star Wars story might be a game Acting for blockbuster video games is no longer necessarily just about providing your voice and face. In addition to sound booth work, McIntyre spent four years off-and-on recording performance capture — which minutely tracks facial as well as whole-body movements — alongside stunt people and a core group of co-stars portraying mutants Sabretooth, Mystique and Jean Grey, who he says have all become friends.



But it was performing opposite prolific video game actor Troy Baker, who McIntyre has known for a long time, that he cites as a highlight of the process. “To work with someone who is that good is such a joy. He’s so in the moment, so fresh ... You don’t get many jobs like this in a career, where you really feel like everybody’s trying to make something truly special.” Releasing on September 15, the game comes at a time when Marvel’s also beginning to pull the X-Men and mutants into its big screen efforts. A key character featured in the game was also just introduced to the Marvel Cinematic Universe in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Troy Baker’s character in the game is Nathaniel Essex, who in the comics becomes the villain Mister Sinister, who was just announced at D23 as heading to the MCU portrayed by Adam Driver. While Insomniac could not have known any of this during development, the game’s senior project director Jess Reiner-Reed said that these characters have decades of history, and that fans are happy to see multiple versions of them at once as long as the stories are compelling and ring true. “Having exposure around all these different characters only enriches the universe. We can take inspiration from the movies and TV shows, and they take some inspiration from us,” she said, referring to the well-documented impact of the Spider-Man video games on Brand New Day’s choreography and effects.



“Audiences trust the care we put into these uniquely Insomniac stories, and they can trust that we’re going to do the same thing with Wolverine.” Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

World.title: High rents a roadblock to productivity
World.content:
NationalNSWRenting Editorial High rents a roadblock to productivity The Herald's View Editorial August 23, 2026 — 6:00am

August 23, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The interests of renters are often treated as a footnote in Sydney’s never-ending conversation about property prices. But even with the recent dip in house prices, buying a property remains out of reach for many – especially buying a home that is within reasonable reach of the workplace. Rents are high in central Sydney. Dominic Lorrimer New data revealed in The Sun-Herald today shows there has been little respite from rental rises across Sydney, with the price of owning your own home keeping large numbers of people in the rental market, especially in the inner cities where they compete with international students to lease apartments. Senior economics correspondent Shane Wright reports that in some parts of the country, rents have risen by 80 per cent since the COVID-era rent freeze.



In Zetland, Chippendale and Haymarket in inner Sydney, rents have jumped by between $367 and $452 a week, Wright reports. The picture is mixed, though, with some Sydney suburbs – such as Hunters Hill, Avalon Beach and Hornsby Heights – recording rental price growth slower than the city’s 23.6 per cent inflation rate since mid-2021. The NSW South Coast has bucked the national trend, with landlords in some towns asking less on average than they were in 2021. These falls are attributed to less demand since the COVID-era surge of people seeking to leave Sydney and Canberra. Effects of the current house price slump on the rental market are unclear, but in theory the slump may enable more renters to become home owners, which in turn would ease price pressure in the broader rental market.



There are many other factors at play, though, including federal changes to negative gearing that some fear will force landlords to lift rents to compensate for their lost tax breaks. Related Article Renting Rents spike up to 80 per cent as people are pushed from homes to units The national data that Wright reports on today suggests local factors – including proximity to major employment and education zones, transport and the regional cost of living – heavily influence how much landlords can charge. The most obvious remedy is to increase housing supply in areas where people want to live. In Sydney, the Minns government has taken steps in the right direction with its overhaul of the planning system and focus on transport-oriented development.



Higher densities are a central mechanism for solving the housing crisis for renters and home owners alike. Related Article Analysis

Home loans Five charts that explain what’s really happening with housing It is true that existing high-density areas of Sydney have been home to some of the nation’s biggest rent rises since COVID. But as more high-rise development takes place in well-located areas of the city, tenants will have more options and landlords can be expected to curb rent rises to attract them. Landlords need a fair return on their investment. But affordable housing lifts overall living standards and can benefit the wider economy, as people are able to spend more of their money on things other than housing.



Young people especially can be caught in the trap of paying high rents and being unable to save a deposit to get their feet on the first rungs of the property ladder. Everyone deserves a place to call home, and the end goal for policymakers must balance the needs of investors with equitable outcomes for ordinary residents of NSW. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Heather and Hugo met at drama school 40 years ago. They haven’t stopped working together since
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is a familiarity within the Australian creative scene that gives audiences a unique kinship with the actors who appear on our screens and stages. These are the faces we have grown up with, who we have aged with, and who we innately feel like — were we to run into them at the pub — we could share a beer with. It gives our home-grown productions a warm, fuzzy feeling because, not only do we recognise familiar streets, landmarks and cafes used as filming locations, but we feel an instant intimacy when recognisable faces appear. The pride is palpable. Occasionally, a production comes along that is so successful in creating that feeling of familiarity you can’t help but smile when you watch it, even if the subject makes you cry or shift uncomfortably in your seat. And that, in a nutshell, is Dalliance. Hugo Weaving and Heather Mitchell in Dalliance. The good friends have worked together for more than 40 years. The six-episode drama series charts the fallout from one big, life-changing event and the ways it radically upends a group of 60-something friends. Exploring everything from female friendship and the path to parenthood to sex, desire and ambition, it’s the latest endeavour from John and Dan Edwards, the father-and-son production duo behind Bump and The F Ward. The series also marks a reunion for long-time friends and collaborators Heather Mitchell and Hugo Weaving, who star as would-be romantic interests, Dani and Billy. Their on-screen rapport is instant, but when you’ve shared stage and screen for over 40 years, that’s to be expected. Related Article Review What to stream this week: A juicy holiday-from-hell Brit drama, plus five more picks “I feel so blessed every time I get to work with him,” Mitchell says of her decades-long friend. “From when we first worked together … there’s always been a lot of laughter, a lot of fun and ease. It hasn’t changed, really, over the years. And that’s the thing about getting older. [With] people you’ve known for a long time, you sort of slot right back to where you were.”



The pair first met at the prestigious National Institute of Dramatic Art (NIDA) in 1979, began working together at Sydney Theatre Company in 1982, and, most recently, shared the screen in Binge’s acclaimed multi-generational drama Love Me. “I adore Heather,” says Weaving. “Working with her is being embraced. She has a capacity to care about others like no one else and I consider myself hugely lucky to get to play with her whenever we work together.” Georgie Parker as Rose, Hugo Weaving as Billy, and Heather Mitchell as Dani in Dalliance. Dalliance is a reunion for many of the cast, and remarkable in that most of them are in their 50s and 60s. Mitchell was most excited by the prospect of giving talented friends, such as Catherine McClements, an opportunity to expand their creative horizons. “I loved watching her play a character who’s sexy, funny and complex when she’s so often cast as brittle and tough.” She also knew the perfect person for the role of Rose, Billy’s wife of 40 years, pleading with Home and Away producer Julie McGauran to release Georgie Parker, who has spent 16 years working on the soap, for Dalliance. “I’ve known Georgie Parker since we were in our 20s, and I think this role shows people the depth of her talent.” Related Article Australian TV This TV legend has guided us through every decade of life. Next up? Our 60s By nature of the series’ time-jumping format, Weaving worked mostly with Mitchell and David Wenham, who plays Billy’s volatile younger brother, but relished the chance to connect with old friends. “Our read-through days were very special, all the cast together for two days. It was so lovely to catch up with everyone.” And like all great 21st-century friendships, Mitchell adds, the WhatsApp group is still going strong. “We’re constantly writing to each other on because we formed such a close relationship between all of us. It’s beautiful.”



For 68-year-old Mitchell, this was a project particularly close to her heart. Despite a career rich with experience (she won her second AACTA Award in February for The Narrow Road to the Deep North), this is her first time in the producer’s seat. She was quick to accept when John Edwards made the offer. “One of the beautiful things about being older is the challenges are less risky because you’ve got less to lose, if that makes sense.” “And I have loved it,” she adds, pointing out that her age gave her the confidence to ask questions. “I haven’t beaten myself up if I don’t know something. I just say, ‘Can you help me with this?’ I’d go to the production manager and say, ‘I have no idea what this means.’ I think as I’m getting older, I ask for help more.” Georgie Parker as Rose and David Wenham as Gary in Dalliance. Camaraderie played a pivotal role in not only the chemistry between the actors and behind the scenes – Mitchell’s husband of 34 years, Martin McGrath, is the show’s director of photography – but also in the writing room, where lived experience and a willingness to be vulnerable gave depth to each character’s journey. Related Article Opinion

Australian TV If you are still complaining about Australian TV, it’s time to shut up Louise Rugendyke National TV editor “We talked a lot about sexuality,” says Mitchell. “Passion, love, sex. People who’ve been through cancer, how medication affects your sexuality, how desire changes for each person as they get older. Some people just do not want to be touched any more. Other people long for it desperately. For me personally, I’m probably saying too much … [but] I’m more sexually satisfied in my 60s than I ever have been. And I know what I want. “We really wanted to explore both men and women and whatever gender, that there is no time limit to love and companionship and sex. And that sex is not the driving thing for everybody. That often people go online looking for very different things. And sometimes it is sex with no other attachments. And other times, someone is really looking for a true love. The past can turn up.



“So we talked at length about what is sexuality, and how is it perceived? And I would hope that for younger people, if any younger people watch this show, that they will also feel that life doesn’t stop. You don’t stop growing. You don’t stop living. You don’t stop wanting.” Mitchell and Weaving in the 1984 miniseries Bodyline. It was the first time they played partners on screen. Dalliance, and Mitchell’s own sharpened focus on life, touches on what psychologists call “socioemotional selectivity theory”. It argues that we shift our priorities and goals depending on how long we think we have left. Young people who see the future as long and open-ended prioritise knowledge and building their social network, while those further along in life, faced with their own mortality, grow more selective. They chase emotionally meaningful goals, avoid obvious risk, and prioritise close relationships over new connections. “The older you get, you’re looking closer to the idea of death. More friends die around you, more things happen which you might feel will result in an ending,” reflects Mitchell. “Certainly within this show, we want to say, no one’s ready to end anything. These characters aren’t thinking of endings, they’re thinking of beginnings, like how do I want to live the rest of my life? How do I want to be with the people I love?” Loading Endings, as it happens, are fresh in Mitchell’s mind. She recently starred in black comedy The Fox, which would become one of the late Sam Neill’s final roles (though with Neill as the voice of a magpie, they didn’t actually share the screen). “Sam was a very, very dear friend of mine,” says Mitchell, who also paid tribute to Neill at the recent Logie Awards. “I’ve spent a lot of time with him, and my husband was a close friend of Sam’s. He’s directed me, I’ve acted with him, but our main relationship is a non-professional one – I actually went out with him when I was 22 – and I still feel his presence enormously. “And there again, a man in his late 70s who was working and had jobs lined up. So much of his identity and his love was in his work, the people and the industry. I think it’s important for people to know, he was not a weakened person. He was strong right up until the end.”

World.title: It was the critics’ pick of Cannes. Now the same film has won Melbourne’s $140,000 cinema award
World.content:
CultureMoviesMIFF It was the critics’ pick of Cannes. Now the same film has won Melbourne’s $140,000 cinema award Kerrie O'Brien August 23, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What would happen when a group of teenagers collides with 2000-year-old ruins? That is the premise of La Gradiva, the French film that has won the Melbourne International Film Festival’s top gong, the Bright Horizons Award. Director Marine Atlan and her creative team win $140,000, one of the richest film prizes around the world. She also co-wrote the film, with Anne Brouillet. La Gravida, winner of the Bright Horizons Award, also won the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival’s Critics’ Week. MIFF Set mainly in Naples, La Gravida follows a group of high school students as they discover Pompeii – and themselves. “I wanted to explore what happens when you become aware that you belong to a span of time far greater than your own lifetime,” Atlan says, speaking from Paris on the eve of the announcement.



It is her first feature, as she emerges from her role as a cinematographer to take the reins. “The most difficult thing was allowing myself to occupy the position of filmmaker and to feel legitimate in doing so.” The winner was announced at Saturday night’s MIFF Awards ceremony. Short-listed for the prestigious Bright Horizons Award, from left to right, are Paloma Schneideman, Beth de Araújo, Maryam Ataei, Hossein Keshavarz, Rakan Mayasi, Abinash Bikram Shah, Alex Huston Fischer, Eleanor Wilson, and, seated in front, are Harvey Zielinski and Sophy Romvari. Also short-listed but not present are Marine Atlan and Félix de Givry. Wayne Taylor Dario Russo took out the Blackmagic Design best Australian director award for the absurdist black comedy The Fox. He pockets $50,000 in cash, plus a fully kitted URSA Cine 12K $27,500 camera. Currently in New South Wales at a writers workshop, Russo was not able to attend the ceremony. The Fox stars Jai Courtney with voiceovers by Olivia Colman and Sam Neill.



Related Article MIFF Young people are struggling like never before. These films ask why Other nominees for the directors awards were Harvey Zielinski for Sweet Milk Lake, Hyun Lee for French Girls and Maddelin McKenna for Mad Rush. Arrernte and Luritja director, writer, and producer Talia Liddle took out the Uncle Jack Charles Award, worth $20,000, for her direction of short film Protest on the Dance Floor. As the name suggests, it explores how Indigenous people in Melbourne use music – and dance floors – to create spaces of sovereignty, connection and liberation. Sad Girls, directed by Fernanda Tovar, won the MIFF Schools Youth Jury Award, worth $10,000. Special mention went to Phenomena, directed by Josef Gatti. The MIFF audience award will be announced next week, after votes have been tallied.



This year’s MIFF judges included president Sophie Hyde, along with Desiree Akhavan, Courtney Eaton, Noora Niasari, Joe Swanberg and Tan Si En. La Gradiva won the prestigious Cannes Critics’ Week Grand Prize and is also a likely contender for Best Foreign Film at the Oscars. French cinematographer turned director Marine Atlan has won the $140,000 Bright Horizons award at MIFF, one of the world’s biggest cinema prizes. Atlan says she puts a lot of herself into making films: “Trying to unfold the opacity of the world, of reality, through images and sounds remains one of the most essential experiences for me.” Her experience as a cinematographer informs how she directs. “Operating the camera and framing are important to my relationship with actors,” she says. “Sometimes being behind the camera gives me a more direct way of working with and directing them.”



Thought it’s hard to nominate just one element of filmmaking that appeals, Atlan says she loves its collective nature, “that moment when an entire crew is completely alert and focused on the same purpose for the duration of a single shot”. Related Article Cinema Total basket case: How Alexander Skarsgard became the perfect husband in Wicker Real-life and filmmaking partners Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, whose film Wicker – starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgard – opened this year’s festival, were also shortlisted for the Bright Horizons Award. Speaking on Friday, they said they didn’t expect quite this explosion of interest. “We knew that he was a beautiful creation and we were excited to share him but it has definitely taken on a life of its own now,” Wilson says with a laugh when asked about the proliferation of memes posted to social media about the Skarsgard’s wickerman. Remarkably, all of her short films were rejected by MIFF, so she’s thrilled to be here and to be nominated.



“When we were writing it, we were thinking about specific characters and their very specific journeys,” says Wilson. “But if you step back and look at it the context of the state of dating now, it does feel strangely prescient.” Related Article Cinema This scientist quit her job in animal testing to fight for monkeys caged in the labs BRIGHT HORIZONS AWARD 2026 SHORTLIST Big Girls Don’t Cry – Paloma Schneideman

Blue Heron – Sophy Romvari

Elephants in the Fog – Abinash Bikram Shah

Goodbye, Cruel World –Félix de Givry

Josephine – Beth de Araújo

La Gradiva – Marine Atlan

Sweet Milk Lake – Harvey Zielinski

The Friend’s House Is Here – Hossein Keshavarz and Maryam Ataei

Wicker – Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer

World.title: Too pretty to be funny? Why Brooke Shields is still fighting to be taken at more than face value
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brooke Shields can’t play funny because she is too pretty. So say some male network executives with whom she locked horns over her new murder-mystery, You’re Killing Me. In the series, by Mother of the Bride writer Robin Bernheim, Shields plays crime-romance novelist Allison Chandler, the bane of the local detective (Tom Cavanagh) in a cosy fishing village in Maine, the kind where nothing much happens – except a worrying number of homicides. Allison is funny, clumsy, sensitive and smart. But, according to the network higher-ups – despite Suddenly Susan, Lipstick Jungle and a legendary guest spot on Friends – Brooke Shields couldn’t be all those things at once. Brooke Shields plays a romance novelist-turned-sleuth in You’re Killing Me. “As an executive producer I’m privy to the comments from our bosses,” she says on a Zoom call from her home, an hour outside of New York City. Her expressive hands embellishing her words, Shields radiates warmth and passion. “A lot of it is still stuck in the old times. It’s like, ‘oh, no, she can’t be clumsy because she’s pretty’. And the more modern way of looking at this is: she’s all of that. She can be sexy and she can be faulted and that’s fine because she’s earned it. At 61 you earn all of your flaws and your experience. And it makes you so much more interesting. It was important for me to play a character like that to show the multifaceted nature of women.” Strong, complex female leads are as old as storytelling itself, she says. Just look at Homer’s Odyssey, now a box-office hit. Editor's pick Streaming Heather and Hugo met at drama school 40 years ago. They haven’t stopped working together since “Anne Hathaway’s character [Penelope] and Calypso [Charlize Theron] – these are unbelievably strong women,” says Shields. “This is since the dawn of time … Women have been the forebears of strength before we even know. It’s why we have the children. I think that’s starting to become more part of the zeitgeist and not as threatening.” The disconnect between Hollywood’s feminine ideal and the female experience is a topic she explored in her memoir Brooke Shields Is Not Allowed to Get Old: Thoughts on Ageing as a Woman.



“You look at Irene Dunne movies and Lucille Ball, who was a beauty queen,” says Shields. “You look at true female comedy back in that day. Even the Marilyn Monroes. They were brilliantly funny and used their looks as a vehicle. So that by the time they had more dramatic moments, your heart was breaking, because they threw you off balance.” Brooke Shields with Andrea Walker, who plays a cocky true-crime podcaster in You’re Killing Me. Much of the comedy in You’re Killing Me stems from the generation gap between Shields’ character and cocky true-crime podcaster Andrea Walker (Amalia Williamson from Canadian romance drama Sullivan’s Crossing), with whom Allison is forced to collaborate to solve the murder of a fellow writer. The Gen X-Gen Z misfires yield hilariously awkward verbal slapstick to match the physical theatre. “A woman of this age needs this young person in her life,” says Shields. “She can teach this young person and she can learn from her, too. And together, they’re stronger.” Related Article Streaming He’s TV Mr Nice Guy, but Nathan Fillion’s ‘unlikeable’ superhero could be his greatest hit She needed look no further for dramatic motivation than her relationships with her daughters, Rowan and Grier, with her filmmaker husband, Chris Henchy. “A lot of [inspiration] came from my trying to set up my phone with Apple Pay, and my daughters being like, ‘Oh my god, Mum! Here!’ Or I’ll be saying to them, ‘Are you on the polly?’ And they’re like, ‘It’s not polly, it’s molly [the street name for party drug MDMA], and no!’ They make fun of me all the time. And so I went to Robin [Bernheim] and said, ‘We’ve got to put this stuff in there’.”



Retaining the dignity of the characters amid the rivalry was “a fine line”. “If you’re the one being made fun of, you get more leeway. And it’s never mean. My older daughter [Rowan] has all this TikTok stuff that she does, and most of it is her making fun of me. I’ll learn the dance or whatever it is. I don’t understand what they’re saying. But it’s funny and I don’t take offence.” Loading After Rowan was born in 2003, Shields suffered postpartum depression, the subject of her memoir Down Came the Rain, and an infamous clash with Scientologist Tom Cruise, who criticised her use of antidepressants. In June this year, Rowan made her reality-television debut, joining the cast of Bravo network’s Next Gen NYC, which follows young professionals making their way in the Big Apple. Her mother wasn’t happy. Related Article Review What to stream this week: A juicy holiday-from-hell Brit drama, plus five more picks “I was horrified. But she held her own,” says Shields. “I got a message from [the show’s host] Andy Cohen that said she maintained her integrity and she is the grounding force. I said to her, ‘Don’t be the one throwing up. Hold the hair back of the person throwing up. Do not succumb to being mean. That’s not going to get ratings. I don’t want to hear that from you because that’s not who you are.’ So she stayed pretty steady.” Shields barely recognises the industry in which she got her break in 1978 in the film Pretty Baby, and then shot to stardom in 1980 with The Blue Lagoon, before becoming a Calvin Klein model and Time Magazine’s Face of the ’80s.



“I’ve had to hire people to help me with social media. I hate it,” she says. “I’m not good at it. My younger daughter was modelling for a while, and she had a contract, and she had to do all of her own photography. I was like, ‘You’re working for Tommy Hilfiger. How are you doing your own photography?’ She’s like, ‘That’s the way it is, Mum’. And I mean, the word ‘influencer’ – what does it mean? And [fame] is so short-lived but that’s where the money is going. Someone has this many followers or this many TikToks and they pay them numbers that they would never get paid for a hard job. How do you battle that?” Brooke Shields with her daughter Rowan. Their relationship inspired some of the plots in You’re Killing Me. Getty Images As president since 2024 of the Actors’ Equity Association, Shields is lobbying the US government for better wages and working conditions for performers, particularly those employed by Disney’s theme parks and the Trey Parker/Matt Stone-owned restaurant Casa Bonita. “The battles we’re fighting right now are heartbreaking,” she says. “You’re watching people work so hard and they’re not compensated. They’re not protected. They weren’t part of the union prior and they want to organise now. We’re going up against this massive industry and this conglomeration that doesn’t care about the people that are busting their asses for them. Related Article ★★★★

Review Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more “At Casa Bonita you’ve got cliff divers and there’s no safety. The idea that ‘the show must go on’ is not fair. I’ve had so many injuries myself from being on Broadway – taping up my knees and continuing to go on. Actors are considered disposable, and the amount they work, and the money they generate, it’s amazing. And that’s male and female.” In Washington, DC, where “everyone wants a selfie”, she has heard shockingly dismissive statements about her craft.



“If you’re a plumber, you don’t have to pay taxes on your plunger, right? Well, under [former US president] Reagan, if actors had to pay for anything to do with their field – tap shoes, headshots, singing lessons – they didn’t have to pay taxes on them,” she says. “And then, in 2017, that miraculously just went away. We obviously know why, and so that’s another thing that I’m fighting for. I’ve had people in DC say, ‘Oh, wait, so you want funding so someone can follow a hobby?’” Brooke Shields and Christopher Atkins in The Blue Lagoon, which launched her career. Her experience at the age of 18, appearing in Bob Hope’s variety show for US troops in Beirut, was an early lesson in the value of entertainment. “Those 20 minutes of gags, monologues and songs for all these fresh-faced young people who were staying on the USS Guam – that was all we could give them. And it meant the world to them. We’re talking about entertainment as a form of escape and medicine, in a way. I’m not overstating it.” Her new show, she says, “is a little escape … It’s just entertainment. It’s not too heavy.” But she hopes You’re Killing Me plays a part in challenging those pervading perceptions about women that she has faced throughout her lifelong career. “Attractive females can also be smart and not afraid to be flawed. I’m OK with not being pristine and perfect.” You’re Killing Me is now streaming on Stan (which is owned by Nine, the publisher of this masthead).

World.title: Rents spike up to 80 per cent as people are pushed from homes to units
World.content:
PoliticsFederalRenting Rents spike up to 80 per cent as people are pushed from homes to units Shane Wright August 23, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rents in parts of the nation’s capital cities have soared by 80 per cent since the end of the COVID-era freeze on rents, but there are pockets of the country where landlords are getting less from their tenants than they did five years ago. Houses have become so unaffordable for many that people are turning their attention increasingly towards either buying or renting inner city units where they also face competition from international students, figures compiled by property data company Cotality show. Rents have climbed by up to 80 per cent in some parts of the country since the end of the Covid-era rental freeze. Louise Kennerley The property market, including the drop in values in Sydney and Melbourne plus record-high rents, has become a political lightning rod since the May budget when Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealed changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. It has sparked accusations from the Coalition that Labor is destroying the economy and the wealth of people invested in the property market, with the government arguing it is giving first home buyers and future generations a chance to own a home.



The pace of growth in rents has slowed this year after they took off in the period after the end of a COVID-era freeze on rents. That freeze ended in early 2021. Since then, the biggest increase recorded by Cotality has been in the working-class Perth suburb of Balga where they have jumped by 80 per cent or more than $320 a week over the past five years. Perth’s overall inflation rate over the same period was a nation-leading 25.8 per cent. International student-loaded areas in Sydney and Melbourne have experienced rent increases almost as large. In Zetland, Chippendale and Haymarket in inner Sydney, rents have jumped by between $367 and $452 a week. Central Melbourne rents have lifted by 72.6 per cent with similarly large increases in Southbank (69.6 per cent) and Docklands (64.2 per cent) while in Carlton, home of Melbourne University, rents have jumped by 58.5 per cent.



All inner city areas of capital cities have seen huge increases except Canberra where a long-run building boom has added to its supply of apartments. Canberra’s largest rent increase, of 22 per cent, was recorded in its southernmost suburb of Banks. Related Article Renting Tenants caught in crosshairs of angry rent-hike debate Cotality’s head of research, Gerard Burg, said the strong growth in rents in capital city centres and nearby suburbs suggested the impact of the return of international students. He said another factor had been the low affordability of homes. Prices exploded during the pandemic, climbing by more than 30 per cent in some markets while the international border was closed. Burg said as standalone homes had become more expensive, potential buyers had moved either into the apartment market or been forced to continue renting.



“You get these spillover effects. We had that big increase in house prices during Covid while rents didn’t move much at all,” he said. “But [we’re] getting to the point that houses aren’t affordable, so we’re seeing the market for units hold up better than houses. And we’re seeing rents for units higher.” Rents have fallen in a handful of places across the country over the past five years, almost all on the south coast of NSW. In the holiday centre of Manyana, rents have dropped by 30.2 per cent since mid-2021 or by $237.50 a week. In the nearby town of Sussex Inlet, rents have tumbled by more than 17 per cent. Parts of the south coast such as Mollymook (minus 7 per cent) and Ulladulla (minus 0.3 per cent), areas that became huge attractions during the pandemic for people seeking to escape Sydney and Canberra, have experienced a fall in absolute rents.



Substantial falls in asking rents over half a decade, even in deeply depressed property markets, are unusual. But there are many more urban and regional centres where rents have fallen by less than inflation, which itself is being pushed up by rent increases. Across Melbourne’s growing western fringe, rental growth has fallen short of inflation in places such as Diggers Rest (15.8 per cent), Eynesbury (16.5 per cent) and Bonnie Brook (16.9 per cent). In Sydney, rents in Hunters Hill (17.8 per cent), Avalon Beach (20.9 per cent) and Hornsby Heights (21.8 per cent) have also grown slower than the city’s 23.6 per cent inflation rate since mid-2021.



There have been some relatively modest rent increases in Brisbane’s south-west, such as Pullenvale (13 per cent), Fig Tree Pocket (15.6 per cent) and Silverbark Ridge (20.8 per cent). But in the hottest rental market in the country, Perth, tenants have been unable to find any respite. The smallest increase since mid-2021 has been in Brigadoon, about 40 kilometres from the Perth CBD, with rents up by 27.2 per cent. Cottesloe is one of the more expensive property markets in the country. Rents there have grown by 35.8 per cent over the past five years, pushing the median weekly impost to almost $1042. Canberra is again the outlier. The smallest increases in the country have been recorded in the nation’s capital, including in well-heeled and central suburbs such as Forrest (3.5 per cent), Ainslie (5.2 per cent) and Reid (8.7 per cent).
